## 1. Regulatory information and recommendations on the procedure

## 1.1. Scientific advice

The applicant did not seek Scientific advice from the CHMP.

## 1.2. Eligibility to the centralised procedure

The applicant Zambon S.p.A. submitted on 31 May 2025 an application for marketing authorisation (MA) to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for Hopledo (levodopa/carbidopa), through the centralised procedure under Article 3(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 726/2004. The eligibility to the centralised procedure was agreed upon by the EMA/CHMP on 25 April 2025.

The eligibility to the centralised procedure under Article 3(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 was based on demonstration of interest of patients at Community level.

The applicant applied for the following indication:

- Treatment of adult patients with Parkinson's disease and moderate to severe motor fluctuations who cannot be stabilised on levodopa/dopa decarboxylase (DDC) inhibitor treatment and/or other available Parkinson oral medicinal products.

## 1.3. Legal basis and dossier content

## The legal basis for this application refers to:

Article 8.3 of Directive 2001/83/EC - complete and independent application.

The application submitted is:

- Composed of administrative information, complete quality data, non-clinical and clinical data based on applicants' own tests and studies and bibliographic literature substituting/supporting certain test(s) or study(ies);
- A fixed-dose combination medicinal product.

## 1.4. Information on paediatrics

Pursuant to Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006, the application included an EMA Decision (EMA/PE/0000258095) on the granting of a product-specific waiver on the grounds set out in Article 11(1)(c) of said Regulation for the above-mentioned medicinal product. The waiver applies to all subsets of the paediatric population from birth to less than 18 years of age.

## 1.5. Information on orphan market exclusivity

Not applicable.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 1.5.1. Similarity with authorised orphan medicinal products

Pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 141/2000 and Article 3 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 847/2000, the applicant did not submit a critical report addressing the possible similarity with authorised orphan medicinal products from the start of the because there is no authorised orphan medicinal product for a condition related to the proposed indication.

## 1.7.3. CHMP Opinion

Based on the CHMP review of data on quality, safety and efficacy, the CHMP considers by consensus that the benefit-risk balance of Hopledo is favourable in the following indication(s):

- Treatment of adult patients with Parkinson's disease and moderate to severe motor fluctuations who have not been sufficiently stabilised with oral levodopa/dopa decarboxylase (DDC) inhibitorbased treatment regimens.

## 2. Introduction

## 2.1. Therapeutic context

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by the loss of dopaminergic neurons. According to the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study, the global prevalence of PD was estimated at 138.6/100,000 people and caused 388000 deaths in the world population. By 2035, age-standardised rates of incidence and prevalence will increase from

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

14.62/100,000 and 139.79/100,000 in 2021 to 20.20/100,000 and 165.05/100,000, respectively (Luo et al 2025). In Europe, in a projection between 2021 and 2050, the all-age prevalence of PD was estimated between 152/100,000 and 267/ 100,000, respectively (Su et al 2025).

Sinemet®, an immediate release (IR) formulation, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1975 as a fixed dose combination of levodopa and carbidopa (LD-CD). In Europe, Sinemet® and Madopar® (containing the fixed dose combination of levodopa and benserazide - LD-BZ), were also approved at the same time. The IR LD-CD formulation offers rapid absorption but is quickly degraded in the periphery. The elimination half-life of LD following Sinemet IR administration was approximately 1.5 hours. Controlled-Release (CR) Sinemet (Sinemet CR 2023), the first CR-LD formulation, was approved in the European Union (EU) in 1990 and in the United States (US) in 1991. CR LD-CD is a polymeric-based drug delivery that slowly erodes and releases LD-CD. Nowadays it is usually administered only for the night-time symptoms of PD to supplement IR LD-CD. After a single dose in healthy young and elderly adult subjects, the mean time to maximum LD concentration (Tmax) was 1.8 to 2.1 hours for the CR LD-CD versus 0.5 to 0.8 hours for the IR LD-CD, with a maximum observed plasma concentration (Cmax) approximately one-third of that noted following IR LD-CD (Yeh et al 1989). In clinical trials of Sinemet CR, patients with moderate to severe motor fluctuations did not experience significant reductions in 'Off' time versus Sinemet IR (Sinemet CR 2023). CR LD-CD has less predictable symptom relief than IR LD-CD (LeWitt et al 2023; Sinemet CR 2023).

Levodopa, in combination with carbidopa, is considered an efficacious treatment for the motor symptoms of PD, and nearly all PD patients require LD treatment as the disease progresses (Jankovic and Poewe 2012). Despite the available treatment options, including adjunctive therapies and rescue medications, disease progression and LD exposure are the major factors in the development of motor complications, and most patients with PD experience motor complications, including wearing-off and peak-dose dyskinesias after several years of LD treatment (Fabbri et al 2023).

As PD progresses, the response to IR LD-CD and CR LD-CD becomes less reliable. To maintain symptom control, it is often necessary to increase the daily dose of levodopa, divide the LD-CD intake into smaller, more frequent doses, and use adjunctive therapies. As dopaminergic medications become less effective, many PD patients experience motor fluctuations, which they report as the most challenging aspect of the disease. These fluctuations typically emerge after several years of levodopa therapy and tend to increase in severity as the disease progresses, though the pattern can vary between patients.

In the 1990's, two catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors, entacapone (Comtan®) and tolcapone (Tasmar®) were approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) as adjunct medications to be combined with LD in patients with motor fluctuations (Comtan SPC 2024, Tasmar SPC 2022). In 2016, the COMT inhibitor opicapone (Ongentys®) was approved by the EMA.

As PD further progresses, motor fluctuations tend to intensify and lose predictability, resulting in a broader range of possible presentations:

- On-off phenomenon may arise: rapid switches between the 'On' and 'Off' states may appear along with sudden 'Off', seemingly without obvious relationship to levodopa dosing;
- Patients can notice an increased latency after LD intake for the beginning of the clinical benefit (delayed 'On'), even after the first-day dose (''prolonged morning akinesia'');
- A complete failure to respond to a levodopa dose (No 'On') can happen (Fabbri et al 2023);

Moreover, motor fluctuations tend to worsen over time, even with optimised oral or transdermal therapies, eventually leading to a point where adequate symptom control can no longer be achieved with these treatment options. At this stage, patients usually become eligible for a device-aided therapy

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

(DAT) (Deuschl et al . 2022). DATs are invasive treatments that require permanent access to the patient's body via a catheter or stimulator and necessitate careful monitoring to ensure tolerability. DATs can be used when motor fluctuations cannot be adequately controlled with an oral medication. They aim to reduce dopaminergic sensitivity by delivering continuous (instead of a pulsatile) stimulation of the dopaminergic terminals. The ideal candidate for DAT should generally have shown good response to previous LD treatment, absence of cognitive impairment and an age threshold of 70 years (75 years old for deep brain stimulation).

The following DATs are available in EU:

- Duodopa® (approved in the EU in 2005) is a gel formulation of LD and CD for continuous intestinal administration for PD patients with severe motor fluctuations and hyperkinesia or dyskinesia. In 2022 the subcutaneous (SC) formulation of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa, was also approved in the EU as Produodopa® for the same indication as Duodopa®.
- APO-go® (SC apomorphine, a short-acting dopamine agonist) has been approved since 2014 for the treatment of motor-fluctuations in PD patients who are not sufficiently controlled by oral antiPD medication.
- Onerji, approved in 2026, is a formulation of LD and CD administered as a continuous solution for SC infusion using a specialised portable delivery pump system (Yurway Delivery System or Crono Twin ND pump). It is indicated for the treatment of motor fluctuations in patients with advanced PD not sufficiently controlled by oral anti-Parkinson medicinal products. Onerji is administered with a levodopa oral morning dose. Additional oral LD can be prescribed as needed. If required, other classes of medicinal products for PD can be taken concomitantly with Onerji and adjusted as needed.
- Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) (approved in the EU in 1998, Gardner, 2013) is based on the finding that high-frequency (100-200 Hz) electrical stimulation of specific brain targets can mimic the effect of a lesion without the need to destroy brain tissue. It requires the implantation of an electrode into the brain tissue.

Electrodes for DBS are implanted in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and in the globus pallidus interna (GPI). Deep Brain Stimulation of the STN has demonstrated significant antiparkinsonian efficacy and is now an established, evidence-based treatment for managing motor fluctuations and dyskinesia in patients with advanced PD (Poewe 2017). Deep Brain Stimulation enables a continuous stimulation, where three main parameters can be adjusted to obtain the maximal benefit with least adverse events (AEs). Despite their efficacy, the effect of DBS remains symptomatic, and no disease-modifying effect has been proved. At the same time, not all patients with advanced PD will be willing to implement DBS and some of them will have a contraindication (e.g., older age, cognitive impairment). Once implanted, patients with deep brain stimulators should not undergo full-body magnetic resonance imaging scans (MRIs), transcranial magnetic stimulation, or diathermy (Pycroft et al . 2018).

- Kynmobi®, a sublingual apomorphine strip, was approved by the FDA in 2020 (and discontinued by the MAH for commercial reasons in 2023), by Health Canada (and in the EU via a decentralised procedure - DCP) in 2023 to treat 'Off' episodes.
- Inbrija®, an inhaled LD, was approved by the EMA in 2019 for the treatment of individual 'Off' episodes.

Currently, there is no curative or disease-modifying treatment available for PD. Fluctuating response to medication was identified as the top concern among patients with PD.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

No long-acting preparation of LD is available in the EU that would combine the advantages of IR and ER components in a modified-release (MR) LD-CD oral combination. In 2015 Numient, the 1 st generation MR oral formulation was registered through a centralised procedure in the EU and withdrawn in 2019 without being commercialised.

## 2.2. Aspects of development

IPX203 was developed by a company subsidiary of Amneal Pharmaceuticals LLC (with which Zambon has an agreement in place for Europe).

IPX203 is a second-generation MR LD-CD formulation proposed for the treatment of adult patients with PD and moderate to severe motor fluctuations who cannot be stabilised on levodopa/dopa decarboxylase (DDC) inhibitor treatment and/or other available PD oral medicinal products.

The IPX203 program has been conducted in line with the principles of the relevant guidelines for drug development and with the 'Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in the treatment of Parkinson's disease' (EMA/CHMP/330418/2012, 2012 rev. 2). All biopharmaceutics and clinical pharmacology studies were conducted according to relevant regulatory guidelines. All safety and efficacy clinical studies were also conducted in accordance with applicable regulatory guidance, ensuring compliance with the current Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki.

No scientific advice has been requested to the CHMP for IPX203. Previous interactions between the applicant and the EMA/CHMP regarding IPX203 included written pre-submission interactions, in January 2025 and a (Co)-Rapporteurs' meeting held on 18 March 2025, upon EMA product team recommendation, as detailed in the pre-submission interactions response dated 31 January 2025. At the meeting, the legal basis initially proposed by Zambon [Article 10(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC], with a proposed Reference Medicinal Product (RMP), was challenged, because the PK/PD clinical study selected to be pivotal for bridging the RMP data was conducted using batches of a corresponding levodopa/carbidopa prolonged-release product authorised outside the EU instead of batches of a product authorised in the EU. In line with these recommendations, Zambon submitted a full mixed application in accordance with Article 8(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC (known Active substances).

The proposed indication for IPX203 is the treatment of adult patients with PD and moderate to severe motor fluctuations who cannot be stabilised on DDC inhibitor treatment and/or other available PD oral medicinal products. The IPX203 clinical development program includes:

- Three Phase 1 PK studies in healthy volunteers (Study IPX203 B16 04 , Study IPX203 B16 05 , and Study IPX203-B16-06 );
- Two Phase 2 studies, a single-dose PK, pharmacodynamics/efficacy, and safety study in advanced PD patients (Study IPX203-B14-02 ), where both Rytary/Numient (MR LD-CD) and Sinemet (IR LD-CD) were used as references, and a single and multiple-dose PK, pharmacodynamics, efficacy, and safety study in advanced PD patients (Study IPX203 B16 01 ).
- Two Phase 3 studies, a randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallelgroup, prospective study in PD patients with motor fluctuations (Study IPX203-B16-02 ), and an open-label 9-month extension study in PD patients with motor fluctuations (Study IPX203 B16 03 ).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 2.3. Description of the product

Hopledo ( IPX203) is a novel oral modified release (MR) LD-CD multi-particulate capsule formulation, with a proprietary innovative release system which allows a better targeting of the active ingredient and a more efficient therapeutic action. Hopledo has two components: an immediate-release (IR) component I in granules, and an extended-release (ER) component II, as coated beads. There are functional excipients designed / intended to:

- prevent pellets disintegration in the stomach;
- prolong residence within the gastrointestinal tract and support extended drug adsorption. The exact site and duration of absorption are unknown;
- provide sustained drug release.

The formulation was developed and designed to combine dual-release mechanism and thereby provide fast attainment of therapeutic LD plasma concentrations to ensure early onset of effect, and to maintain the desired concentrations for a longer duration with minimal peak-to trough-fluctuations than provided by the authorised oral administered LD-CD products. When administering IPX203, LD from IR granules produces an initial boost of LD exposure, with a rapid onset of effect followed by a continuous LD supply from the ER beads. With prolonged duration of stable therapeutic concentrations after each dose, IPX203 is designed to provide better control of PD symptoms, fewer motor fluctuations or unfavourable side effects such as dyskinesia, less frequent dosing, enhanced patient compliance, and possibly improved quality of life in PD patients. Additionally, IPX203 design would allow for dosing intervals of approximately 6-8 hours (3 times/day, range: 2 to 4 times/day) in patients with PD with motor fluctuations.

This product formulation was designed to avoid the limitation of slow initial release and the consequent latency to improvement of motor symptoms seen with CR formulations.

This product was authorised in the US on 7 August 2024, under the brand name Crexont TM  and is marketed by Amneal. Subsequently, Zambon signed an agreement with Amneal to apply for IPX203 MA in the EU. The proposed legal basis for the IPX203 marketing authorization in EU is a full-mixed application under Article 8(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC.

## 2.4. Inspection issues

## 2.4.1. Good manufacturing practice (GMP) inspection(s)

The CHMP agreed that no inspection was required.

## 2.4.2. Good laboratory practice (GLP) inspection(s)

Some nonclinical studies were conducted and published before 1980 due to the research timeline in this field. These studies were not conducted in accordance with Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) conditions. However, the review of these pre-GLP published studies outlined consistency in the reported findings in comparison to those studies performed post-GLP. Furthermore, the quality of these investigations corresponds to that of most studies conducted for other medicinal products during the same period of time. The CHMP agreed that, overall, these studies provided a clear overview of the properties of LD and CD, and additional studies adhering to the current GLP requirements did not reveal new information.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In summary, the CHMP agreed that no GLP inspection was required

No ethical or clinical issues have been suspected from the assessment of the clinical trials presented in this initial MAA submission.

Therefore, the CHMP agreed that no inspection was required.

## 3.1. Introduction

The finished product is presented as modified-release hard capsules containing 140 mg, 210 mg, 280 mg and 350 mg of levodopa and carbidopa monohydrate equivalent to 35 mg, 52.5 mg, 70 mg and 87.5 mg carbidopa as active substances.

Other ingredients are:

Capsule contents: microcrystalline cellulose, mannitol, sodium lauryl sulfate, povidone, cellulose acetate, copovidone, basic butylated methacrylate copolymer, talc (E553b), triethyl citrate (E1505), croscarmellose sodium, magnesium stearate, methacrylic acid and methyl methacrylate copolymer (1:1)

Capsule shell: gelatine, titanium dioxide (E171), iron oxide red (E172), iron oxide yellow (E172), quinoline yellow (E104), brilliant blue FCF (E133), and erythrosine (E127)

Printing ink: shellac glaze 45% (E904), ferrosoferric oxide/iron oxide black (E172), propylene glycol (E1520), ammonium hydroxide 28% (E525), shellac NF (E904), sodium hydroxide (E524), povidone, and titanium dioxide (E171).

The product is available in opaque, white, high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottle with a white polypropylene (PP) child resistant screw closure fitted with an induction inner-seal. Desiccant, silica gel in high-density polyethylene fibre packs, is included in the bottle as described in section 6.5 of the SmPC.

## 3.2.1. General information

The chemical name of carbidopa is (2S)-3-(3, 4-dihydroxyphenyl)-2-hydrazino-2-methyl propanoic acid corresponding to the molecular formula C10H14N2O4.H2O. It has a relative molecular weight of 244.24 and the following structure:

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Figure 1: Carbidopa structure

<!-- image -->

Characterisation of the active substance is covered by the Certificate of Suitability, and the control of potential mutagenic impurities is considered adequately addressed.

Carbidopa is a slightly hygroscopic white or yellowish white powder slightly soluble in water, practically insoluble in methylene chloride, soluble in dilute solution of mineral acids.

Carbidopa exhibits stereoisomerism due to the presence of one chiral centre. The 2S laevorotatory form is used as therapeutic agent. Enantiomeric purity is controlled routinely.

Polymorphism has not been observed for carbidopa.

## 3.4. Finished medicinal product

## 3.4.1. Description of the product and pharmaceutical development

## Description of the product

The finished product is presented as follows:

140 mg levodopa and 35 mg carbidopa: hard capsules with white opaque body and yellow opaque cap. Body imprinted with '140' in black ink and cap imprinted with 'IPX203' in white ink. Filled capsules are 18 mm x 6 mm in size and contain white to off-white granules and beads.

210 mg levodopa and 52.5 mg carbidopa: hard capsules with white opaque body and green opaque cap. Body imprinted with '210' in black ink and cap imprinted with 'IPX203' in white ink. Filled capsules are 20 mm x 7 mm in size and contain white to off-white granules and beads.

280 mg levodopa and 70 mg carbidopa: hard capsules with white opaque body and purple opaque cap. Body imprinted with '280' in black ink and cap imprinted with 'IPX203' in white ink. Filled capsules are 23 mm x 8 mm in size and contain white to off-white granules and beads.

350 mg levodopa and 87.5 mg carbidopa: hard capsules with white opaque body and medium orange opaque cap. Body imprinted with '350' in black ink and cap imprinted with 'IPX203' in white ink. Filled capsules are 23 mm x 9 mm in size and contain white to off-white granules and beads.

## Pharmaceutical development

The goal of the finished product development was to develop a modified-release levodopa (LD) and carbidopa (CD) formulation which attains therapeutic LD plasma concentrations rapidly and maintains a therapeutic concentration profile for the duration longer than the currently approved products.

The capsules contain two components: component I contains immediate release (IR) granules and component II contains extended release (ER)-coated beads.

The formulation development focused on the design of a multiparticulate modified-release dosage form combining immediate-release and prolonged-release characteristics. The selected formulation was developed to support rapid onset of action while maintaining levodopa plasma concentrations over an extended period, thereby achieving the intended therapeutic profile.

The different product strengths are proportional and are distinguishable by colour, imprinting and size of the capsules.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

All excipients are well known pharmaceutical ingredients, and their quality is compliant with Ph. Eur. standards. There are no novel excipients used in the finished product formulation. The list of excipients is included in section 6.1 of the SmPC.

The formulation development started with the quality target product profile (QTPP) which defined the critical quality attributes (CQAs). A comprehensive finished product Quality Target Product Profile (QTPP) was established which enabled the appropriate identification of the finished product critical quality attributes (CQAs)

Pharmaceutical development activities included formulation optimisation, development of an appropriate dissolution methodology and confirmation of in vivo product performance. The overall development programme supported the selection of the final formulation, establishment of a suitable control strategy and demonstration of comparable performance of products manufactured at the relevant manufacturing sites.

## Manufacturing process development

The selected manufacturing process of each component of the finished product was based on the manufacturer's prior experience with a similar finished products consisting of the same combination of active substances. The manufacturing process was developed to produce immediate-release and modified-release components that together provide the intended release characteristics and therapeutic performance of the finished product. The final dosage form consists of hard capsules containing both formulation components The manufacturing process for each component was characterised in order to identify which parameters were important to process predictability and to identify process parameters which may impact the component's CQAs. Characterisation studies were conducted during manufacturing process development and the scale-up from pilot batch to registration batch for each component of the finished product. Parameters which were found to influence the component or product CQAs based on the risk assessment activity were identified as impacting process parameters.

## 3.4.2. Manufacture of the product and process controls

The finished product is manufactured in a dedicated manufacturing site

Satisfactory evidence of GMP compliance has been provided for all sites involved in the manufacturing, testing and batch release of the finished product.

- The manufacturing process consists of three main stages. Component I, a granule formulation manufactured by a wet granulation process, followed by drying, milling, and blending.
- Component II, a multi-particulate bead formulation manufactured by wet granulation, extrusion, spherization, drying, and screening process, followed by Wurster coating, drying and screening.
- Encapsulation, filling of Components I and II into hard gelatine capsule shells

The process is considered to be a nonstandard manufacturing process.

The description of the manufacturing process has been presented with all necessary relevant details, including equipment and normal operating ranges (NORs) for process parameters.

The IPCs are defined and specifications and analytical procedures are described.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Satisfactory process validation protocols and reports are presented for three batches manufactured at commercial manufacturing scale. The results support the consistency of the manufacturing process in meeting the IPCs and finished product specifications. The product processing times and hold times were qualified for the maximum allowable times during manufacturing. The IPCs are adequate for this type of manufacturing process and contribute to the ensuring consistent product quality. The consistency of the manufacturing process and the quality of the finished product were demonstrated based on extensive IPC, release and stability results obtained from the process validation batches.

Major steps of the manufacturing process have been validated by a number of studies on three fullscale batches per strength. It has been demonstrated that the manufacturing process is capable of producing the finished product of intended quality in a reproducible manner. All the results generated during the process validation met the acceptance criteria and it can be concluded that the manufacturing process of the finished product is fully validated for all product strengths. The inprocess controls are adequate for this type of manufacturing process.

## 3.4.3. Control of Finished Product

## Specifications

The finished product release and shelf-life specifications include appropriate tests for this kind of dosage form: appearance (visual), identification (HPLC, HPLC/UV), loss on drying (Ph. Eur.), uniformity of dosage units (Ph. Eur.), dissolution carbidopa (HPLC), dissolution levodopa (HPLC), related substances (HPLC), assay carbidopa (HPLC), assay levodopa (HPLC), hydrazine (LC/MS), residual solvents (GC), and microbial limits (Ph. Eur.).

During evaluation, two Major Objections (MO) were raised on the control of the product for purity profile. Following submission of additional justification and supporting evidence by the applicant for both clinical and commercial batches of the finished product, the CHMP considered the objections satisfactorily addressed and the Major Objections were resolved.

The potential presence of elemental impurities in the finished product has been assessed following a risk-based approach in line with the ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities. The risk assessment of elemental impurities in the finished product evaluated the different potential sources of elemental impurities, including, active substances, excipients, manufacturing, equipment, container closure systems and water. The results showed that the elemental impurities in the finished product of all the batches met the requirements and are below the established control limit of 30% PDE. Based on the assessment, risk of presence of elemental impurities in the finished product is low and no control has to be included in the finished product specification.

## Analytical procedures and reference standards

The analytical methods used have been adequately described and appropriately validated in accordance with the ICH guidelines. Satisfactory information regarding the reference standards used for testing has been presented.

## Batch analysis

Batch analysis results are provided for three commercial scale batches per strength confirming the consistency of the manufacturing process and its ability to manufacture to the intended product specification.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Container Closure system

The container closure system is opaque, white, high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottle with a white polypropylene (PP) child resistant screw closure fitted with an induction inner. The material complies with Ph. Eur. and EC requirements. The choice of the container closure system has been validated by stability data and is adequate for the intended use of the product.

## 3.4.4. Stability of the product

The shelf life of of 3 years and store in the original package due to sensitivity to moisture in the proposed container, as stated in the SmPC, is justified by the available stability data. Use 100 days after first opening of the bottle.

Real time stability data from 3 commercial scale batches per strength of finished product stored under long term conditions (25ºC / 60% RH) and for up to 6 months under accelerated conditions (40ºC / 75% RH) according to the ICH guidelines were provided. The batches of medicinal product are representative to those proposed for marketing and were packed in the primary packaging proposed for marketing.

Samples were tested for appearance, appearance of container, loss of drying, dissolution, related substances, assay levodopa, assay carbidopa, hydrazine, and microbial limits. The analytical procedures used are stability indicating.

Stability studies were designed in accordance with applicable regulatory guidance, also based on ICH Q1D Bracketing and Matrixing Designs for Stability Testing of New Drug Substance and Product and included representative container closure systems and commercial presentations. The data generated were considered supportive of the proposed shelf life and storage conditions for the marketed product; the batches used in stability studies are representative to those proposed for marketing.

All results were within the specifications with no significant changes in the tested attributes under long term and accelerated conditions.

Appropriate photostability and in-use stability studies were conducted in accordance with relevant regulatory requirements. No significant changes affecting product quality were observed, and the data supported the proposed product presentation, storage conditions and in-use use of the finished product..

The stability results justify the proposed shelf-life of 3 years and store in the proposed container due to sensitivity to moisture as stated in the SmPC (section 6.3) are acceptable. Use 100 days after first opening of the bottle.

## 3.4.5. Adventitious agents

Gelatine obtained from bovine sources is used in the product. Valid TSE CEP from the suppliers of the gelatine used in the manufacture is provided.

## 3.5. Discussion and conclusions on chemical, pharmaceutical and biological aspects

Information on development, manufacture and control of the active substances and finished product has been presented in a satisfactory manner.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

During the evaluation, two MOs were raised on the control of the product for purity profile. Appropriate additional justification and supporting information were provided by the applicant for both MOs, and the CHMP considered both issues satisfactorily addressed.

The results of the quality assessment indicate consistency and adequate control of the critical quality attributes relevant to product performance.

The quality of this product is considered to be acceptable when used in accordance with the conditions defined in the SmPC. Physicochemical and biological aspects relevant to the uniform clinical performance of the product have been investigated and are controlled in a satisfactory way.

## 3.6. Recommendation(s) for future quality development

Not applicable.

## 4. Non-clinical aspects

## 4.1. Introduction

Zambon submitted a full-mixed MAA under Article 8(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC, for LD and CD MR hard capsules (oral use), relying on pharmacology, pharmacokinetics (PK) and toxicology studies from the published literature, considering that the constituents of IPX203 (levodopa and carbidopa) have a well-established medicinal use with recognised efficacy and an acceptable level of safety.

Levodopa/carbidopa modified hard capsules are intended to provide improved control of plasma LD levels compared with currently available LD-CD products for the treatment of PD. Considering the available  published nonclinical information, the long history of LD-CD for PD treatment, and the clinical data generated in the IPX203 clinical development program, no new nonclinical pharmacology, pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies were conducted with IPX203 by the Applicant in support of this application.

Fixed combinations of LD and CD have been used extensively worldwide for the treatment of PD since the 1970s. The safety and efficacy of these combinations have been established through numerous non-clinical studies reported in the literature and many decades of clinical dosing experience. To support the well-established safety and efficacy of LD and CD and summarise the findings from published non-clinical studies that might have an impact on the product labelling, the following search strategy was applied to retrieve articles related to pharmacology, PK, and toxicology of LD, CD, and LD:CD between January 2012 and June 2022 using EMBASE (Elsevier B.V.). The following search terms were applied:

Published pharmacological and safety pharmacology studies detailed beneficial and adverse effects of modifying brain and peripheral dopamine (DA) levels in laboratory animals via LD administration. The PK characteristics of LD, CD, and LD:CD, including absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, are well characterised. Published literature on general toxicology of LD, CD, and CD:LD includes acuteand repeat-dose studies in mice, rats, dogs, and monkeys, an assessment of genetic toxicity and carcinogenicity, reproductive and developmental toxicology studies, as well as other toxicity, immunotoxicity and neurotoxicity studies.

Safety considerations of excipients and degradants present in the drug product were based on information obtained from the FDA Inactive Ingredients Database (IIG), FDA Generally Recognised as Safe (GRAS) food ingredient listings and notices, the United States Pharmacopoeia (USP)-National Formulary (NF), and Drug Master Files.

Following the review of the published literature above mentioned, Zambon concluded that there were no new relevant non-clinical findings that would have an impact on the product labelling.

## Analytical methods

The analytical methods used to quantify levodopa (LD), carbidopa (CD) and their metabolites are described in the historical literature. Early studies employed radiolabelling at various carbon positions of LD and CD, enabling tracking of metabolic fate and excretion patterns in multiple species. Classical chromatographic techniques (e.g., gas-liquid and thin-layer chromatography) were used initially, while later studies employed more sensitive and specific methods such as high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with electrochemical or mass spectrometry detection. Available data indicate acceptable assay sensitivity and specificity for the intended pharmacokinetic evaluations. Overall, the methods described appear appropriate and consistent with the standards applied at the time the studies were conducted and are considered acceptable in the context of the long-standing clinical use of LD and CD.

## 4.2. Pharmacology

## 4.2.1. Pharmacodynamics

## 4.2.1.1. Primary pharmacodynamics

The primary pharmacodynamic properties of LD and its combination with CD are comprehensively described in the published literature and considered adequately addressed in the present MAA.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Levodopa, a precursor of dopamine (DA), restores dopaminergic neurotransmission in the striatum through decarboxylation by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), thereby compensating for the loss of dopaminergic neurons characteristic of PD. Carbidopa, a peripheral AADC inhibitor, prevents premature metabolism of LD in peripheral tissues, enhancing its delivery to the central nervous system (CNS).

The pharmacodynamic effects of LD and LD:CD have been consistently demonstrated in several wellestablished and pharmacologically relevant PD animal models, including 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA)-lesioned rats and 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-lesioned non-human primates. These studies have shown that LD administration resulted in increased striatal DA levels and improved motor behaviour. In animals with dopaminergic denervation, LD led to more pronounced behavioural effects than in intact controls, consistent with the hypersensitivity of DA-depleted systems.

In vitro and in vivo studies confirm that LD increases DA release both in brain slices and in whole animals, and these effects are potentiated by CD or benserazide co-administration. The observed enhancement of DA and its metabolites (e.g., Dihydroxyphenylacetic Acid [DOPAC], Homovanillic Acid [HVA]) in the striatum following LD:CD treatment provided further evidence of central dopaminergic activation. Moreover, studies demonstrated that the behavioural efficacy of LD is closely associated with increases in extracellular, rather than tissue, DA levels, supporting the relevance of extracellular DA as a pharmacodynamic biomarker.

Additional pharmacodynamic (PD) insights include the involvement of serotonergic terminals in LD metabolism and DA release in DA-denervated striatum, which may contribute to levodopa-induced dyskinesias (LID). Experimental interventions targeting serotonergic neurons or their receptors (e.g., 5-HT1 agonists, D2 autoreceptor gene transfer) have been shown to modulate this phenomenon, further elucidating the mechanism of LD's action and its long-term effects.

Taken together, in the applicant's view, the primary PD data available in the literature outlined the mechanism of action of LD:CD in the treatment of PD and are considered adequate to support the indication and posology proposed for IPX203. The relevance of the animal models used was considered acceptable. Therefore, no additional primary pharmacodynamic studies were deemed necessary.

## 4.2.1.2. Secondary pharmacodynamics

The secondary pharmacodynamic profile of levodopa (LD) was addressed throughout a selection of published studies that explored the potential effects of LD beyond its primary action in the central dopaminergic system. While these effects are not directly related to the treatment of PD, they may provide additional insights into the pharmacological activity and safety of LD.

The applicant summarised evidence of LD's effects in several non-motor domains, including neuroinflammation, visual and cognitive function, gastrointestinal motility and pain modulation. In models of sepsis-associated encephalopathy, LD administration improved cognitive outcomes and reduced neuroinflammatory markers, in part via D1 and D2 receptor mechanisms. In diabetic rat models, LD preserved retinal function and prevented progression of visual dysfunction, an effect associated with increased retinal DA levels. These findings suggested a broader neuroprotective potential of LD in disease states involving dopaminergic pathways or oxidative stress.

Furthermore, LD was shown to exert antinociceptive effects in rats, increasing the threshold for colonic distension via D2 receptor activation, and to enhance synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus following global cerebral ischemia. While these findings do not bear directly on the claimed indication, they contributed to the understanding of the compound's pharmacodynamic profile and may support aspects of tolerability or ancillary clinical benefits observed in patients.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Overall, the secondary pharmacodynamic data were consistent with the known pharmacology of LD and provided no evidence of off-target activities that would raise concern. Although these studies are not pivotal for the benefit-risk assessment of Hopledo, they were informative and reinforced the plausibility of DA-mediated effects outside the striatum. No issues requiring further clarification were identified in this context, and no additional studies are considered necessary.

## 4.2.1.3. Safety pharmacology

The safety pharmacology profile of LD and CD was characterised throughout a wide range of published studies covering the CNS, cardiovascular, respiratory, and gastrointestinal (GI) systems in several animal species. While most of these studies were conducted prior to the implementation of the current ICH S7A and ICH S7B guidelines, the data are consistent and reflected the extensive clinical experience with LD/CD fixed combinations.

Regarding CNS effects, LD/CD administration has been shown to induce dose-dependent behavioural responses across species, including hyperactivity in rodents and motor alterations in monkeys. These effects were attributable to central dopaminergic stimulation and were consistent with the intended pharmacological action. Emesis, commonly observed in dogs, is mediated by stimulation of dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and is attenuated by peripheral AADC inhibition with CD.

In the respiratory system, LD alone had limited effects on ventilation under normoxic and hypoxic conditions; however, a modest stimulation of ventilatory response was observed in combination with CD. These findings suggested that the central control of respiration may be modulated through dopaminergic mechanisms but with limited clinical relevance.

Cardiovascular studies demonstrated that LD can increase blood pressure (BP) via peripheral conversion to catecholamines, with secondary hypotension observed thereafter. In dogs and rats, intravenous LD induced transient pressor responses and, at higher doses, arrhythmias. Importantly, these effects were significantly reduced or prevented when LD was co-administered with CD, supporting the rationale for peripheral decarboxylase inhibition in clinical use.

Gastrointestinal effects of LD and CD include reduced gastric acid secretion, delayed intestinal transit, and modulation of smooth muscle tone. These effects were generally observed at high doses and are likely to reflect dopaminergic influences on enteric nervous system activity.

Overall, the safety pharmacology findings did not raise concerns and are consistent with the known pharmacological profile of LD/CD. The effects observed in animals are largely reflective of the clinical safety profile and appear to be dose-related, reversible, and consistent with dopaminergic stimulation. Although dedicated safety pharmacology studies were not conducted under GLP, the historical data are considered sufficient in the context of the long-standing clinical use of these substances.

No new safety signals emerged from the literature review, and no additional safety pharmacology studies are considered necessary.

## 4.2.1.4. Pharmacodynamic drug interactions

The pharmacodynamic interactions of levodopa, particularly in combination with carbidopa, have been addressed throughout a review of relevant non-clinical studies evaluating co-administration with compounds that may influence dopaminergic transmission or modulate motor function. These interactions are of particular importance in the context of Parkinson's disease, where polypharmacy is common.

The available literature demonstrated that the antiparkinsonian effects of LD can be potentiated by agents acting via complementary mechanisms. For example, co-administration with glial cell linederived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) in MPTP-lesioned non-human primates enhanced the therapeutic efficacy while reducing LD-associated adverse effects such as dyskinesia and vomiting. This suggested that neuroprotective or neurorestorative agents may synergise with LD therapy in advanced disease stages.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Further non-clinical studies indicated that co-administration of LD with remacemide hydrochloride, a glutamate receptor antagonist, or with phosphodiesterase 9 (PDE9) inhibitors, resulted in enhanced motor performance in PD models. These findings supported potential synergistic effects when LD is combined with agents targeting excitatory neurotransmission or intracellular signalling cascades.

In addition, the combination of LD/CD with opicapone, a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor, significantly increased plasma LD exposure in non-human primates, consistent with clinical pharmacokinetics and current treatment strategies. Similar enhancement of LD effects was reported with celecoxib, a COX-2 inhibitor, suggesting potential interactions involving neuroinflammation.

Taken together, the pharmacodynamic interaction data support the rationale for co-treatment strategies commonly used in clinical practice. No unexpected or deleterious interactions were identified, and the studies are consistent with the known mechanisms of action of LD and CD. These interactions are relevant for the optimisation of clinical therapy but do not alter the safety profile of the fixed LD/CD combination as such.

In conclusion, the pharmacodynamic interaction profile of LD/CD is well described and adequately supported by the published data. No further non-clinical studies are required in this regard.

## 4.2.2. Pharmacokinetics

## 4.2.2.1. Absorption

The absorption of LD and CD was described based on published studies in both animals and humans. LD is consistently shown to be rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations typically occurring within one hour after oral administration. However, the oral bioavailability of LD is limited due to extensive presystemic metabolism, with reported values around 35% in rats and dogs, and 30-50% in humans. CD is absorbed more slowly and incompletely, with time to peak levels between 1-2 hours in animals and 3-5 hours in humans. The co-administration of CD with LD enhances LD systemic exposure and prolongs its half-life, confirming its role in inhibiting peripheral AADC activity. The data also indicated that chronic administration of LD and CD does not significantly alter the peripheral pharmacokinetics of LD. The findings are in line with the known pharmacological properties and support the expected absorption behaviour of the fixed-dose combination.

## 4.2.2.2. Distribution

Distribution data for LD and CD were drawn from published studies in both animals and humans. LD distribution across tissues, including the gastrointestinal tract and brain, is mediated by the large neutral amino acid (LNAA) transport system, which may be subject to competition by dietary amino acids. LD is not highly protein-bound in plasma (&lt;30%) and is evenly distributed between plasma and erythrocytes. Tissue distribution studies in rodents indicated an uptake of radiolabelled LD in multiple organs, including the brain, kidney, liver, lung, skin, pancreas and muscle. CD shows high concentrations in peripheral tissues such as kidney, liver, lungs, and intestines, but does not appear to cross the blood-brain barrier. Both LD and CD have been shown to cross the placenta in animal studies, and LD also in humans. Overall, the distribution profiles were consistent with the established knowledge and did not raise any new safety concerns. Overall, the data presented were considered adequate to support the distribution characteristics of the fixed combination.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 4.2.2.3. Metabolism

The metabolic pathways of LD and CD are well described in the literature and consistent across species. LD undergoes rapid decarboxylation by AADC to dopamine in the GI tract and liver, accounting for its limited oral bioavailability. This decarboxylation is saturable and can be inhibited by CD. LD is also metabolised by the COMT to 3-O-methyldopa (3-OMD), and subsequently to other metabolites such as DOPAC and HVA. CD metabolism involves loss of the hydrazine group and formation of α - methyl derivatives, with no indication of toxicologically relevant species-specific metabolites. Importantly, LD and CD metabolism does not involve cytochrome P450 enzymes, minimising the risk of metabolic drug-drug interactions. The metabolic profiles described support the known pharmacological activity and safety of the substances and are adequate for the purpose of this MA application.

## 4.2.2.4. Excretion

Excretion data from literature indicate that both LD and its metabolites are primarily eliminated via the renal route in all species studied, with the majority of the administered dose recovered in urine within 24 hours. Only a small fraction is excreted as unchanged LD, confirming extensive metabolic conversion. CD is also primarily excreted in urine, with variable amounts of unchanged drug depending on species. Faecal excretion reflects incomplete absorption rather than biliary elimination. Excretion of both compounds in milk has been reported in rats, and transplacental passage has also been demonstrated. The excretion profiles are consistent with historical data and support the lack of accumulation or retention concerns. The data are considered sufficient and relevant for the proposed clinical use of the fixed-dose combination of LD and CD under evaluation.

## 4.2.2.5. Pharmacokinetic drug interactions

Co-administration with magnesium oxide reduced the plasma levels of both LD and CD in rats, consistent with human findings and likely due to altered GI absorption. Other interactions include increased LD exposure when administered with catechin, benserazide, and opicapone, as expected from inhibition of LD metabolism. These interactions are well understood and aligned with the known pharmacology of these substances. The data supported the need to consider possible absorption or metabolic interactions in clinical use but did not raise any new safety issues.

## 4.2.2.6. Other pharmacokinetic studies

Additional studies, such as those in hepatectomised rats, further supported the role of the liver in firstpass metabolism of LD. These findings reinforced the conclusion that pre-systemic metabolism is a major determinant of LD bioavailability, and that formulation's approaches designed to modify release and absorption profiles are pharmacologically justified. No new concerns arose from these supplementary data.

## 4.3. Toxicology

## 4.3.1. Single-dose toxicity

Data on single dose toxicity for levodopa, carbidopa and the two active substances in combination were provided from published literature. Reported oral LD50 of levodopa in rats ranged from 1780 up to &gt;8000 mg/kg; oral LD50 of carbidopa in mice was 1750 mg/kg and, in male and female rats, 5610

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

and 4080 mg/kg, respectively. In mice, the oral LD50 of a 1:10 mixture of carbidopa and levodopa was 3440 mg/kg.

## 4.3.2. Repeat-dose toxicity

Data on repeated dose toxicity for levodopa, carbidopa and the two active substances in combination were provided from published literature.

Repeated dose toxicity of LD was tested in rats and monkeys with a treatment duration of approximately 12 weeks in both species. Toxicity of CD was tested in rats, dogs and monkeys, with treatment durations up to 96 weeks, 34 weeks and 1 year, respectively. Toxicity of levodopa/carbidopa combinations, employing the two active substances in different proportions, was tested in rats, monkeys and minipigs with treatment durations up to 2 years, 1 year and 13 weeks, respectively.

## Levodopa

The 12-week studies with LD alone showed no treatment-related effects in monkeys (which received levodopa at doses up to 1000 mg/kg/day). Organs with histopathological changes identified in rats included salivary glands and adrenals, at all tested doses (i.e., 250 to 1000 mg/kg/day), kidneys, at ≥500mg/kg/day, and stomach, at 1000 mg/kg/day.

## Carbidopa

For CD alone, the longer-term study in rats, with administration of doses of up to 135 mg/kg/day, revealed no effects other than a slight degree of flaccidity during the first year of the treatment. No pathologic changes related to carbidopa were observed in a shorter-term study (14-day) that employed doses up to 400 mg/kg/day.

The longer-term study with CD alone in dogs, with administration of 5, 15, 45, 135 mg/kg/day, showed tremors, emesis, soft stools or diarrhoea sometimes with blood in the faeces, anorexia, and weight loss at &gt;15 mg/kg/day. At 135 mg/kg/day all dogs were killed in the 4 th  week, at 45 mg/kg/day, all dogs were killed in the 6 th  week; all other dogs survived until termination of the experiment. Another study in dogs, a 43-day study, revealed that coadministration of pyridoxine hydrochloride markedly attenuated the development of lesions associated with carbidopa administration.

In the studies with carbidopa alone conducted in monkeys, the animals received doses of up to 400, 45 and 135 mg/kg/day for 14 days, 86 days and 1 year, respectively. No significant effects were observed.

## Levodopa/carbidopa combination

In rats, administration of LD in combination with CD resulted in reduced activity, ptyalism, irregular respiration, and weakness or flaccidity at all doses investigated across all studies. Organs with histopathological changes included the stomach, adrenal and salivary glands, which were observed at the maximum tested dose (500 mg/kg/day of levodopa in combination with carbidopa [25, 50 and 100 mg/kg/day], tested in a 30-day study).  These histomorphologic changes were attributed to LD.

Effects observed in the longest-term study in monkeys (1 year, with administration of up to 100/10 mg/kg/day levodopa/carbidopa) were limited to transient increase in activity (at 50/10 and 100/10 mg/kg/day levodopa/carbidopa), muscular incoordination and weakness (at 100/10 mg/kg/day levodopa/carbidopa). Deaths were observed in a shorter-term study (85 days) with administration of doses of 120/30 mg/kg/day levodopa/carbidopa.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

A study in minipigs employed a formulation of LD/CD administrated by subcutaneous infusion. This study did not reveal any systemic effects. Only local effects were noted at the infusion sites.

## 4.3.3. Genotoxicity

Data from studies on genotoxicity of dopamine, levodopa and carbidopa were provided from published literature. Studies on the genotoxic potential of dopamine included an Ames assay, mouse lymphoma assay, sister chromatid-exchange analysis in human lymphocytes in vitro , DNA single strand breaks in human skin fibroblast in vitro and an in vivo micronucleus assay. Studies with LD included an Ames assay, in vitro micronucleus and in vivo micronucleus and Comet assay. Additionally, data was also provided on a clinical study with levodopa that investigated a potential induction of chromosomal damage in peripheral blood lymphocytes. Regarding CD, data was provided on an in vivo micronucleus and Comet assay.

According to available data, dopamine was positive (genotoxic) in the mouse lymphoma assay and in the assay for single strand breaks in human fibroblasts in vitro ; it was negative in the remaining conducted assays.

Levodopa was weakly positive in the Ames assay and in vitro micronucleus assay and was positive in the in vivo micronucleus and Comet assays. In a clinical study, it has not induced an increase in the frequency of micronuclei in peripheral blood lymphocytes.

Carbidopa was negative in both in vivo micronucleus and Comet assays.

The observed positive results for dopamine in two in vitro assays were suggested to be related to the oxidation of dopamine and generation of reactive oxygen radicals, semiquinones, and quinones. For the genotoxicity observed for levodopa, reference was made to oxidative damage.

## 4.3.4. Carcinogenicity

No data on carcinogenicity-specific studies were provided. However, the repeated dose toxicity studies in rats with administration of carbidopa and LD/CD combination (lasting 2 years) did not provide any evidence of a carcinogenic effect.

## 4.3.5. Developmental and reproductive toxicity

## Fertility

Regarding studies on fertility, submitted data from public literature were limited to information from a study in mice with near-lifetime dietary administration of levodopa. No effects were observed at 10 and 20 mg/g diet, but only at the maximum tested dose of 40 mg/g diet, the maximum tolerated dose, which showed a reduction in the number of pregnancies and offsprings. Therefore, SmPC section 4.6 details that there are no data on the effects of levodopa or carbidopa on human fertility. No effects on fertility were observed in animal studies .

## Embryo-foetal development

Data was provided on embryo-foetal development studies with LD, CD and the two substances in combination. Studies with levodopa alone were conducted in mice and rabbits; with carbidopa alone and the combination, in mice, rats and rabbits.

Embryo-foetal development studies revealed foetal (e.g., visceral and skeletal) malformations in rabbits upon administration of LD or LD/CD combination. This information is reflected in SmPC section 5.3.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Prenatal and postnatal development

No data on conventional prenatal and postnatal development studies have been provided. Instead, information from literature was submitted, specifically pertaining to one study in mice, describing administration of LD from gestation day 11 up to birth, and one study on milk excretion of CD conducted in rats. The publications describing studies focusing on mice given LD revealed persistent increases in dopamine content in the brain and behavioural changes in the progeny. The study where rats received CD showed its excretion in milk.

The above is reflected qin SmPC section 4.6, where it is stated that levodopa and possibly levodopa metabolites are excreted in human milk. There is evidence that lactation is suppressed during treatment with levodopa. It is unknown whether carbidopa or its metabolites are excreted in human milk. Animal studies have shown excretion of carbidopa in breast milk.

## 4.3.6. Toxicokinetics and exposure margins

Only published data were provided by the applicant. Toxicokinetic data were limited to one LD/CD combination study in minipigs receiving the fixed-dose combination via SC infusion.

## 4.3.7. Local tolerance

No data on dedicated local tolerance studies were submitted. This was considered acceptable by the CHMP.

## 4.3.8. Other toxicity studies

Data from published literature was provided on immunotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Studies on immunotoxicity were conducted with both LD and LD/CD combination; those on neurotoxicity, with LD.

Levodopa and the combination were found to suppress immuno-inflammatory skin reactions in mice and rats. Both in vitro and an in vivo study with LD revealed a potential neurotoxic effect.

## 4.3.9. Ecotoxicity/environmental risk assessment

The environmental risk assessment (ERA) report was prepared in accordance with the Guideline on the Environmental Risk Assessment of Medicinal Products for Human Use (EMEA/CHMP/SWP/4447/00 Rev.1 , 2024).

The justification for the absence of a complete ERA for LD and CD was documented separately for each active substance.

Levodopa and CD are naturally occurring substances, and the exclusion of an ERA is in line with Question 1, related to the Phase I Decision tree (Figure 2) of the above noted guideline:

- In the case of medicinal products comprised of naturally occurring substances (e.g., vitamins, electrolytes, amino acids, peptides, proteins, nucleotides, carbohydrates and lipids) as active substances, the ERA may consist of a justification for not submitting ERA studies, as they are unlikely to result in significant risk to the environment. Alternatively, given their environmental fate and/or common presence, these products are unlikely to alter the concentration or distribution of the substance.

Due to the nature of LD and CD, a risk to the environment arising from their use is therefore not expected. Levodopa/Carbidopa finished products currently approved and marketed in the EU for the treatment of Parkinson's disease patients are most commonly formulated as oral tablets. Hopledo prescribed use is not expected to increase significantly environmental exposure to LD/CD. This supported and contributed to the applicant's justification for not performing ERA studies for CD

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

following the prescribed use of Hopledo 140 mg/35 mg, 210 mg/52.5 mg, 280 mg/70 mg, and 350 mg/87.5 mg modified-release hard capsules.

The applicant's justification for the absence of ERA studies was accepted by the CHMP. In addition, the applicant applied suitable precautionary and safety measures to inform patients and healthcare professionals (HCPs), mitigate environmental risks, and promote environmental protection, in accordance with guideline EMEA/CHMP/SWP/4447/00, 2024.

## 4.4. Overall discussion and conclusions on non-clinical aspects

The PK profile of LD and CD, based on extensive published data, is also considered well established. Information submitted by the applicant adequately supported the description of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion characteristics of both active substances. No new PK concerns have been identified.

The PD profile of LD and CD is well established and sufficiently characterised in the non-clinical literature. Data presented by the applicant are consistent across species, models and study types, providing robust support for Hopledo proposed indication and posology. Observed PD effects are predictable, reproducible and aligned with extensive clinical experience. No additional pharmacology studies were considered necessary by the CHMP to support this MA application.

Regarding toxicological data, no new non-clinical studies have been provided. Instead, published literature on single and repeated dose toxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity and other toxicity studies was submitted.

This information was considered sufficient: and no further studies were considered necessary by the CHMP.

With regard to non-clinical safety data, the wording included in Hopledo SmPC is generally consistent with that encountered for already approved medicinal products containing LD and CD.

Levodopa and CD active substances are natural compounds, the utilisation of which is unlikely to modify the concentration or distribution of these substances within the environment. Consequently, the authorisation of Hopledo (levodopa/carbidopa) 140 mg/35 mg, 210 mg/52.5 mg, 280 mg/70 mg, and 350 mg/87.5 mg modified-release hard capsules is not anticipated to pose an environmental risk.

## 5. Clinical aspects

## 5.1. Introduction

## 5.1.1. Good Clinical Practice (GCP) aspects

The applicant claimed that the clinical trials presented in this initial MAA were performed in accordance with GCP.

In addition, it was also confirmed that the clinical trials conducted outside the European community were carried out in accordance with the ethical standards of Directive 2001/20/EC.

Based on the review of clinical data, the CHMP did not identify the need for a GCP inspection of the clinical trials included in this MAA dossier.

## 5.2. Clinical pharmacology

## 5.2.1. Methods

Validated bioanalytical methods were used for the determination of LD and CD in human plasma samples collected during the clinical development programme, across IPX203 clinical protocols (IPX203-B16-04/-05/06; IPX203-B14-02; IPX203-B16-01). Method validation activities were conducted in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements to demonstrate that the analytical procedures were suitable for their intended use and capable of generating reliable data to support the clinical studies.

## 5.2.2. Pharmacokinetics

## 5.2.2.1. Introduction

The (PK of IPX203 was studied in three Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (Studies IPX203-B1604, IPX203-B16-05 , and IPX203-B16-06 ). Pharmacokinetics and PD have been studied in two Phase 2 studies following a single dose (Study IPX203-B14-02 ) and multiple therapeutic doses (Study IPX203-B16-01 ) in subjects with advanced PD.

## 5.2.2.2. Evaluation and qualification of models

## 5.2.2.2.1. Population pharmacokinetics

No PopPK models were used.

## 5.2.2.2.2. Physiology based pharmacokinetic model

No PBPK models were used.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.2.3. Absorption

The PK of IPX203 was studied in three Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (Studies IPX203-B1604 , IPX203-B16-05 and IPX203-B16-06 ). Pharmacokinetics and PD have been studied in two Phase 2 studies following a single dose (Study IPX203-B14-02 ) and multiple therapeutic doses (Study IPX203-B16-01 ) in subjects with advanced PD. Phase 2 studies were conducted between 2015 and 2017 and Phase 1 studies were conducted in 2019. A tabular summary of the conducted studies is provided below.

## Phase 1 studies

## Study IPX203-B16-04

## Levodopa

In comparison to the fasted state condition, when IPX203 is administered on fed state condition, all point estimates (Cmax and AUC) for LD are &gt;100%, indicating higher exposure with food. The geometric mean ratios (A/C) are ~119% for Cmax and ~118% for both AUC metrics, showing a consistent ~18-19% increase of levodopa bioavailability under fed conditions. Intra-subject CVs are modest (≈12 -17%), not suggestive of a highly variable drug.

In the course of the procedure, the applicant provided partial AUC estimates for LD. These results showed a marked redistribution of LD exposure over time under fed conditions, with a very pronounced reduction in early exposure. Specifically, LD pAUC0-1h (fed/fasted) is 4.53% (90% CI 3.13-6.56), i.e., far outside the usual 80-125% range, while later exposure is increased, e.g., pAUC5-10h (fed/fasted) is 181.80% (90% CI 157.31-210.11).

Based on these study results, the applicant revised the wording of SmPC sections 4.2 and 5.2 to describe the food effect in PK terms only. Of note, following administration of IPX203 with high-fat, high-calorie meal, absorption of levodopa may be slower/delayed, as reflected by a delayed median Tmax compared with the fasted state, while overall systemic exposure (AUC) remains unchanged. In addition, for patients in whom a rapid onset of IPX203 effect is considered important, such as at the first dose of the day, administration on an empty stomach may be considered.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In comparison to the fasted state condition, when IPX203 is administered springled in applesauce, all point estimates (Cmax and AUC) for levodopa were &lt;100%, indicating slightly lower exposure when sprinkled. Intra-subject CVs were modest (≈12 -17%), and the analysis was highly powered (~100%).

Administration by sprinkling the contents of IPX203 on apple sauce was however considered bioequivalent to the administration in the fasted state, for both rate and extent of exposure. The ~812% decreases are unlikely to be clinically meaningful, and no dose adjustment is needed. These data supported inclusion of sprinkling on applesauce as an acceptable alternative administration method in the product labelling, with appropriate sprinkling instructions, as detailed in SmPC section 4.2 (and PL).

## Carbidopa

In contrast to LD, a very large decrease in exposure with food was observed for CD, with point estimates ~36% of fasted for Cmax and AUC (i.e., ~64% lower under fed conditions). Nevertheless, a modest decrease in exposure was observed for CD when sprinkled: Cmax 86.9%, AUCs ~90.9%. Of note, a 'no food effect' claim cannot be made for carbidopa, as food reduces both rate and extent of exposure substantially. Sprinkling supports comparable extent of exposure (AUC) but a lower peak.

## Study IPX203-B16-05

## Levodopa

When comparing the new modified-release (MR) LD/CD 280/70 mg (IPX203 - treatment A) with Sinemet IR 100/25 mg (treatment B), and although the dose of IPX203 is 2.8-fold higher (280 mg vs 100 mg), levodopa Cmax was essentially the same as IR, whereas AUCs were ≈2.7× those of IR. However, in IPX203 MR capsules 25% of LD dose (corresponding to 70 mg) is contained in the immediate release granules. The attained Cmax was probably mostly driven by such IR amount and partially from the ER beads, given the delayed Tmax (the median LD Tmax was 2.0 hours for IPX203 versus 0.5 hours for IR LD-CD). When dose-normalised (using the least square means), the IPX203 product yielded ~38% lower peak than IR.

Extent of exposure (AUC) scaled as expected with dose. When dose-normalised, represented ~9798% of IR (based on the geometric least square means of AUC0-∞ ), indicating comparable bioavailability to IR on a per-mg basis.

These findings are consistent with a MR profile that reduces peak-to-trough fluctuation while maintaining ( versus IR) an overall exposure.

As dose differ between treatments, this is not a bioequivalence assessment; dose-normalised metrics would provide the appropriate relative bioavailability context. In the course of the procedure, as requested, the applicant provided partial AUC analyses. Overall, the data supported that IPX203 maintains early LD exposure while providing substantially greater later exposure compared with IR, consistent with a comparable onset by about 2 hours and a more sustained LD profile thereafter. In particular, LD AUC0-2h was broadly similar between IPX203 and IR, whereas LD exposure was markedly higher with IPX203 in the 2-6h and 6-12h intervals, supporting the prolonged duration of action and the proposed BID/TID dosing.

On the other hand, for LD, exposure in the first hour (AUC0-1h) was lower with IPX203 than IR, even though AUC0-2h is similar, suggesting that very early onset may differ while overall early exposure by 2 hours was comparable. In addition, the statement that early partial AUCs are 'similar' for both IPX203 and IR does not apply to CD, for which early partial AUCs appear higher with IPX203. However, these observations did not change the main conclusion on LD onset and sustained exposure.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

When comparing the new IPX203 MR LD/CD 280/70 mg (A) with Sinemet CR 100/25 mg (C), LD Cmax was approximately 2.2-fold higher, whereas AUCs were ≈3.1 fold higher. On a per -mg basis the MR product yielded ~21% lower peak and ~11% higher total exposure than Sinemet CR 100/25 mg, indicating slight supra-bioavailability in the extent of LD absorption. In summary, it can be concluded that the new MR provided greater total exposure than CR but with a lower peak.

## Carbidopa

When comparing the new IPX203 MR LD/CD 280/70 mg (A) with Sinemet IR 100/25 mg (B), CD Cmax and AUC were approximately 3.2 and 3.4-fold higher, respectively, in line with the higher dose of the MR formulation, i.e., 2.8-fold higher (70 mg vs 25 mg). On a per-mg basis (using the least square means), the MR product yielded ~18% higher peak and ~22% higher total exposure than IR, indicating slight supra-bioavailability vs IR. In the new MR formulation, the IR granules contained 100% of CD dose.

When comparing the new IPX203 MR LD/CD 280/70 mg (A) with Sinemet CR 100/25 mg (C), CD Cmax was approximately 4.6-fold higher, whereas AUCs are ≈ 4.8 fold higher. In a per mg analysis based on the least square means, the MR formulation delivered ~65-73% higher exposure and peak than CR, implying substantially greater bioavailability than the CR tablet.

## Study IPX203-B16-06

For both levodopa and carbidopa, study results showed bioequivalence between the two IPX203 batches (IPX203 MR LD-CD 140-35 mg), one manufactured in the US and the other in Taiwan.

For both LD and CD, a dose proportionality was observed in the dose range of IPX203 MR LD-CD 14035 mg to IPX203 MR LD-CD 350-87.5 mg. The elimination pattern of both drugs was not modified with an increased dose.

## Phase 2 studies

Phase 2 studies (single and multiple dose) were conducted using IPX203 capsules 180 mg (LD-CD 18045 mg) and 270 mg (LD-CD 270-67.5 mg), which are not the proposed to be marketed dose strengths. However the derived PK results were bridged to results from the to-be-marked (TBM) formulations (IPX203 MR capsules LD-CD 140-35 mg, LD-CD 210-52.5 mg, LD-CD 280-70 mg and LD-CD 350-87.5 mg) through the dose proportionality study IPX203-B16-06 , as well as through the food effect study IPX203-B16-04 , given that both LD and CD showed dose-normal linearity PKs (within the range of LD-CD 140-35 mg to LD-CD 350-87.5 mg), which assures a predictable exposure scaling across strengths. Moreover, no accumulation and time-invariant pPKs were observed with the multiple dose regimens tested in the Phase 2 study IPX203-B16-01 . Of note, the Phase-3 pivotal trial was conducted using the TBM IPX203 MR capsules LD-CD 140-35 mg.

## Study IPX203-B14-02

In this randomised, open-label, rater-blinded, three-period crossover conducted in fasted subjects with advanced PD, all treatments contained LD and CD at a fixed 4:1 ratio, with IPX203 and Rytary given at doses roughly three times higher than the comparator IR LD-CD.

## Levodopa

Following IPX203, LD showed a median Tmax of 2.0 h (range 0.5-7.0 h); as anticipated for modified/extended-release products, Tmax for both IPX203 and Rytary exceeded that of IR LD-CD. Despite the higher doses, the early rise in LD concentration with IPX203 was similar to that seen with IR LD-CD and Rytary, indicating comparable performance of the IR fraction. The mean Cmax (all doses)

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

after IPX203 was 3161 ng/mL with a mean half-life of about 2.3 h; on average, Cmax was only ~27% higher with IPX203 and ~14% higher with Rytary than with IR LD-CD, whereas AUC0-t was larger for both modified/extended-release regimens, consistent with the higher administered dose.

The bioavailability of LD based on dose-normalised natural-log-transformed AUC0-inf following IPX203 administration was approximately 85.5% relative to IR CD-LD.

A useful indicator of profile 'flatness' was the time for which plasma concentrations remained above 50% of Cmax. By this measure IPX203 sustained LD levels the longest-about 4.7 h above 50% Cmax compared with 3.9 h for Rytary and 1.9 h for IR LD-CD-and this pattern was consistent across all IPX203 dose strengths studied. The time to reach 50% of Cmax was broadly similar for IPX203 and Rytary and slightly shorter for IR LD-CD; importantly, the time to attain a clinically meaningful concentration (~430 ng/mL) was comparable across all three treatments. Overall, IPX203 delivered a smoother and more prolonged LD exposure than IR LD-CD and somewhat longer than Rytary, with only modest increases in peak concentrations despite higher doses-an exposure profile consistent with reduced peak-trough fluctuation while preserving prompt onset.

As requested in the course of the procedure, the applicant provided a model-based sensitivity analysis to check if the first sampling time at 0.5 h was sufficient to capture the true IR LD Cmax in Studies IPX203-B14-02 and and IPX203-B16-01.

This analysis used individual one-compartment PK fits and different absorption rate constants. The predicted Tmax values were close to the first sampling time, mainly around 0.44-0.78 h, and predicted Cmax values for plausible ka values were within about ±10% of the reference estimate. Therefore, a clinically relevant underestimation of IR Cmax due to the 0.5 h first sample is unlikely. The applicant also provided early exposure metrics, including AUC0-0.5h, AUC0-1h, and AUC0-2h, dose-normalised to 100 mg LD. These results were broadly similar between studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 and supported the early exposure assessment, as detailed below.

A total of 51 subjects with PD (24 in study IPX203-B14-02 and 27 in study IPX203-B16-01), were considered for sensitivity analyses estimating the true IR Tmax/Cmax. Measured plasma LD exposure data were obtained from patients resulting from a single morning dose or multiple dosing uptake of 100-250 mg Sinemet IR.

In a first step, for all study individuals (one) compartment structural PK models were fitted to their LD exposure profiles (total n = 24 + 2x27 = 78). Diagnostic plots of observed LD plasma exposure versus model predicted LD exposure were used to verify fit quality. Such plots are shown in the figure below for IPX203-B14-02 (left) and IPX203-B16-01 (right), with lines of identity plotted for guidance.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Calculated LD exposure correlates well with measured LD exposure. Due to the higher complication of study IPX203-B16 (a multi-dose Phase 2 study) observed variability to model calculated exposure is higher but still in an acceptable range. In both studies, variability increases at higher plasma concentrations, i.e., at exposure levels at which Cmax is located, and also observed plasma levels have a slight tendency to be higher than their predicted counterparts. As requested, sensitivity analyses to estimate the true IR Tmax and Cmax were then run by estimating Cmax and Tmax using best-fit one compartment PK models individual by individual. This was performed by using a common dose of 100 mg LD, fixed population geometric mean Vd (47.8 L) and CL (36.9 L/h) values, and variable ka values. As a lower boundary for ka, kel = CL/Vd (0.772 h -1 ) was selected, since individual LD plasma exposure analyses showed that kel&gt;ka in more than 80% of individual analyses, indicating that exposure is an elimination rate limited clearance. In addition, lower (1.97) and upper (3.11) ka values of the 95% confidence interval (CI), population mean ka (2.54), and the geometric mean ka value + 1 SD (5.7) estimated in the subject population were used.

In the remaining four other cases, small differences in Tmax and Cmax are observed in the 0-1-hour post-dose period. Importantly, Tmax values range from 0.44-0.78 h and are thus close to the first sampling time point of 0.5 h. Observed plasma levels at 0.5 h should therefore capture the real Cmax quite well.
