Descriptive statistics results of individual profiles support the sensitivity analysis. Comparison of Tmax, Cmax, and partial AUCs from both Phase 2 studies shows a good congruity across these studies. Although having wide ranges, estimated geometric mean values of all analysed parameters are comparable from study to study. Geometric mean Tmax is estimated at 0.75 hours again sustaining that sampling at 0.5 hours post-dosing is deemed acceptable for capturing Cmax correctly.

In summary, the Applicant adequately justified that the 0.5 h first sampling time was acceptable for estimation of IR Cmax , and any possible underestimation is unlikely to have a major impact on the 2.8× conversion factor.

Moreover, in the course of the procedure, the applicant confirmed that the proposed unit-dose conversion factor (x2.8) was derived using Cmax matching approach.

A more complete justification of the proposed IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm was provided, including additional clinical evidence, quantitative PK simulations for the illustrative cases, and one additional example with the same IR total daily dose. The Applicant also proposed a targeted mitigation at the upper end of the conversion range, allowing initiation with the next lower available capsule strength for patients with a most frequent IR LD dose of 200 mg or higher.

Interim data from a Phase 4 real -world evidence (RWE) study conducted in the United States (ELEVATE-PD study interim analysis with 111 patients) were supplied. This study evaluated the performance of the current IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm in routine clinical practice.

These real-world data provided additional external validation that the proposed conversion approach is robust, predictable, and clinically workable across a heterogeneous patient population, and directly addressed concerns that the algorithm would result in unstable or disproportionate dosing in practice.

It was explained that the conversion algorithm is intended as an initial dosing recommendation, followed by individual titration based on efficacy and tolerability. This is clinically relevant, as dose adjustment is expected in advanced Parkinson's disease. The currently available Phase 4 data are

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

interim and supportive, but they provided useful reassurance that the 2.8× unit -dose conversion can be used in routine clinical practice, with a median of one titration step after conversion. The Phase 3 and Phase 4 data also support BID initiation in patients receiving &lt;500 mg/day IR LD, with maintained clinical benefit and no new safety concern.

The simulations for the proposed cases showed that large nominal increases in total daily LD do not necessarily lead to excessive Cmax. They also suggest that IPX203 provides more sustained exposure above the proposed efficacy threshold and less fragmented exposure compared with IR. Importantly, in higher-dose scenarios, the proposed lower-dose starting option reduces Cmax and total exposure, while maintaining predicted ON-time. This addressed the main concern that the algorithm could lead to excessive exposure in some patients after switch.

In addition, the Applicant proposed a revised SmPC wording for the conversion algorithm. This keeps the 2.8-fold conversion principle but allows starting with the next lower strength when the most frequent IR levodopa dose is 200 mg or higher. The recommendation for follow-up after 1 to 3 days and further dose or dosing-frequency adjustment based on individual response is also clinically relevant and supports safe use during conversion.

Some uncertainty remains because the simulations are model-based and the proposed efficacy threshold may vary between patients. In addition, patients with the same IR TDD but different IR dose patterns may still receive different nominal IPX203 TDD after conversion. However, the Applicant's explanation was considered acceptable in the context of the initial nature of the conversion algorithm, the need for later individual titration, supportive Phase 3/4 data, and the proposed mitigation option for the upper conversion range.

## Carbidopa

In the same crossover study, CD was absorbed relatively rapidly after IPX203, with a median Tmax of 2.5 h (range 1.5-6.0 h). The mean Cmax (all doses) was 571 ng/mL and the mean half-life about 2.3 h. Both IPX203 and Rytary produced a more sustained CD profile than IR LD-CD, maintaining concentrations for longer and indicating extended-release behaviour. As expected from the higher CD dose in IPX203, systemic exposure was greater: Cmax and AUC were approximately 3 to 3.5-fold higher than those observed with IR LD-CD. Overall, IPX203 achieved higher and more prolonged CD levels than IR LD-CD, with stability over time comparable to Rytary.

The bioavailability of CD based on dose-normalised natural-log-transformed AUC0-inf following IPX203 administration was approximately 112% relative to IR CD-LD.

## Study IPX203-B16-01

In this phase-2, randomised, open-label, rater-blinded, two-period crossover in advanced PD, IPX203 (LD:CD 4:1) was compared with IR LD-CD under steady dosing after individual titration. For LD, IPX203 delivered a smoother, longer-lasting profile than IR: on Day 15, concentrations were maintained above 50% of Cmax for 6.2 h versus 3.9 h and above 430 ng/mL for 9.0 h versus 7.4 h (both statistically significant), with broadly similar time to 50% Cmax and dose-normalised Cmax across treatments; fluctuation over 10 h was lower with IPX203 (1.7 vs 2.7) and accumulation over 15 days was minimal and comparable (≈1.0 -1.1). The larger AUC with IPX203 reflected the higher LD dose used, and the IR fraction supported a similar onset to clinically meaningful concentrations. The applicant clarified, based on literature data, that the clinically relevant LD threshold for onset of effect is approximately 1000 ng/mL, and that 430 ng/mL was only an internal working reference.

The adequacy of the 0.5h hour as the first sampling timepoint in study IPX203-B16-01 was supported by the model-based sensitivity analysis discussed above for study IPX203-B14-02.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

For CD, IPX203 produced higher and more sustained exposure than IR at both single and multiple doses. On Day 15, Tmax was similar (2.5 h vs 2.0 h), while Cmax averaged 479 vs 146 ng/mL and AUC τ 1892 vs 416 ng·h/mL (≈4.5 -fold), consistent with the higher CD dose and modified-release design; fluctuation indices were comparable (1.7 vs 1.5) and accumulation was low (≈1.1) for both treatments. It is emphasised that the non-clinical margin based on the 1-year rhesus monkey NOAEL (≥135 mg/kg/day) corresponds to an estimated 4.4 -fold margin over the proposed maximal daily CD dose (595 mg/day), which is considered acceptable in the context of the absence of toxicological findings at high chronic doses in primates and the lack of clinically relevant QTc effects at supratherapeutic CD exposure.

Overall, relative to IR LD-CD, IPX203 provided extended coverage with modest peaks for levodopa and substantially higher, sustained carbidopa exposure, without meaningful accumulation over 15 days.

IPX203 PK properties, as summarised above, are reflected in the SmPC.

## 5.2.2.4. Bioequivalence

No bioequivalence studies were conducted. This was considered acceptable by CHMP.

## 5.2.2.5. Distribution

The apparent volume of distribution (V/F) was not determined from the conducted phase 1 and phase 2 studies. No PopPK analysis, or in vitro and ex vivo protein binding studies of LD and CD were performed. However, in the context of a full-mixed application under Article 8(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC, the characterisation of LD and CD PK distribution (as outlined in SmPC section 5.2) was substantiated with literature references.

## 5.2.2.6. Metabolism

No dedicated in vitro metabolism studies were conducted. Instead, the Applicant substantiated with appropriate literature references the statements in SmPC section 5.2 regarding metabolism of both levodopa and carbidopa, including the PKs of its metabolites.

## 5.2.2.7. Elimination

No mass balance study was conducted.

The elimination half-life was estimated for both LD and CD in the conducted phase 1 and phase 2 studies. The estimates are summarised in the Table below (t1/2 (h) (mean ± SD):

Table 9: Elimination half-life of levodopa and carbidopa

| Drug           | IPX203-B16-04 (n=27)   | IPX203-B16-05 (n=25)             | IPX203-B16-06 (n=40)   |
|----------------|------------------------|----------------------------------|------------------------|
| 1.988 ± 0.3000 | 1.997 ± 0.2620         | 1.668 ± 0.1629 to 2.113 ± 0.6700 | Levodopa               |
| 3.903 ± 0.5606 | 3.886 ± 0.4117         | 3.684 ± 0.5868 to 3.770 ± 0.3606 | Carbidopa              |

The applicant substantiated with literature references the statements in SmPC section 5.2 regarding the biotransformation and elimination of LD and CD. Levodopa and CD are primarily eliminated via non-renal routes. According to the population PK analysis done with extended-release LD/CD, creatinine clearance is unlikely to have a clinically meaningful effect, given the minor contribution of estimated creatinine clearance to the variability in levodopa exposures. The magnitude of the effect for creatinine clearance above 30 mL/min is not considered clinically meaningful .

Special consideration was given to CD and its metabolites, eliminated in the urine (with a notable fraction excreted unchanged), and possible accumulation in patients with advanced renal disease: during IPX203 administration the exposure to CD was about four times higher than with IR forms administration, thus additional accumulation is possible, and the applicant discussed accordingly the

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

possible clinical consequences of CD accumulation in patients with renal impairment. Even though in PD patients with renal impairment CD accumulation can cause neuropsychiatric, autonomic, gastrointestinal, metabolic, and motor complications, data from IPX203-B16-01 study confirmed that accumulation ratios for CD following 15 days of IPX203 or IR LD-CD treatment were low and comparable (1.1 for each).  In patients with renal impairment, theoretical risks include enhanced peripheral LD exposure, potentially increasing dopaminergic adverse effects (e.g., nausea, orthostatic symptoms) and increased frequency of known LD - related ADR rather than new safety concerns. In the applicant's view, no evidence suggested nephrotoxicity or direct renal adverse effects from CD.

A phase I study to evaluate the effect of high-dose CD on LD PK (Hayashi et al ., 2025) brought additional data. In previous non-clinical studies using rats, more than 3-fold prolongation of the LD t1/2 was achieved when combined with a high CD dose. This Phase I study aimed to evaluate the effects of high-dose CD on the PK of LD. The study was performed to examine the effects of a combination of LD, CD, and entacapone in healthy male volunteers. Levodopa and entacapone doses were set at approved dose levels. The CD dose ranged from the approved 10 mg-600 mg. In addition to plasma concentrations of LD, those of the metabolites were also determined to evaluate their inhibitory effects on LD-metabolising enzymes. The plasma concentrations of LD and its metabolites were monitored by LC/MS\\_MS up to 24 h after administration. The observed AEs were mild, and all participants completed the study. At higher CD doses, the area under the LD plasma concentration-time curve increased by approximately 2-fold, and the half-life of LD was slightly prolonged by &lt; 1.4-fold. These changes were much smaller than those observed in rats. The ratios of LD metabolites suggested that dopa deoxycarboxylase inhibition was saturated at a CD dose of 300 mg. In conclusion, higher CD doses were confirmed as tolerable, and the effect of CD on LD half-life limited.

While CD and its metabolites are eliminated renally and higher CD exposure is expected with IPX203, clinical data from Study IPX203-B16-01 showed low and comparable accumulation for CD after repeated dosing (accumulation ratio ~1.1 for both IPX203 and IR LD-CD), suggesting no meaningful build-up over 15 days in the studied population. The proposed SmPC approach (no dedicated data in renal impairment and recommendation for cautious use) was therefore considered acceptable by the CHMP. For transparency, it is stated that IPX203 has not been specifically studied in patients with renal impairment and that appropriate clinical monitoring during titration is recommended in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (and severe hepatic impairment).

## 5.2.2.8. Dose proportionality and time dependency

A dose proportionality study ( IPX203-B16-06 ) was conducted to assess the PK of LD and CD following single dose administration of IPX203 capsules (140-35 mg LD-CD, 210-52.5 mg LD-CD, 28070 mg LD-CD, and 350-87.5 mg LD-CD). For both LD and CD, a dose proportionality was observed in the dose range of IPX203 MR LD-CD 140-35 mg to IPX203 MR LD-CD 350-87.5 mg. The elimination pattern of both drugs was not modified with an increased dose.

Time dependency PK of both LD and CD were assessed in the phase 2 study IPX203-B16-01 . No time dependent PK were observed for both LD and CD following multiple dose administration of IPX203 in PD patients. Therefore, in SmPC section 5.2 'linearity', is reflected stating that Hopledo shows dose proportional pharmacokinetics for both carbidopa and levodopa over the levodopa dosage strength range of 140 mg to 350 mg.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.2.9. Pharmacokinetics in the target population

As already summarised in section 5.2.2.3, the PKs of LD and CD were studied in two Phase 2 studies following IPX203 administration as a single dose (Study IPX203-B14-02 ) and multiple therapeutic doses (Study IPX203-B16-01 ), in subjects with advanced PD.

## 5.2.2.10. Special populations

No dedicated renal or hepatic impairment studies were conducted following administration of IPX203.

However, the applicant provided an literature-based justification, supported by the known disposition of LD and CD, together with available experience with other LD/CD containing medicinal products already in the EU market, and the individualised titration approach used for this therapeutic class.

With regard to Hopledo administration in patients with hepatic impairment , it was justified accordingly that a clinically relevant impact on LD/CD exposure is not expected in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment, considering that LD and CD are not primarily dependent on hepatic microsomal metabolism and that LD is mainly metabolised through aromatic AADC and COMT pathways in peripheral tissues. The absence of dedicated PK data is likewise appropriately reflected in SmPC section 5.2, and the recommendation for caution in patients with severe hepatic impairment is considered adequate. Moreover, the applicant revised SmPC section 4.2, recommending caution on dose adjustment in patients with severe hepatic impairment, with appropriate clinical monitoring.

Concerning Hopledo administration in patients with renal impairment , the applicant clarified that unchanged LD represents only a minor component of urinary excretion and that renal elimination mainly concerns metabolites rather than parent LD. Of note, the available literature describes that, following a single 50 mg oral dose of  14 C-carbidopa in Parkinsonian patients, about 64% and 33% of the radioactivity were recovered in the urine and faeces, respectively, with a radioactivity amount of 32% in the 0-24-hour urine due to unchanged carbidopa. Three metabolites were identified in urine (2-methyl-3-methoxy-4-hydroxy-phenylpropionic acid, 2-methyl-3,4- dihydroxy-phenylpropionic acid, and 3-hydroxyα -methylphenylpropionic acid), and each accounted for approximately 10% of the radioactivity excreted in the urine. Therefore, renal excretion is not a major elimination pathway for CD. The applicant amended SmPC section 4.2, recommending caution on dose adjustment in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment, with appropriate clinical monitoring. Supportive information was provided from a population PK analysis performed with an extended-release LD/CD capsule formulation that combined IR and ER beads. This analysis suggested that renal impairment is unlikely to have a clinically significant effect on ER carbidopa-levodopa PK, given the minor contribution of estimated creatinine clearance to the variability in LD exposures. This is appropriately reflected in SmPC section 5.2.

## 5.2.2.11. Pharmacokinetic interaction studies

## 5.2.2.11.1. Special populations

Regarding the potential effects of gender, ethnics, and body weight in the pharmacokinetics of levodopa and carbidopa, no dedicated study was performed. Instead, in response to CHMP request, the applicant reviewed literature data accordingly.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Effect of gender

Sex has been recognised as an intrinsic factor contributing to the substantial interindividual variability of LD PK. In clinical studies conducted with ER LD-CD formulation (Numient/Rytary), plasma concentrations of LD were higher in women compared with men, in both healthy subjects and patients with Parkinson's disease (Mittur et al ., 2017). In healthy subjects, mean dose-normalised LD Cmax values were approximately 25% greater and AUC0-∞ values approximately 38% higher in females than in males, while in patients with PD, mean dose-normalized Cmax was 35% greater and AUC0-∞ was 37% higher in females than in males. Median tmax and t1/2 of LD were comparable in men and women for both healthy subjects and patients with PD (Mittur et al ., 2017).

Miyaue et al . concluded that sex influences LD PK but has little effect on CD (Miyaue et al ., 2025). In the study by Zappia et al ., women were significantly lighter in terms of body weight and had significantly greater AUC than men (Zappia et al ., 2002). Similar results were seen in other studies (Conti et al ., 2022), irrespective of age (Kumagai et al ., 2014). Among the underlying suggested mechanisms, sex-mediated differences in COMT activity and incorrectly normalizing body weight difference between men and women have been accounted for (Martinelli et al ., 2003; Chen et al , 2012a; Chen et al ., 2012b).

## Effect of body weight

In the study by Mittur et al . (2017), dose-normalised Cmax and AUC0-∞ of LD from ER LD-CD were negatively correlated with body weight in healthy subjects and patients with PD. No difference in tmax and t1/2 was observed between the weight groups (Mittur et al ., 2017). In the study by Adamiak-Giera et al ., body weight has been shown to impact Tlag; very short times correspond to patients with motor complications and times of order of 20 minutes were observed in patients without that impairment. The authors concluded that the higher Cmax, a large AUC0-∞ (p &lt; 0.01), a smaller V/F, and CL/F (p &lt; 0.01) seen in patients with motor fluctuations as compared to those without such fluctuations may be explained partly because the mean body weight of this group (68.2 ± 12.3 kg) was lower than that of patients without motor complications (88.7 ± 18.6 kg) (Adamiak-Giera et al ., 2021). The automatic model selection procedure selected neither age nor body weight as statistically significant covariates of the population model for V/F. The patient's age but not the weight proved to be one of predictors of k10 and, consequently, of the Cmax and AUC (Adamiak-Giera et al ., 2021).

## Effect of race

The majority of patients with PD in whom PK data were collected were white, therefore, very limited data are available regarding the LD PK across racial and ethnic groups. Studies on ER LD-CD (Rytary/Numient) found that in the healthy population, LD Cmax and AUC0-∞ values were 10-17% higher in Black versus White subjects. Median tmax and t1/2 were comparable in the two groups.

In summary, some literature data suggested LD bioavailability to be slightly higher in females than in males. However, there may be confounding factors such as body weight. No difference in tmax and t1/2 were reported between genders and different weight groups. Comparison data regarding PK of LD across racial and ethnic groups are scarce. Nevertheless, individual studies (cited above) conducted in different populations did not indicate any meaningful differences between races.

In summary, IPX203 dosing is individually titrated for patients, and such individualisation considers the differences between gender, race, and body weight. Therefore, the following text, included in SmPC section 5.2. was considered duly justified by the CHMP:

- There are no clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetic of levodopa or carbidopa based on gender, race, or body weight.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Effect of age

Elderly patients were well represented in the PK studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01, with more than half of participants aged 65 years or older and approximately 20% aged 75 years or older (see also section 5.3.3 of this AR).

In addition, the applicant described the impact of elderly in the PKs of both LD and CD within a review of literature data.

It is well-known that the incidence of PD is closely related to ageing. Ageing may influence PK factors following IR LD-CD administration in the elderly, where the PK of LD-CD was characterised by lower systemic clearance and higher bioavailability, leading to an increased AUC and Cmax (Robertson et al ., 1989). Other published studies demonstrated LD absorption to be consistent regardless of age. Increasing patient's age has been associated with a statistically significant, albeit clinically negligible, increase in LD t1/2 and a decrease in apparent oral clearance (Contin et al ., 1991). In a population PK model, Othman et al . showed that age almost reached significance for inclusion as a covariate for LD clearance but was not included in the final model (Othman and Dutta, 2014).

Some differences in PK parameters between age groups were reported for the ER LD-CD formulation by Mittur et al . (2017). Dose-normalised LD AUC0-∞ increased with increasing age in healthy subjects and patients with PD. Age accounted for approximately 4% and 15% of the variability in LD AUC0-∞ in healthy volunteers and patients with PD, respectively, and mean dose-normalised Cmax and AUC0-∞ were 27% and 52% higher, respectively, in PD patients older than 65 years of age compared with those younger than 50 years of age. However, the authors admitted that majority of patients with PD in whom PK data were available were significantly older than healthy subjects, whereas majority of healthy subjects were younger than 50 years of age.

For IPX203, Cmax and AUC0-∞ exposure for LD and CD were plotted using data from all Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies (as per the Figures below). Results indicated that LD and CD exposure are not influenced by the age of the patients.

Figure 5: Dose-normalised Cmax for LD and CD as a Function of Age

<!-- image -->

Figure 6: Dose-normalised AUC0-∞ for LD and CD as a Function of Age

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

<!-- image -->

In summary, the totality of evidence indicated no PK basis for dose adjustment of LD-CD products by age, particularly in the elderly. Therefore, as outlined in SmPC section 5.2, as the peak concentrations of LD and CD are generally similar between younger (45 to 60 years) and older (60 to 75 years) subjects, no dose adjustment is needed in the elderly. However, as discussed in the safety sections of this AR (and detailed in the SmPC), in patients aged 75 years and older experience serious AEs with IPX203. Consequently, these patients should be converted cautiously from IR LD/DDCI into IPX203. Close clinical monitoring is also recommended during the conversion period and subsequent dose optimisation, in line with standard clinical practice for older patients during dopaminergic therapy adjustments.

## 5.2.2.11.2. PK drug-drug interactions

No in vivo drug-drug interaction (DDI) studies were performed during the development of IPX203. However, in the absence of dedicated DDI studies literature data was supplied. Levodopa/Carbidopa derived from IPX203 is subjected to the same, known drug interactions that are common to other products containing LD/CD, as described in SmPC section 4.5.

## 5.2.2.11.3. Dose proportionality/time independence/accumulation

A dose proportionality study ( IPX203-B16-06 ) was conducted to assess the PK of LD and CD following single dose administration of IPX203 capsules (140-35 mg LD-CD, 210-52.5 mg LD-CD, 28070 mg LD-CD, and 350-87.5 mg LD-CD). For both LD and CD a dose proportionality was observed in the dose range of IPX203 MR LD-CD 140-35 mg to IPX203 MR LD-CD 350-87.5 mg. The elimination pattern of both drugs was not modified with an increased dose.

Time dependency PK of both LD and CD were assessed in the phase 2 study IPX203-B16-01 . No time dependent PK were observed for both LD and CD following IPX203 multiple dose administration in PD patients.

## 5.2.3. Pharmacodynamics

## 5.2.3.1. Mechanism of action

As already outlined in this assessment report (AR), LD is a precursor of dopamine (DA). When administered orally, it is rapidly decarboxylated to DA in extracerebral tissues so that only a small portion of a given dose is transported unchanged to the CNS. Carbidopa is a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that prevents metabolism of LD to DA in the peripheral circulation, ensuring that a higher proportion of the dose reaches the brain, where DA can act by restoring dopaminergic stimulation. This mechanism of action (MoA) is extensively documented in the literature.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.3.2. Primary and secondary pharmacology

## Primary pharmacodynamics

Primary PD was established throughout the measurement of effects on clinical scores of Parkinson's disease. Therefore, the PD endpoints used were concomitantly efficacy endpoints as well.

## Study IPX203-B14-02

The subject motor state assessment results demonstrated a 2.7-hour advantage in total 'OFF' time during IPX203 treatment compared with IR CD-LD treatment (p &lt; 0.0001) and a 0.9-hour advantage compared with Rytary (p = 0.023). During IPX203 treatment, this reduction in 'OFF' time was accompanied by increased in 'ON time' without troublesome dyskinesia (\"Good ON time\"), on average, 2.6 hours more than IR CD-LD and 0.9 hours more than Rytary (p &lt; 0.0001 and p = 0.0259, respectively).

The MDS-UPDRS Part III score results showed a similar pattern of effect in favour of IPX203. In the first 2 hours postdose, IPX203, Rytary, and IR CD-LD each exhibited rapid improvement in motor function. Starting at hour 3, both IPX203 and Rytary maintained significantly greater improvement in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores than did IR CD-LD, which lasted through Hour 5 with Rytary and through the last measurement at Hour 10 with IPX203. IPX203 had a longer duration of effect compared with IR CDLD (p &lt; 0.0001) and Rytary (p ≤ 0.0290), respectively, based on 4, 7, and 13-point improvements in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average predose value.

## Study IPX203-B16-01

With IPX203 treatment, subjects experienced less \"OFF time' as a percentage of their waking hours (mean 19.3% compared with 33.5% with IR CD-LD). In addition, subjects had more total \"Good ON Time' with IPX203 compared to IR CD-LD, whether measured out (of clinic) by the subject with a home diary or by the investigator in the clinic. The average durations of \"Good ON\" episodes or any \"ON\" episodes based on patient's diary entries were longer with IPX203 compared to IR CD-LD. Treatment with IPX203 was also associated with fewer motor fluctuations per day than IR CD-LD.

With IPX203, subjects were 73.3% less likely to receive rescue medication (Day 1) and 72.1% less likely to receive a re-dose (Day 15) than during IR CD-LD treatment.

Improvements in MDS-UPDRS Part III mean scores were greater for subjects receiving IPX203 than IR CD-LD from 3 to 8 hours postdose on Day 1, and from 2 to 4 hours post-dose on Day 15. On Day 15, when subjects had not had a study treatment for at least 5 hours, mean predose Part III scores were lower in IPX203-treated subjects.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that the results from the MDS-UPDRS Part III scores were much more relevant than for the MDS-UPDRS Part IV scores, both in terms of statistical and clinical significance.

It is unquestionable that MDS-UPDRS Part III remains the classical and well-established endpoint to demonstrate motor benefit, as stated in the EMA Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in the treatment of Parkinson's disease (EMA/CHMP/330418/2012 rev. 2). It is also unquestionable that MDS-UPDRS Part IV is not relevant for the assessment of dyskinesias, as also stated in this EMA guideline. Nevertheless, the purpose of the guideline is to guide in the clinical development of investigational products for the treatment of PD, which implies the assessment of their efficacy in treating the motor symptoms, aspect in which MDS-UPDRS Part III is considered the best score.

However, in the specific development of Hopledo, the efficacy of LD-CD in treating motor symptoms in PD had been already thoroughly established, while the main objective of the clinical development was to specifically demonstrate that this formulation shows improvements in motor fluctuations and treatment-related motor complications.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

While it can be agreed that measurement of 'OFF'-time or 'On-time' is the main efficacy variable, an operational definition of what will be considered an 'OFF' and 'ON' period should be established. It should be also clear to what extent 'On'-time with dyskinesia and 'On'-time without dyskinesia is increased. Patients changing from 'OFF' to 'ON' with dyskinesia should be asked whether they consider this an improvement or not, as per the EMA guideline above mentioned.

Taking this into consideration, the assessment of MDS-UPDRS Part IV added value in these particular development goals.

While for Part III results were consistently improved with IPX203, in several questions of Part IV that was not the case. Of note, the only statistical difference obtained (in questions) from MDS-UPDRS Part IV was outlined for question 4.3: 'Time spent in the OFF state'. However, in the analysis of 'change from baseline' the differences in the mean of change from baseline was 0.5 (+/-0.51). If considering the median, there was no difference. A reduction of approximately 1 hour/day of 'OFF' time is generally regarded as the minimal clinically important improvement.

There was a lack of correlation of the MDS-UPDRS Part III positive results with the absence of results in Part IV, specifically given the limited clinical relevance of the results in the time spent in the 'OFF state'. The applicant provided a largely acceptable methodological explanation for the discordance between MDS-UPDRS Part III and Part IV. However, this response was generally descriptive and partially evasive of the main issue raised in this question: whether the observed Part III improvements translated into clinically meaningful benefit in a formulation specifically intended to modify levodopa exposure and, therefore, motor complications.

It can be acknowledged that the short-duration Phase 2 studies were not designed to capture Part IV changes and that the general design is broadly consistent with the EMA Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in Parkinson's disease. Although the applicant's explanation is methodologically reasonable it is scientifically insufficient and the absence of correlation between Part III and Part IV remains a concern, not merely a design artefact. Overall, the response failed to address the central PD expectation that a modified-release levodopa formulation is specifically intended to smooth plasma concentrations and reduce motor complications, which in this case still lacks sufficient PK/PD translation. Nevertheless, the CHMP agreed not to pursue further this matter, as not impacting Hopledo overall benefit-risk profile.

## Secondary pharmacodynamics

Hopledo intendeds to provide a peak LD plasma concentration (Cmax) that does not exceed the exposures reached with other currently marketed formulations to treat PD. However, the CD Cmax following maximum dosing was expected to exceed that (of other currently marketed preparations).

QT prolongation effects were assessed in a supratherapeutic study with moxifloxacin as positive control. No significant ECG changes were detected, and C-QT analysis did not show any statistically significant relationship between CD and QTc.

In the course of the procedure the applicant was asked to provide the empirical distribution of clinical Cmax for CD (including the data from studies IPX203-B14-02, IPX203- B16-01 or pooled PK and fasting status) at the maximal per-dose 175 mg (per SmPC conversion), reported as the 50 th  and 95 th percentile (the median), and overlaid against the TQT 400 mg Cmax distribution.

In the TQT study with IPX203 ( study IPX203-102-23 ), 35 healthy subjects received IPX203, placebo and moxifloxacin in separate treatment periods using a 3-way crossover design. The primary objective was to evaluate the effect of a single supratherapeutic dose of CD (400 mg) on cardiac repolarisation relative to placebo in healthy adult subjects. CD at the studied concentrations did not have a relevant effect on heart rate and therefore, change-frombaseline QTcF (∆QTcF) was used as the primary endpoint. Carbidopa did not have an effect on the placebo-corrected, change-from-baseline QTc interval (∆∆QTcF) and an effect exceeding 10 ms could be excluded within the full range of observed range of plasma concentrations up to ∼ 3000 ng/mL.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Based on data from healthy subjects in studies IPX203-B16-04, IPX203-B16-05, and IPX203-B16-06, in which the highest studied CD dose was 70 to 87.5 mg, mean Cmax of a 175 mg dose could be estimated to levels between 740 and 1010 ng/mL, with a median value between 700 and 940 ng/mL and the 95 th  percentile between 1250 and 1710 ng/mL. It should be noted that these values were extrapolated from lower doses assuming PK linearity.

In the targeted patient population with advanced PD, PK data were available from 25 to 28 subjects in studies, IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01. In these studies, the highest studied CD dose was 67.5 mg. In this patient's population, mean Cmax of a 175 mg dose of CD could be estimated to levels between 570 to 650 ng/mL, with a median value between 540 and 595 ng/mL and 95 th  percentile between 990 and 1370 ng/mL (Day 15 in Study IPX203-B16-01, n= 27).

The Figure below displays the Goodness-of-fit plot of placebo-adjusted, change-from-baseline QTcF vs CD concentrations from the TQT study (Study IPX203-102-23).

Overall, the requested exposure-margin context for CD at the maximal per-dose level (175 mg), linked to the TQT exposure-QTc model provided by the applicant was considered adequate. The CHMP noted that, in the target PD population (Study IPX203-B16-01, Day 15), the estimated Cmax distribution for a 175 mg CD dose (mean 613 ng/mL; median 539 ng/mL; 95 th  percentile 1371 ng/mL) falls within the concentration range covered by the TQT study, where an effect &gt;10 ms was excluded across observed concentrations (up to 3000 ng/mL). Using the final concentration-QTc model, the predicted ΔΔ QTcF at mean/median/P95 clinical Cmax values is small (0.5-0.6 ms), and remains well below the regulatory threshold, supporting a low QT risk for CD.

While the 175 mg estimates were derived by extrapolation from lower CD doses assuming PK linearity, this was considered acceptable in the context of the clearly negative TQT results, the shallow (slightly negative) concentration-QTc slope, and the substantial exposure coverage provided by the TQT dataset.

However, because the achieved exposure margin versus the worst-case clinical Cmax was below the ICH E14 preference, in the course of the procedure, the applicant was also requested to demonstrate, using the final concentration-QTc model, that the predicted ΔΔ QTcF and its upper 90% CI remain &lt;10 ms up to the clinical 95th percentile Cmax from clinical studies. Thus, an exposure-QTc bridging assessment, using the final concentration-QTc model from study IPX203-102-23 and the observed clinical Cmax data from studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 , was submitted and it is summarised below.

In study IPX203-B14-02, where subjects with advanced PD were given a single dose of IPX203, mean Cmax (±SD) across all dose groups was 571 (400) ng/mL (n= 24). In the highest IPX203 dose group (202.5 mg; n= 5), mean Cmax was 1022 (615) ng/mL.

At steady state on Day 15 in study IPX203-B16-01, mean Cmax across all dose groups was 479 (291) ng/mL (n= 27) and in the highest dose group with a mean dose of 225 mg (n= 2), mean Cmax was 862 (9.2) ng/mL.

## 5.2.3.3. Pharmacodynamic interactions with other medicinal products or substances

The Applicant included relevant interactions in the SmPC, which overlap with those of other currently approved LD/CD-containing medicinal products.

## 5.2.3.4. Genetic differences in PD response

No genetic difference that can affect Hopledo PD response in a clinically significant way was foreseen.

## 5.2.3.5. Immunological events

Not applicable.

## 5.2.4. Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD)

## Pharmacodynamics

Study IPX203-B14-02 aimed to assess, amongst other objectives, the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of IPX203 single doses in subjects with advanced PD, using Rytary and IR CD-LD as references.

The initial rates of decrease in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline (corresponding to an improvement in motor symptoms) were comparable for all three treatments. However, the MDSUPDRS Part III score decrease(s) lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than following IR CD-LD or Rytary. Maximum decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline occurred at times that lagged behind the time of peak plasma concentrations of LD for the particular treatment.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Study IPX203-B16-01 intended to assess also PK/PD correlations in both single and multiple doses. In the single dose setting the initial decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline (corresponding to an improvement in motor symptoms) were comparable between the two treatments. However, decrements in the MDS-UPDRS Part III scores lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than following IR CD-LD treatment. Maximum decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline occurred at times that lagged behind the time of peak plasma concentrations of LD for this particular treatment.

In the multiple dose setting, at predose on Day 15, treatment with IPX203 showed a greater mean decrement (-9.3) in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores than did treatment with IR CD-LD (+0.1). As observed following the first dose on Day 1, a qualitative concordance was noted between the LD plasma concentration profile and changes in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. The initial rates of improvement in motor symptoms were comparable between the two treatments. However, improvements in the MDSUPDRS Part III scores lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than IR CD-LD, which may be associated with less frequent dosing of IPX203 than IR CD-LD.

Given the uncertainties on whether the improved duration of motor benefit with IPX203 was driven by higher total levodopa exposure (dose/AUC) or by a true pharmacokinetic advantage (PK profile, longer time above effective concentration or other), the applicant was asked to provide further data. Specifically, it was requested to provide a simple exposure-matched comparison (IPX203 vs IR at comparable LD AUC ₀ - τ or comparable total daily LD dose), presenting key clinical outcomes (e.g., Area Under the Effect Curve [AUEC] of Δ MDS-UPDRS III, time in 'Good ON' / time to rescue or second dose, and dyskinesia-related tolerability if available).

The applicant submitted accordingly an exposure-response analysis using data from Studies IPX203B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01. Individual Cmax, AUC, time above the proposed LD efficacy threshold of 750 ng/mL, and AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS Part III were assessed and presented by treatment. The applicant explained that a fully exposure-matched comparison is difficult, because IPX203-B14-02 was a single-dose study and IPX203-B16-01 included multiple-dose treatment with individual dose adjustments and limited PK/PD sampling. This limitation was acknowledged and considered acceptable by CHMP. Study IPX203-B16-01 was designed to compare plasma exposure and anti-parkinsonian efficacy following Sinemet IR or IPX203 administration. Efficacy data were only recorded during PK days after the first dose until rescue in study IPX203-B14-02. From the 24 PK completers, during IR treatment 11 subjects took rescue administration at less than 6 hours. To avoid exposure and efficacy readings due to unscheduled rescue dose administration, only IPX203-B14-02 PK-PD data were evaluated for data readings limited to the period post-dose until rescue. However, this data set was the cleanest available as all dose (exposure) responses were associated with a single dose administration.

The administration regimen on day 15 in study IPX203-B16-01 did, however, better reflect the typical clinical use. On day 15, PK sampling and MDS-UPDRS part III scores were performed over 10 hours during which dose amounts, frequency, and intervals were different from individual to individual.

## Plasma exposure data compilation

For both studies, Cmax and AUC values were extracted from the respective study analysis data model (AdAM) database. Time above threshold was calculated from each individual's LD exposure data. To assure better precision before evaluating the time above threshold periods, LD exposure profiles were enriched with additional time-concentration data. This was done by interpolating concentration at time t (Ct) levels for time points in-between measured values in a step size of 0.05 hours.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## MDS-UPDRS part III data compilation

Data of Δ MDS-UPDRS part III scores were extracted from the AdAM data base of IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 recordings. Using these data, AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS part III scores were compiled for each individual over the period from dose administration until rescue medication for study IPX203-B1402 and over 10 hours for study IPX203-B16-01.

## PK-PD relations

All data sets (time above 750 ng/mL threshold, Cmax, AUC, and AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS part III scores) were combined by subject and treatment and used for the evaluation of PK-PD relations. The Figure below shows the correlation of LD Cmax with efficacy expressed as AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS part III scores. Treatment results with Sinemet IR plotted as orange and those with IPX203 as green dots.

In this representation, it is evident that Sinemet IR and IPX203 data sets separate. Most of Sinemet IR AUC exposure is located in the left lower quadrant of the plot (blue dots). Due to IPX203 formulation design and conversion requirements, there is limited overlap in AUC exposure (green dots in lower left quadrant). <div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Figure 10: Correlation of time&gt;750 ng/mL with AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS part III scores

## IPX203 vs IR, n=24

<!-- image -->

As derived from the AUC vs AUEC plots, also in this comparison Sinemet IR results reside in the lower left quadrant for study IPX203-B14-02 (single dose). All but one Sinemet IR administrations result in limited times above efficacy threshold (left lower quadrant, &lt;4h). In both study reports it was already documented that Δ MDS-UPDRS part III changes from baseline had a significantly longer duration of effect (from 2 to up to 10 hours) compared with Sinemet IR (p &lt; 0.0001).

Due to multiple dosing on day 15 in study IPX-B16-01, time above threshold following Sinemet IR or IPX203 administration is no longer clustered. However, these were achieved with mean periods between daily doses of 7 hours (IPX203) versus 4 hours (Sinemet IR), thus, with fewer LD plasma level fluctuations when using IPX203. Moreover, as in IPX203-B14-02 best efficacy linked to longer periods above threshold is nearly exclusively seen following IPX203 administration.

It is difficult to identify a clear driver of efficacy, AUC or time above efficacy threshold are however potential candidates. In particular this is challenging for time above efficacy threshold in the multiple dosing situation on day 15 in study IPX203-B16-01. What is obvious is that IPX203 administration results in higher efficacy whatever comparison is used. Only IPX203 reaches maximum efficacy levels (AUEC). In general, equivalent Cmax and AUC exposures result in similar efficacy regardless of whether administered as Sinemet IR or IPX203. Thus, the concept of the new IPX203 design to provide sustained LD supply over a longer period of time was achieved by delivering more LD amount from an extended-release component. These higher LD amounts leaded to an augmented AUC (=D/CL) and similarly longer time above efficacy threshold while limiting peak dose levels efficiently.

As seen in IPX203-B14-02, TEAEs did not seem to be related to Cmax or AUC exposure. These events were similar in number and type for both treatment arms and were basically observed over the entire Cmax and AUC range determined.

In summary, the provided analyses suggested that Cmax alone is not the main driver of the longer motor benefit with IPX203, as Cmax values overlap between IPX203 and IR. Higher AUC and longer time above the efficacy threshold seemed to be more relevant for the sustained response. This is consistent

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

with the formulation concept of IPX203, where additional LD is delivered from the extended-release (ER) component, leading to higher overall exposure and longer time above an effective concentration.

The applicant also noted that, where similar Cmax or AUC values were observed, clinical efficacy was generally similar between IR and IPX203. Higher AUEC values of Δ MDS-UPDRS Part III and longer duration of effect were mainly observed with IPX203, which is consistent with the longer time above threshold.

In conclusion, presented data supported the notion that the prolonged clinical benefit of IPX203 is driven mainly by higher total LD exposure and longer time above an effective LD concentration, rather than by higher Cmax.

## 5.2.5. Dose selection and therapeutic window

The selection of doses for IPX203 and Rytary (LD/CD formulated in an ER capsule) was primarily based on achieving peak LD plasma concentrations within ±20% of those resulting from the corresponding doses of IR LD-CD. This approach aimed to ensure comparable peak exposure while minimising potential side effects.

Studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 provided key PK insights:

- The mean Cmax (maximum concentration) and AUC0∞ (area under the curve from time zero to infinity) values of LD increased in an approximately dose-proportional manner with the LD dose following IPX203 and Rytary administration.
- For IPX203, doses of 270 to 360 mg were estimated to provide peak LD concentrations comparable to those of 100 mg LD from IR LD-CD, based on previous PK data.
- The dose-proportional increase in LD Cmax and AUC0∞ was consistent across the dose range of 360 mg to 900 mg studied in the trials, indicating predictable PK.

The typical IPX203 dosing regimen was three times a day, approximately every 7 to 8 hours, allowing for adjustments during the first 9 days of each treatment period to optimise efficacy, tolerability, and safety.

The ability to adjust dosing frequency and amount enabled personalised treatment regimens, aiming to minimise \"OFF\" time and dopaminergic side effects.

IPX203 demonstrated a lower degree of peak-to-trough fluctuation in plasma LD concentrations and was associated with less frequent dosing compared to IR LD-CD.

The PK profile of IPX203 showed low accumulation and predictable PK following multiple doses, supporting its use as a therapeutic option with potentially favorable dosing profile.

The estimated comparable doses of IPX203 to IR LD-CD (e.g., 280-370 mg IPX203 to 100-250 mg IR LD-CD) provided a preliminary basis to shift patients from IR LD-CD to IPX203, with the aim of maintaining therapeutic efficacy while potentially reducing side effects associated with peak-to-trough fluctuations.

The applicant proposed a conversion table from IR formulations to IPX203. Although, the general concept of such conversion table could be understandable, some clarifications were required in the course of the procedure. This table appeared to prioritise Cmax matching (100 mg IR → 280 mg IPX203), which results in a ~2.7-fold AUC increase at that dose level. In addition, the applicant proposed two split rules (&lt; 500 mg/day vs ≥ 500 mg/day IR). Such calculation seemed to give a large difference in doses in patients which at the beginning used very similar LD IR doses. Based on Study IPX203-B16-05 , the dose-normalised exposure of levodopa with IPX203 was essentially equivalent to IR (GMR AUC about 1.0 per mg) with a lower Cmax. Therefore, a systematic increase of total daily LD at switch seemed not fully supported pharmacokinetically. Such increases seemed also not fully justified by other PK results.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Two hypothetical cases illustrate that, according to the rules in the table, the total daily dose of LD would increase markedly in patients that at the beginning used very similar LD IR doses:

- Case 1: LD 100-200-200-100 mg (Total LD 600 mg). Table → LD 560 mg TID = 1680 mg/day (+180% LD), with CD 420 mg/day.
- Case 2: LD 100-200-100-100 mg (Total LD 500 mg). Table → LD 280 mg TID = 840 mg/day (+68% LD), with CD 210 mg/day.

The Applicant was asked to revise the conversion algorithm to better anchor on total daily IR LD (±10%) with explicit BID/TID splits and rounding rules to available strengths, and to provide PK/PD simulations comparing IR baseline vs proposed IPX203 regimens for AUC, Cmax, time-above threshold, and expected 'ON-time'.

Therefore, it explained accurately the rationale for a conversion approach based on the most frequent single IR LD dose (using a 2.8× factor aimed at LD C max matching) and referred to supportive Phase 3 data from study IPX203-B16-02 (RISE-PD). The illustrative concentration-time plots (see below) for the two hypothetical cases were helpful to understand the intended concept.

The conversion from IR LD to IPX203 was based on the most frequent single daily IR LD dose rather than the total daily dose (TDD) because IPX203 is designed to extend the effect of each individual dose over a longer period, maintaining therapeutic plasma levels with fewer administrations. In other words, IPX203's PK are structured around how a single dose is absorbed and sustained, not how multiple IR doses accumulate across the day. IPX203 rapidly achieves therapeutic plasma concentrations and then maintains them for a longer duration compared to IR LD, with less peak-to-trough fluctuation. Because of this, each IPX203 dose is intended to replace multiple IR LD doses spread throughout the day.

At the end of the Phase 3 IPX203-B16-02 (RISE-PD) study, the mean ratio of TDD of IPX203 to IR LD was 1.79, and the mean ratio of the most frequently administered single dose of IPX203 to the most common single dose of IR LD was 2.8 (median).

These differences are attributable to two key factors:

- Slightly lower bioavailability of IPX203 vs . IR LD-CD, ranging from 88% to 99% based on AUC data
- The need for a higher amount of LD required to compensate for the PK troughs associated with IR LD-CD and thereby maintain a smoother clinical response

When converting patients with motor fluctuations from IR LD-CD to IPX203, the primary objective is to match the LD Cmax to preserve anti-Parkinsonian efficacy during the 'ON time' while avoiding an increase in dyskinesia. IPX203 was designed to match the peak of the most frequent IR dose, which is expected to be the dose with the optimal benefit-risk ratio for that patient. Less frequent adjustments with higher or lower doses are typically used to tailor daily LD administration to individual needs. For example, a higher dose in the morning may compensate for reduced levels after overnight fasting, while a lower dose in the evening can better match the naturally lower dopamine requirements during night-time.

Since the Cmax of IPX203 is approximately 38% of the Cmax achieved with IR LD-CD, it is recommended that the LD content of IPX203 be increased by a factor of approximately 2.8 relative to the corresponding IR LD dose.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Clinical recommendations suggested multiplying the most frequent IR LD dose by 2.8 to determine the starting IPX203 dose. This strategy ensured that the MR capsule provides sufficient LD to cover the time interval during which the patient would typically require multiple IR doses.

Conversely, the total daily IR LD intake reflects multiple short-acting doses, each with its own absorption and wearing-off pattern. If conversion is based on the TDD, it could lead to overdosing or under-dosing because IPX203 does not mimic the cumulative peaks of IR LD-it smooths them out into a prolonged exposure. The most frequent single IR dose better represents the patient's 'effective unit' of therapy, which IPX203 is designed to extend.

The plot in the Figure below shows LD dosing, LD plasma exposure, MDS-UPDRS Part III response, and motor states for a typical IPX203-B16-01 study participant.

Patients switched from IR LD to IPX203 experienced a longer 'Good ON time' per dose, with fewer daily administrations. This was also confirmed based on Phase 3 data suggesting a conversion factor of 2.8 as the most appropriate.

This validated that matching IPX203 to the most frequent single IR LD dose provided consistent symptom control without requiring the same total daily milligram amount.

The primary concern might be the patient safety, specifically the risk of AEs associated with potentially excessive LD peak exposure, especially in patients who were previously controlled on lower doses of IR LD-CD, such as &lt;500 mg.

Since the 2.8 conversion ratio for the individual IPX203 dose (100 mg IR LD converting to 280 mg IPX203) had been already established to ensure patients experienced an 'ON time' comparable to their previous IR LD-CD regimen, the only remaining variable to control the total daily LD exposure was the dosing frequency, giving the drug less frequently.

In the applicant's view, the twice-per-day dosing recommendation for patients on IR LD-CD doses &lt;500 mg would provide a more controlled and gradual approach to dose titration, prioritising patient's safety while still aiming for effective symptom control.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

While it is important to recognise that the 2.8x conversion factor from study IPX203-B16-02 (RISE-PD) provides a useful starting point , in real-world practice, IPX203 conversion and dose optimisation would often require an individualised approach, including adjustments to dosing frequency and intervals. Clinicians may also consider a lower starting dose or reduced dosing frequency based on concomitant PD therapies and should ensure closer monitoring during titration. Finally, also important to note that in the RISE-PD study, more than half of the patients required no further dose adjustments as the 2.8× conversion factor immediately provided them with an optimal IPX203 dose.

Even when using the highest amount of IPX203 (Case 1, green line) also in case 2, peak LD concentrations are still in the same range as for both Cases of Sinemet IR doses used at study entry. Hence, peak-dose related side effects would have already been registered on Sinemet IR dosing. In addition, initial IPX203 doses determined by conversion are subject to optimisation (i.e., reduction and increase for case 1 and case 2, respectively). Furthermore, doubling of AUC when using IPX203 (case 2 vs case 1) was noted as rather advantageous because it leads to an augmented risk-benefit ratio by keeping LD plasma concentrations inside the therapeutic window for longer, even at reduced administration frequency.

The assessor considered the illustrative concentration-time plots for the two hypothetical case above discussed helpful to understand the intended concept.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

However, the applicant's response did not resolve the concerns raised. In particular, the proposed split at 500 mg/day combined with a single-dose based algorithm could result in disproportionate differences in the starting IPX203 total daily dose for patients with similar baseline IR regimens (as illustrated by Case 1 versus Case 2). Moreover, patients receiving the same baseline IR total daily LD dose but using different IR dosing patterns may still be assigned materially different starting IPX203 doses, which indicates limited algorithm stability around the 500 mg/day cut-off. The statement that this is 'only a starting dose', in the assessor's view, did not mitigate the clinical relevance during the switch period.

In addition, the applicant did not provide requested quantitative outputs to support the conversion approach. Thus, it was required to further revise and justify the proposed IR-to- IPX203 conversion algorithm, while retaining the 2.8× unit -dose conversion factor as a starting principle, it was needed to (re)assess the 500 mg/day cut-off and the associated BID/TID split to avoid disproportionate differences in starting total daily LD after switch.

Within a more complete justification of the proposed IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm, additional clinical evidence, quantitative PK simulations for the illustrative cases, and one additional example, with the same IR TDD, were supplied. The applicant also proposed a targeted mitigation at the upper end of the conversion range, allowing initiation with the next lower available capsule strength for patients with a most frequent IR LD dose of 200 mg or higher.

In addition, it explained that the conversion algorithm is intended as an initial dosing recommendation, followed by individual titration based on efficacy and tolerability. This is clinically relevant, as dose adjustment is expected in advanced PD.

Of note, since the initial submission, in the course of the procedure the applicant supplied new, relevant interim data from a Phase 4 RWE study conducted in the US, (ELEVATE-PD study interim analysis with 111 patients), evaluating the performance of the IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm in routine clinical practice. This provided useful reassurance that the 2.8× unit -dose conversion can be used in routine clinical practice, with a median of one titration step after conversion. The combined Phase 3 and 4 data supported BID initiation in patients receiving &lt;500 mg/day IR LD, with maintained clinical benefit and no new safety concern.

The simulations for the proposed cases showed that large nominal increases in total daily LD do not necessarily lead to excessive Cmax. They also suggest that IPX203 provides more sustained exposure above the proposed efficacy threshold and less fragmented exposure compared with IR. Importantly, in higher-dose scenarios, the proposed lower-dose starting option reduces Cmax and total exposure, while maintaining predicted 'ON time'. This addressed the main concern that the original algorithm could lead to excessive exposure in some patients after switch.

The applicant also proposed a revised SmPC wording for the conversion algorithm, which keeps the 2.8-fold conversion principle, but it allows starting with the next lower strength when the most frequent IR LD dose is 200 mg or higher. The recommendation for FU after 1 to 3 days, and further dose or dosing-frequency adjustment, based on individual response, is also clinically relevant and supports safe use during conversion.

Overall, some uncertainty would remain because the simulations are model-based and the proposed efficacy threshold may vary between patients. In addition, patients with the same IR TDD but different IR dose patterns may still receive different nominal IPX203 TDD after conversion. However, the applicant's explanation was considered acceptable in the context of the initial nature of the conversion algorithm, the need for later individual titration, supportive Phase 3/4 data, and the proposed mitigation option proposed for the upper conversion range.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

With regard to the apparent discrepancy between the maximum dose suggested by the conversion table, i.e., 700 mg LD three times daily corresponding to 2100 mg LD/day, and the previously proposed maximum daily dose of 2380/595 mg LD/CD, as mentioned above, the conversion algorithm is intended to define the initial conversion dose only, and that such (initial) conversion should not exceed 2100 mg LD/day, administered as 700 mg three times daily. Therefore, in SmPC section 4.2, the higher value of mg LD/CD is presented as a maximum daily dose not to be exceeded after subsequent individualised titration, based on clinical response and tolerability.
