The applicant acknowledged that, in the clinical programme, the exposure to doses at or above 2380/595 mg of LD/CD was limited, and that robust patient-level dose-history analyses, focused safety analyses and formal exposure-response assessments at this dose level would not provide reliable or clinically meaningful conclusions. This limitation is acceptable in the context of the agreed SmPC wording, where the dose of 2380/595 mg is presented only as an upper limit for selected patients after titration.

The agreed text in (SmPC) sections 4.2 and 4.4 likewise detailed the limited clinical experience with the total daily Hopledo doses above 2100 mg of levodopa, recommending that care should be exercised when considering further dose increases, and that patients receiving higher doses should be monitored closely for dopaminergic adverse reactions, including orthostatic hypotension, syncope, falls and dyskinesia. Also, of note, the total daily dose (TDD) can be divided up to four doses per day (QID).

## 5.2.6. Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical pharmacology

## 5.2.6.1. Discussion

The PK of IPX203 have been characterised in three Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (Study IPX203-B16-04 , IPX203-B16-05 and IPX203-B16-06 ) and two Phase 2 studies in patients with advanced PD receiving single (Study IPX203-B14-02 ) and multiple therapeutic doses (Study IPX203-B16-01 ). Although the Phase 2 studies used non-to-be-marketed (non-TBM) strengths of LD-CD (180-45 and 270-67.5 mg), the applicant bridged accordingly to the TBM LD-CD capsule strengths (140-35, 210-52.5, 280-70 and 350-87.5 mg) throughout a dedicated dose-proportionality study and food-effect data, demonstrating dose-normal linear PKs for both LD and CD across the commercial range and time-invariant PK under multiple dosing. Of note: the Phase 3 pivotal trial employed the TBM capsule strengths.

In terms of absorption , across studies, IPX203 achieved a profile consistent with a typical MR formulation: the median LD Tmax was delayed relative to the IR comparator, and concentrations were sustained longer, while the initial rise attributable to the IR fraction was preserved. Collectively, the findings summarised in previous sections of this AR showed a smoother, longer-lasting LD exposure

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

with reduced peak-to-trough fluctuation. Furthermore, adequate CD bioavailability was also demonstrated with the proposed MR formulation. Greater CD bioavailability with the proposed MR formulation was also confirmed.

Study IPX203-B16-04 assessed the food effect on IPX203 PK. In healthy volunteers, a high-fat meal delayed LD absorption and increased exposure. Sprinkling on apple sauce gave exposure close to fasted yet remained bioequivalent for LD under standard 80-125% bounds. Half-life was similar across arms. In contrast, CD exhibited a pronounced negative food effect (~64% lower exposure and a later Tmax), whereas sprinkling yielded AUCs close to fasted with a modestly lower Cmax (about 1015% lower) with similar half-life. These data supported the proposed label statements about administration with or without food, recognising that a high-fat (or high-calorie) meal may delay/slow down LD absorption by ~2 h (as reflected by a substantially later Tmax and marked reduction in early systemic exposure compared with the fasted state, while the overall exposure is not reduced and shifted to later time intervals), and acceptability of sprinkling on apple sauce, with appropriate instructions. The distribution of LD and CD was not studied. Instead, the applicant supplied literature data. Levodopa is bound to plasma proteins in the range of 10-30%, while CD at approximately 36%. Levodopa and CD distribution parameters were also not investigated, as well described in the literature.

Across the clinical programme study IPX203-B16-04, IPX203-B16-05, IPX203 - B16-06), LD and CD elimination was consistent and similar to IR/CR comparators.

Metabolism was not investigated, as the pathways for LD and CD are well established in the literature. The PK of 3-OMD, the major metabolite of LD was likewise not investigated. Instead, literature data was supplied by the applicant. The to-be-marketed (TBM) LD-CD formulations range (LD-CD 140-35 to 350-87.5 mg) showed dose proportionality, with no change in elimination behaviour. Bioequivalence was demonstrated between US and Taiwan-manufactured batches (140-35 mg), supporting manufacturing flexibility and predictable dose-scaling. Across the tested strengths, IPX203 showed approximate dose proportionality under fasting conditions.

Study IPX203-B16-01 demonstrated that results were consistent with a modified-release profile: later Tmax, a flatter peak, and longer maintenance of LD within a dosing interval. Time above predefined concentrations and the fluctuation index favoured IPX203). However, some issues initially limited data interpretation and the proposed conversion scheme. In this study the first post-dose sample was at 0.5 h; therefore, for IR LD-CD Tmax was censored at 0.5 h and IR Cmax seemed likely underestimated.

Nevertheless, the applicant provided a model-based sensitivity analysis to confirm if the first sampling time at 0.5 h was sufficient to capture the true IR LD Cmax in studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B1601. The analysis used individual one-compartment PK fits and different absorption rate constants (ka). The predicted Tmax values were close to the first sampling time, mainly around 0.44-0.78 h, and predicted Cmax values for plausible ka values were within about ±10% of the reference estimate. Therefore, a clinically relevant underestimation of IR Cmax due to the 0.5 h first sample was noted as unlikely. The applicant also provided early exposure metrics, including AUC0-0.5h, AUC0-1h, and AUC02h, dose-normalised to 100 mg LD. These results were broadly similar between studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01, supporting the exposure assessment.

In summary, the 0.5 h first sampling time is acceptable for estimation of IR Cmax, and any possible underestimation is unlikely to have a major impact on the 2.8× conversion factor, confirmed as derived using Cmax matching approach.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In addition, a plausible clinical rationale for the IR-only delivery of carbidopa in IPX203 was submitted, together with a demonstrated higher CD exposure versus IR LD-CD, consistent with the higher CD dose, and low accumulation after repeat dosing.

The non-clinical margin based on the 1year rhesus monkey NOAEL (≥135 mg/kg/day), corresponding to an estimated 4.4-fold margin over the proposed maximal daily CD dose (595 mg/day), can likewise be considered acceptable in the context of absence of toxicological findings at high chronic doses in primates, and lack of clinically relevant QTc effects at supratherapeutic CD exposure.

Moreover, the applicant confirmed that the clinically relevant published levodopa threshold for onset of effect is approximately 1000 ng/mL.

The pharmacokinetics in the target population were investigated in IPX203-B14-02, a single-dose study in patients with advanced PD. The study results were generally consistent with what may be expected for a modified-release LD/CD: later Tmax, a flatter peak, and longer maintenance of LD than IR. Time above 50% Cmax was longer with IPX203 than IR (4.7 h vs 1.9 h) and numerically longer than Rytary, an ER LD-CD formulation (3.9 h). Carbidopa exposure with IPX203 was several-fold higher than IR, as anticipated from the higher CD dose. Across dose levels, the reported 'bioavailability vs IR' for LD with IPX203 was roughly comparable to IR (about 80-109%), suggesting that per-mg exposure is similar.

Levodopa has an individual therapeutic window , and the dose must be titrated to clinical response (adequate motor control without troublesome dyskinesia). Carbidopa has no independent symptomatic effect: it is administered to ensure sufficient peripheral AADC inhibition. Within the IPX203 programme, differences between regimens were driven by absorption; elimination was unchanged. On this basis, plasma targets are not considered, and dosing is guided by effect and tolerability.

The concerns raised in the course of the procedure regarding IR LD/CD to Hopledo conversion algorithm were adequately addressed. The applicant clarified that the proposed conversion table defines only the initial conversion dose, which should not exceed 2100 mg levodopa per day, administered as 700 mg TID. The higher dose of 2380/595 mg LD/CD is not intended as a routine recommended conversion dose, but as a maximum daily dose not to be exceeded, after individualised titration according to clinical response and tolerability. Although clinical experience at doses at or above 2380/595 mg is limited and does not allow robust exposure-response or focused safety conclusions, this approach was considered acceptable, supported by detailed SmPC wording. Sections 4.2 and 4.4 clearly distinguish initial conversion from subsequent titration, state that experience above 2100 mg/day is limited, and recommend close monitoring for dopaminergic ADRs, including orthostatic hypotension, syncope, falls and dyskinesia.  Also, of note, the TDD can be divided up to QID.

Concerning multiple-dose behaviour under steady dosing in patients, IPX203 reduced LD fluctuation over 10 h (≈1.7 vs 2.7 with IR), extended time above 50% C max  (6.2 h vs 3.9 h) and above 430 ng/mL (9.0 h vs 7.4 h), and showed minimal accumulation for both LD and CD (≈1.0 -1.1), confirming time-invariant PK at therapeutic use.

Looking at special populations , no dedicated renal or hepatic impairment studies have been conducted. Instead, the applicant's literature-based justification is considered generally acceptable from a PK perspective, given the known disposition of LD and CD, the clinical experience with other LD/CD-containing medicinal products, and the individualised titration approach to be used in clinical practice.

In addition, the applicant justified that a clinically relevant impact on LD/CD exposure is not expected in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment , since neither LD nor CD is primarily dependent on hepatic microsomal metabolism, and levodopa is mainly metabolised through peripheral AADC and COMT pathways. The absence of dedicated PK data is adequately reflected in SmPC sections 4,2 and 5.2, where caution on dose adjustment and appropriate clinical monitoring is recommended.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In relation to renal impairment , unchanged levodopa represents only a minor component of urinary excretion and renal elimination mainly concerns metabolites rather than parent LD. In addition, available literature describes that, following a single 50 mg oral dose of 14C-carbidopa in Parkinsonian patients, about 64% and 33% of the radioactivity are recovered in urine and faeces, respectively, with a radioactivity amount of 32% in the 0-24-hour urine due to unchanged carbidopa. Three metabolites were identified in the urine, and each accounted for approximately 10% of the radioactivity excreted. Therefore, renal excretion is not a major elimination pathway for carbidopa.

The applicant revised adequately SmPC section 4.2and 5.2 r, detailing that PK of Hopledo in subjects with renal impairment have not been established, and recommending caution on dose adjustment in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment, with appropriate clinical monitoring.

No PK interaction studies have been performed as LD/CD interactions are also well described in the literature.

Overall, for a full-mixed (Article 8(3) application, characterisation of distribution and elimination is limited. No mass-balance study , no popPK , no dedicated protein-binding or in vitro and in vivo metabolite PK assessments and no dedicated DDI and renal or hepatic impairment studies have been conducted. However, the Applicant presented adequate literature data supporting the proposed SmPC wording in sections 4.2, 4.5 and 5.2.

Primary pharmacodynamics were established through measurement of effects on clinical scores of Parkinson's disease. Therefore, the PD endpoints used were concomitantly efficacy endpoints. Levodopa mechanism of action is well known and sufficiently described in the literature.  In study IPX203-B14-02 the subject motor state assessment results demonstrated a 2.7-hour advantage in total 'OFF' time during IPX203 treatment compared with IR CD-LD treatment (p &lt; 0.0001) and a 0.9-hour advantage compared with Rytary (p = 0.023). During IPX203 treatment, this reduction in 'OFF' time was accompanied by increased 'ON time' without troublesome dyskinesia (\"Good ON time\"), on average 2.6 hours more than IR CD-LD, and 0.9 hours more than Rytary (p &lt; 0.0001 and p = 0.0259, respectively).

The MDS-UPDRS Part III score results showed a similar pattern of effect in favour of IPX203.

In study IPX203-B16-01 , subjects receiving IPX203 experienced significantly less \"OFF\" time as a percentage of their waking hours (mean 19.3% compared with 33.5% with IR CD-LD). In addition, they had more total \"Good ON time' with IPX203 compared with IR CD-LD, whether measured out of clinic by the subject himself (with a home diary) or by the investigator in the clinic. The average durations of \"Good ON\" episodes or any \"ON\" episodes based on patient's diary entries were longer with IPX203, in comparison to IR CD-LD. Treatment with IPX203 was also associated with fewer motor fluctuations per day than IR CD-LD.

Subjects on IPX203 treatment were 73.3% less likely to receive rescue medication (at Day 1), and 72.1% less likely to receive a re-dose (at Day 15) in comparison to those on IR CD-LD treatment.

Improvements in MDS-UPDRS Part III mean scores were greater for subjects receiving IPX203 than IR CD-LD, from 3 to 8 hours postdose on Day 1, and from 2 to 4 hours postdose on Day 15. On Day 15, when subjects had not had a study treatment for at least 5 hours, mean predose Part III scores were significantly lower in IPX203-treated subjects.

The results from the MDS-UPDRS Part III scores were more relevant than for the MDS-UPDRS Part IV scores, both in terms of statistical and clinical significance. It is unquestionable that MDS-UPDRS Part III remains the classical and well-established endpoint to demonstrate motor benefit, as stated in the EMA 'Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in the treatment of Parkinson's disease'.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

However, in the specific development of Hopledo, the efficacy of LD-CD fixed-dose combination in treating motor symptoms in PD had been already thoroughly established, while the main objective was to specifically establish that this formulation shows improvements in motor fluctuations and treatment-related motor complications.

While it can be agreed that measurement of 'OFF time' or 'ON time' is the main efficacy variable, an operational definition of what will be considered an 'OFF' and 'ON' period should be established. It should be also clear to what extent 'ON time' with dyskinesia and 'ON time' without dyskinesia is increased. Patients changing from 'OFF' to 'ON' with dyskinesia should be asked whether they consider this an improvement or not, as per the EMA guideline already mentioned. Taking this into consideration, the assessment of MDS-UPDRS Part IV added value in these particular development goals.

While for Part III results were 'consistently improved' with IPX203, in several questions of Part IV that was not the case. The only statistical difference obtained in (questions from) MDS-UPDRS Part IV was for question 4.3 'Time spent in the OFF state'. However, in the analysis of 'change from baseline' the differences in the mean of change from baseline was 0.5 (+/-0.51). If considering the median, there was no difference. A reduction of approximately 1 hour/day of 'OFF time' is generally regarded as the minimal clinically important improvement.

Even though MDS-UPDRS Part III remains the classical and well-established endpoint to demonstrate motor benefit in assessing an effect on PD, while assessing new formulations of levodopa/carbidopa the measurement of Part IV gains an added usefulness by assessing therapy induced motor complications.

There was a lack of correlation of the MDS-UPDRS Part III positive results with the absence of results in Part IV, specifically given the limited clinical relevance of the results in the 'time spent in the OFF state'. The applicant provided a largely acceptable methodological explanation for the discordance between MDS-UPDRS Part III and Part IV. However, this response was generally descriptive and partially evasive of the main issue raised in this question: whether the observed Part III improvements translated into clinically meaningful benefit in a formulation specifically intended to modify levodopa exposure and, therefore, motor complications.

It can be acknowledged that the short-duration Phase 2 studies were not designed to capture Part IV changes and that the general design is broadly consistent with the EMA Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in Parkinson's disease. Although the applicant's explanation is methodologically reasonable, it is scientifically insufficient, and the absence of correlation between Part III and Part IV remains a concern, not merely a design artefact. In summary the applicant's response failed to address the central pharmacodynamic expectation that a modified-release levodopa formulation is specifically intended to smooth plasma concentrations and reduce motor complications, which in this case still lacks sufficient PK/PD translation. Nevertheless, the CHMP agreed not to pursue this matter further, as it does not impact IPX203 overall benefit-risk profile. Looking at IPX203 secondary pharmacodynamics , attention was paid to the peak LD plasma concentration (Cmax) and the effects of carbidopa (CD) on cardiac repolarization (QTc) and other ECG parameters.

Study IPX203-B16-01 was designed to assess the effects of supratherapeutic doses/exposures of CD on QTc and other ECG parameters, using moxifloxacin as a positive control. The results showed no significant ECG changes, and the concentration-QT (C-QT) analysis did not reveal any statistically significant relationship between carbidopa and QTc.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Due to the achieved exposure margin versus the worst-case clinical Cmax being below the ICH E14 preference, an exposure-QTc bridging assessment was conducted using the final concentration-QTc model from Study IPX203-102-23, and the observed clinical Cmax data from Studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01. The predicted placebo-adjusted QTc effects ( ΔΔ QTcF) at both the mean Cmax and the clinical 95 th  percentile Cmax values were small (0.3-0.7 ms), and the upper bound of the 90% CI at these concentrations remained below the regulatory threshold of 10 ms.

The applicant submitted the empirical distribution of clinical Cmax for CD, including data from studies B14-02, B16-01, or pooled PK and fasting status, at the maximal per-dose 175 mg (per SmPC conversion). The distribution was reported as the 50 th  and 95 th  percentile (the median) and overlaid against the TQT 400 mg Cmax distribution.

The requested exposure-margin context for CD, at the maximal per-dose level (175 mg), was linked to the TQT exposure-QTc model. The estimated Cmax distribution for a 175 mg CD dose (mean 613 ng/mL; median 539 ng/mL; 95th percentile 1371 ng/mL) fell within the concentration range covered by the TQT study, where an effect &gt;10 ms was excluded across observed concentrations (up to 3000 ng/mL).

Using the final concentration-QTc model, the predicted ΔΔ QTcF at mean/median/P95 clinical Cmax values was small (0.5-0.6 ms) and remained well below the regulatory threshold, supporting a low QT risk for CD. Although the 175 mg estimates were derived by extrapolation from lower CD doses assuming PK linearity, this was considered acceptable in the context of the clearly negative TQT results, the shallow (slightly negative) concentration-QTc slope, and the substantial exposure coverage provided by the TQT dataset.

Since CD is eliminated via renal route, the applicant also provided an exposure-margin sensitivity showing predicted ΔΔ QTcF (upper 90% CI) at the upper tail of Cmax expected in low-eGFR subgroups (e.g., pooled PK stratified by eGFR categories), confirming that the upper bound remains &lt;10 ms at those exposures, including a sensitivity cut stratified by age ≥65/≥75 years to account for age -related decline in renal function. Supportive empirical data from the Phase 2 programme were likewise submitted, by listing subjects with CD Cmax &gt;900 ng/mL and subjects with eGFR &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m², including age and observed Cmax. These data did not indicate a consistent increase in CD Cmax in the low-eGFR subgroup, and the observed peak concentrations in this subgroup remain within the concentration range covered by the TQT exposure-QTc assessment, where a clinically relevant QTc effect was excluded. Although the response did not present a formal model-based 'exposure-margin sensitivity' by eGFR category (with predicted ΔΔ QTcF and upper 90% CI) as originally requested, the provided patient-level listings adequately addressed the underlying concern by showing that reduced renal function (including in older subjects) is not associated with materially higher peak CD exposure in the available clinical dataset. Relevant pharmacodynamic interactions, overlapping with those outlined for other currently approved levodopa/carbidopa-containing medicinal products, are accurately included in the PI.

No genetic difference that can affect the PD response in a clinically significant is foreseen.

With regard to the relationship between plasma concentration and effect and safety Study IPX203-B14-02 aimed to assess, amongst other objectives, PD and PK of single doses of IPX203 in subjects with advanced PD, using Rytary and IR CD-LD as the references.

The initial rates of decrease in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline (corresponding to an improvement in motor symptoms) were comparable for all three treatments. However, the MDSUPDRS Part III score decreases lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than following IR CD-LD or Rytary. Maximum decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline occurred at times that lagged behind the time of peak plasma concentrations of LD for the particular treatment.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Study IPX203-B16-01 intended to assess also PK/PD correlations in both single and multiple doses.

In the single dose setting the initial decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline (corresponding to an improvement in motor symptoms) were comparable between the 2 treatments. However, decrements in the MDS-UPDRS Part III scores lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than following IR CD-LD treatment. Maximum decreases in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from average baseline occurred at times that lagged behind the time of peak plasma concentrations of LD for the particular treatment.

In the multiple dose setting, at predose on Day 15, treatment with IPX203 showed a greater mean decrement (-9.3) in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores than did treatment with IR CD-LD (+0.1). As observed following the first dose on Day 1, a qualitative concordance was noted was noted between the LD plasma concentration profile and changes in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. The initial rates of improvement in motor symptoms were comparable between the two treatments. However, improvements in the MDS-UPDRS Part III scores lasted for a longer duration following IPX203 treatment than IR CD-LD, which may be associated with less frequent dosing of IPX203 than IR CDLD.

The applicant was asked to prove whether the improved duration of motor benefit with IPX203 was driven by higher total LD exposure (dose/AUC) or by a true PK advantage (PK profile, longer time above effective concentration or other).

Across study IPX203-B14-02 (single dose, PD) and IPX203-B16-01 (single and multiple doses, PD), the time-course of clinical response was followed by the LD concentration-time profile. The onset of improvement (MDS-UPDRS III) was similar for IPX203 and IR LD-CD, but the duration of improvement was longer with IPX203, consistent with its sustained LD exposure. Peak clinical effect was behind LD Cmax, which is expected for dopaminergic response.

Comparisons on Day 15 were confounded by higher total daily LD with IPX203 (2:1 vs IR) and lower dosing frequency (3.1 vs 4.7 doses/day); dose-normalised efficacy was not shown. Single-dose results used strengths not identical to the to-be-marketed strengths. Taken together the PK-PD data demonstrated a coherent exposure-response: similar onset but longer maintenance of effect with IPX203, fewer rescues, and longer time to redose. However, because Day-15 superiority coincided with higher LD exposure, the magnitude of benefit could be attributed solely to the release profile.

Therefore, the applicant provided dose-normalised PK-PD analyses (Emax and/or indirect-response) showing the relationship between LD exposure (Cmax, AUC ₀ - τ , and time above a clinically relevant concentration) and MDS-UPDRS III, adjusted for total daily LD dose and dosing frequency. Report Cmax/D and AUC ₀ - τ /D for LD (and CD) by regimen and day.

A plausible mechanistic rationale for IPX203 (rapid IR component plus prolonged ER component) and an illustrative individual time-course plot linking LD concentrations with MDS-UPDRS III and motor states were also supplied.

In addition, the applicant provided an exposure-response analysis using data from studies IPX203B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01. Individual Cmax, AUC, time above the proposed LD efficacy threshold of 750 ng/mL, and AUEC of Δ MDS-UPDRS Part III were assessed and presented by treatment. It was also explained that a fully exposure-matched comparison is difficult, because IPX203-B14-02 was a single-dose study and IPX203-B16-01 included multiple-dose treatment with individual dose adjustments and limited PK/PD sampling. This limitation is acknowledged and considered acceptable by CHMP.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The provided analyses suggested that Cmax alone is not the main driver of the longer motor benefit with IPX203, as Cmax values overlap between IPX203 and IR. Higher AUC and longer time above the efficacy threshold seem to be more relevant for the sustained response. This is consistent with the formulation concept of IPX203, where additional LD is delivered from the extended-release component, leading to higher overall exposure and longer time above an effective concentration.

The applicant also noted that, where similar Cmax or AUC values are observed, clinical efficacy is generally similar between IR and IPX203. Higher AUEC values of Δ MDS-UPDRS Part III and longer duration of effect were mainly observed with IPX203, which is consistent with the longer time above threshold. The presented data supported the notion that the prolonged clinical benefit of IPX203 is driven mainly by higher total LD exposure and longer time above an effective LD concentration, rather than by higher Cmax.

The PK/PD correlation performed in the studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 was established by using only MDS-UPDRS Part III score as main endpoint. For a new LD/CD formulation, especially with the current claims, the clinically important PD question was not just whether Part III can be modelled against plasma LD, but whether the PK profile also translates into functionally meaningful benefit, such as reduced 'OFF time', improved 'ON time' without troublesome dyskinesia, or reduced motor complication burden. The applicant's response was partially acceptable as MDS-UPDRS Part III is the only component suitable for dense within-day PK/PD modelling in the cited studies. For a novel LD/CD formulation intended to improve motor response consistency and fluctuations, it would be expected the inclusion of longitudinal exposure-response analyses exploring clinically relevant outcomes beyond Part III, including MDS-UPDRS Part IV, patient diary-derived OFF time, ON time without troublesome dyskinesia, or related fluctuation endpoints. Therefore, although the explanation was methodologically reasonable it was however scientifically insufficient and the absence of correlation between Part III and Part IV remains a concern, not merely a design artefact. Nevertheless, the CHMP agreed that, in the absence of an impact on Hopledo overall benefit/risk profile, the matter would not be further pursued with follow-up questions.

## Dose justification

In the (single dose, PD) study IPX203-B14-02 , IPX203 and Rytary were dosed to target IR-like peaks (±20%). Mean Cmax and AUC ₀ - ∞ increased 'approximately dose-proportionally' across the tested doses. In study IPX203-B16-01 (patients, Day 1 and multiple dose), IPX203 doses (≈270 - 900 mg LD) were chosen from study IPX203-B14-02 to target IR 100 mg peaks; redosing every ~7-8 h was typical. Across Day-1 PK, peak-to-trough fluctuation was lower and dosing frequency reduced vs IR; accumulation was low.

The applicant proposed a conversion table from IR formulations to IPX203. Although, the general concept of such conversion table was understandable some clarifications were required in the course of the procedure.

Thereafter, the applicant explained accurately the rationale for a conversion approach based on the most frequent single IR LD dose (using a 2.8× factor aimed at LD Cmax matching) and referred to supportive Phase 3 information (RISE-PD study).

The applicant further provided a more complete justification of the proposed IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm. The response included additional clinical evidence, quantitative PK simulations for the illustrative cases, and one additional example with the same IR TDD. It was also proposed a targeted mitigation at the upper end of the conversion range, allowing initiation with the next lower available capsule strength for patients with a most frequent IR LD dose of 200 mg or higher.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Furthermore, the response explained that the conversion algorithm is intended only as an initial dosing recommendation, followed by individual titration based on efficacy and tolerability. This is clinically relevant, as dose adjustment is expected in advanced Parkinson's disease.

The Phase 3 and Phase 4 data also supported BID initiation in patients receiving &lt;500 mg/day IR LD, with maintained clinical benefit and no new safety concern.

Furthermore, the Applicant proposed revised SmPC wording for the conversion algorithm. This text keeps the 2.8-fold conversion principle but allows starting with the next lower strength when the most frequent IR levodopa dose is 200 mg or higher. The recommendation for follow-up after 1 to 3 days and further dose or dosing-frequency adjustment based on individual response is also clinically relevant and supports safe use during conversion.

Some uncertainty would remain because the simulations are model-based and the proposed efficacy threshold may vary between patients. In addition, patients with the same IR TDD but different IR dose patterns may still receive different nominal IPX203 TDD after conversion. However, overall, the applicant's explanations are considered acceptable by the CHMP in the context of the initial nature of the conversion algorithm, the need for later individual titration, supportive Phase 3/4 data, and the proposed mitigation option for the upper conversion range.

## 5.2.6.2. Conclusions

In general, the PK/PD clinical programme can be considered acceptable.

IPX203 delivers the intended MR performance preserving onset, flattening LD peaks relative to IR, and extending coverage, while providing higher and more sustained CD exposure to support peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibition. The clinical programme demonstrated predictable, proportional PK across the TBM strengths range, bridging strengths used in phase 2 studies, confirms manufacturing site equivalence, and characterises relevant effects of food and alternative sprinkle IPX203 in applesauce. The CHMP agreed that the text detailed in SmPC section 4.2 and 5.2 is well supported by the submitted evidence.

The clinical PD section was also considered generally adequate.

## 5.4. Dose response studies

## 5.4.1.1. Phase 2 Study IPX203-B14-02

Study IPX203-B14-02 was a Phase 2 randomised, open-label, rater-blinded, multicentre, 3treatment, 3-period, single-dose, crossover study that assessed the PK, PD/efficacy and safety of single doses of IPX203 in subjects with advanced PD, using Rytary/Numient (MR LD-CD) and Sinemet (IR LD-CD) as reference products, and characterised the safety of single doses of IPX203 in these subjects. Males or females diagnosed with idiopathic PD at age ≥40 years were enrolled. Idiopathic PD was defined by the United Kingdom Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Diagnostic Criteria. There were no known secondary causes (e.g., vascular, toxin or medication-induced, metabolic, or infectious) for subject's Parkinsonism nor did the subjects had another neurodegenerative disorder with Parkinsonism symptoms (e.g., progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, multiplesystem atrophy).

Subjects received a single oral dose of each of the three study treatments (IR LD-CD, Rytary/Numient and IPX203) in the fasted state in a randomised sequence.

A crossover study design was selected to allow each subject to serve as his or her own control. IR LDCD was the primary active comparator and Rytary/Numient was included as an additional active treatment. Subjects received single doses of each study treatment with washout periods of approximately 1 week between doses. Subjects continued taking IR LD-CD between study visits. During the IR LD-CD treatment period, the dosing regimen of IR LD-CD was expected to be the same as the subject's pre-study (stable) morning baseline dosing regimen. The dosing regimens for IPX203 and Rytary/Numient were selected based on the amount of LD in the subject's pre-study morning dose of IR LD-CD (as per Table below). All treatments were administered to subjects with 240 mL of roomtemperature water in a fasted state. All study treatments contained LD and CD at a fixed ratio of 4:1.

Note: CD and LD present at a fixed ratio of 1:4 in each strength and treatment.

The subjects' motor state was assessed by a qualified blinded rater at -1 hour and -0.5-hour pre-dose, just before dosing (pre-dose), and every half hour following dosing through each 10-hour measurement period as one of the following states: 'Asleep', 'OFF', 'ON' without dyskinesia, 'ON' with non-troublesome dyskinesia, and 'ON' with troublesome dyskinesia. 'OFF' was defined as the typical functional state when the medication no longer provided benefit with regard to mobility, slowness, and stiffness despite taking medications. 'ON' was defined as the typical functional state when a subject's medication provided benefit with regard to mobility, slowness, and stiffness. Dyskinesia was defined as involuntary and irregular twisting and/or turning movements that were an effect of medication and occurred during 'ON' time. Non-troublesome dyskinesias did not interfere with function or cause meaningful discomfort. Troublesome dyskinesias interfered with function or caused meaningful discomfort. The Movement Disorders Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III (motor examination) was assessed pre-dose and hourly up to 10 hours post-dose by qualified site staff who were blinded to treatment. If rescue medication was required within 10 hours post-dose, no further PK or pharmacodynamic assessments were conducted following rescue at that visit.

## The study endpoints were:

- 'OFF' time based on the assessment of subject's motor state (primary endpoint);
- 'ON' time without troublesome dyskinesia; also called 'Good ON' time (the sum of 'ON' time without dyskinesia plus 'On' time with non-troublesome dyskinesia), based on the assessment of subject's motor state;
- 'ON' time without dyskinesia based on the assessment of subject's motor state;
- 'ON' time with non-troublesome dyskinesia;
- 'ON' time with troublesome dyskinesia based on the assessment of subject's motor state;
- 'Asleep' time based on the assessment of subject's motor state;
- Change in MDS-UPDRS Part III score from pre-dose value at each time point;
- Duration of effect estimated from the time at which an improvement of at least 4 points in the MDS-UPDRS Part III score from pre-dose was first observed until the time at which the improvement was no longer observed (duration was also estimated for at least 7 and 13 points);
- Proportion of subjects with an improvement of at least 20%, 25%, 30%, and 35% in MDS-UPDRS Part III score from average pre-dose score;

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- Proportion of subjects who required rescue provided by treatment group, along with a distribution by time point of rescue using the following categories: &lt;2 hours, 2 to &lt;4 hours, 4 to &lt;6 hours, 6 to &lt;8 hours, and ≥8 hours.

The primary PD endpoint was the mean total post-dose 'OFF' time based on the assessment of the subject's motor state; the primary comparison was between IPX203 and IR LD-CD using a mixed-effect analysis of variance (ANOVA) model with treatment, period, and sequence as fixed effects and subjectwithin-sequence as a random effect. Mean times in each motor state were compared by treatment. The mean change from average pre-dose in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores was summarised and compared between treatments using mixed-effect ANOVA models. Duration of effect was examined by comparing improvement from average pre-dose MDS-UPDRS Part III scores for each treatment using prespecified thresholds (4-, 7-, and 13-point improvements). Percentages of subjects who required rescue medication and time to rescue were compared by treatment. If the subject withdrew prior to the 10hour evaluation, the assessment of subject's motor state was imputed to be 'OFF' for the remainder of the evaluation period, and the baseline observation (average pre-dose) was carried forward for the MDS-UPDRS Part III score.

## Deviations from study plan

Major protocol deviations occurred in study IPX203-B14-02: cases of incorrect dosing, dosing from a wrong bottle, continued PK samples collection after administration of a rescue medication, wrong sample volume collected and stabilizer solution volume that was not adjusted correctly, exit labs collected prior to study assessment completion all have occurred during the study. Considering the number and seriousness of such deviations, in the course of the procedure the applicant was requested to further justify why these did not impact the study results.

Among the 26 randomised subjects, 12 subjects (46.2%) had at least one major deviation. These deviations were isolated, infrequent, and managed according to prespecified procedures. Their nature and impact are described below.

1. Dosing Deviations.

Incorrect dosing occurred in 2 subjects (7.7%), and dosing from the wrong bottle occurred in 1 (3.8%). In all cases, the deviations involved minor differences in the administered dose (e.g., 250 mg instead of 200 mg, or 200 mg instead of 150 mg). Importantly, these deviations did not compromise the integrity of PK analyses because the actual dose received by each subject was used in all summaries and statistical analyses. This ensured accurate estimation of PK parameters and preserved the validity of efficacy assessments.

2. PK sampling after rescue medication

In cases of PK samples collected after administration of rescue medication (in 1 subject, 3.8%), these samples were excluded from the PK analysis, as prespecified in the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP). This approach ensured that any potential confounding effect of rescue medication on PK parameters was avoided.

3. Sample handling and early lab collection

Deviations related to sample handling, such as incorrect sample volume or stabiliser solution errors, were observed in 1 subject (3.8%), while early collection of exit labs occurred in 4 subjects (15.4%). Additionally, 5 subjects (19.2%) had safety labs collected pre-dose at Visit 3. For these cases, laboratory summaries were analysed both including and excluding affected subjects, and no clinically meaningful differences were observed. These findings confirm that such deviations did not impact safety evaluations or overall study conclusions.

4. Severity Assessment and Data Handling

The applicant confirmed that all protocol deviations were documented, and their severity assessed before database lock, in accordance with the SAP. This process ensured that any potential impact of deviations could be identified and addressed prior to final data analysis, minimising the risk of bias and preserving the validity of the study results.

In spite of the high number of major protocol deviations, affecting 12 (46.2%) out of the 26 randomised subjects, it is agreed that none of them impacted the credibility of the study findings.

## 5.4.1.2. Phase 2 Study IPX203-B16-01

Study IPX203-B16-01 was a Phase 2 randomised, open-label, rater-blinded, 2-treatment, 2-period, multiple-dose, crossover, multicentre study that assessed the PK and PD of single and multiple doses of IPX203 and IR LD-CD in subjects with advanced PD.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Male or female subjects diagnosed with idiopathic PD at age ≥40 years who were being chronically treated with stable regimens of LD-CD but experiencing motor complications were enrolled. Motor complications were defined as the subject experiencing daily 'wearing OFF' episodes with periods of bradykinesia and rigidity and experiencing an 'OFF' state upon awakening on most mornings by history. The definition of idiopathic PD was the same as in Study IPX203-B14-02.

Eligible subjects were randomised 1:1 to one of two dosing sequences: IPX203 followed by IR LD-CD, or IR LD-CD followed by IPX203, according to their randomised sequence for Periods 1 and 2. A crossover study design was selected to allow each subject to serve as his or her own control thereby reducing confounding factors due to inter-subject variability. IR LD-CD was the primary active comparator. Subjects completed two 15-day treatment periods, one for each study treatment, with a washout period of approximately 1 week (±2 days) between the 2 treatment periods. Given the expected short half-lives of IPX203 and IR LD-CD, a 1-week washout period was considered sufficient to minimise any carryover effects. The investigators could adjust each subject's IPX203 or IR LD-CD dose regimen for optimal efficacy, tolerability, and safety. The number of dose adjustment steps was not limited during the 9-day dose adjustment period. The study design of Study IPX203-B16-01 is presented below.

The study was open-label with specific PD assessments done by qualified raters who were blinded to treatment assignments (i.e., assessment of subject's motor state and MDS-UPDRS).

The efficacy and pharmacodynamic assessments in this study were intended to evaluate and quantify the treatment effect-time profile of the two different formulations of LD-CD on the motor symptoms of PD. The PD measures were typically responsive to LD.

The efficacy endpoints of the study were:

- Subject PD diaries (Days 12-14 of each treatment period):
- o Average percent 'Off' time during waking hours, based on subject PD diaries (primary efficacy endpoint);
- MDS-UPDRS (Parts I-IV);
- Kinesia 360 sensors.

The PD endpoints were:

- Investigator Assessment of the Subject's Motor State;

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- MDS-UPDRS, Part III.

All PD analyses (i.e., investigator's assessment of Subject Motor State and MDS-UPDRS Part III) were conducted using the Pharmacodynamic Completers analysis set. Pharmacodynamic Completers included all subjects who received both treatments and had at least 1 pre-dose and 4 post-dose motor state assessments at each visit.

The MDS-UPDRS Part III figures were plotted using all randomised subjects. randomised set included all subjects who were randomised into the study and received at least one dose of study drug.

Kinesia 360 data were analysed using the Kinesia 360 Completers analysis set. Kinesia 360 Completers included all subjects who received both treatments and had at least 2 hours of evaluable Kinesia 360 data during at least 1 of the 3 days prior to each of Visits 1, 2, and 4. Evaluable Kinesia 360 data was defined as at least 2 hours of Kinesia 360 data for the particular day.

## Results

Twenty-eight subjects were randomised, and 27 (96.4%) completed both treatments. One withdrew, because of an AE while receiving IPX203, and did not receive IR CD-LD.

For the 28 randomised subjects, the mean (SD) age was 66.4 (10.1) years. Males slightly outnumbered females (16 versus 12, respectively). The majority (92.9%) of the subjects were white.

## Pharmacokinetic results

## Single-dose PK on Day 1 (Table A)

In the 27 subjects who received both treatments, the mean LD first dose taken in the clinic on Day 1 was 159 mg for IR CD-LD and 573 mg for IPX203. Following IPX203 treatment, LD was absorbed with a median Tmax of 2.0 hours (range: 0.5-5.0 hours). As expected, Tmax values were greater for IPX203 than for IR CD-LD due to continued drug release from the extended-release (ER) component.

The initial increase in LD concentration from IPX203 was comparable to that from IR CD-LD. The time to reach therapeutic or clinically meaningful plasma LD concentrations (e.g., 430 ng/mL) was similar for both treatments. After a single dose, LD plasma concentrations were sustained longer above 50% Cmax after IPX203 treatment than after IR CD-LD (on average, 4.6 vs. 1.5 hours, respectively) and above 430 ng/mL (6.8 vs. 2.8 hours, respectively). Plasma exposure to LD (based on Cmax and AUC∞ values) increased in an approximately dose-proportional manner following IPX203 treatment across the dose range of 360 mg to 900 mg studied in the trial.

a Bioavailability relative to IR CD-LD

Carbidopa had a median Tmax of 2.5 hours (min, max 1.5, 4.0) on Day 1 following the first dose of IPX203. Mean CD Cmax following IPX203 was 500 ng/mL, and mean t½ was 2.0 hours. Values of AUC and Cmax for CD following a single dose of IPX203 were higher than for the IR CD-LD treatment, as expected from the higher dose of CD in IPX203 and formulation characteristics. The bioavailability values for LD and CD in IPX203 relative to IR CD-LD, based on arith metic mean AUC∞ ratios, were 89% and 117%, respectively.

## Multiple-dose PK on Day 15 (Table B)

The mean morning dose of LD administered in the clinic on Day 15 of a stable dosing regimen was 159 mg for IR CD-LD and 560 mg for IPX203. Following the first dose of IPX203 on Day 15, LD was absorbed with a median Tmax of 1.5 hours (min, max 0.5, 6.0). The initial rate of increase in LD concentration from IPX203 was comparable to that of IR CD-LD. The mean LD Cmax following IPX203 treatment was only 15% greater than that of IR CD-LD in spite of a 3.5-fold greater LD dose. The mean LD AUCtau value following IPX203 treatment was approximately 2.9-fold greater than that of IR CD-LD, consistent with the higher dose of LD administered.

The duration that plasma LD concentrations remained above 430 ng/mL was significantly longer for IPX203 (on average 9.0 hours vs. 7.4 hours with IR CD-LD).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Following the first dose of IPX203 on Day 15, CD was absorbed with a median Tmax of 2.5 hours (min, max 1.5, 4.0). The mean CD Cmax following IPX203 treatment was 479 ng/mL. The mean CD AUCtau value following IPX203 treatment was approximately 4.6-fold greater than that of IR CD-LD. The mean fluctuation index for LD over the 10-hour in-clinic assessment duration on Day 15 of a stable dosing regimen was lower with IPX203 than IR CD-LD (1.7 vs. 2.7, respectively) and comparable for CD (1.7 vs. 1.5, respectively). Accumulation ratios for LD and CD were low with both treatments.

In terms of efficacy, during IPX203 treatment, subjects had less \"OFF\" time as a percentage of their waking hours compared with IR CD-LD (mean 19.3% vs. 33.5%, respectively), based on PD diary data collected on Days 12 to 14 of each treatment period (primary efficacy measure). On average, treatment with IPX203 was associated with approximately 2.3 hours less \"OFF\" time than was IR CDLD during waking hours; most of this improvement (1.9 hours) was \"Good ON\" time. The durations of \"Good ON\" episodes or any \"ON\" episodes were significantly longer with IPX203 (LS means differences 2.89 hours and 3.79 hours, respectively). Treatment with IPX203 was also associated with significantly fewer motor fluctuations per day than IR CD-LD. Significantly higher proportions of subjects experienced a reduction in \"Off\" time of at least 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 hours during IPX203 treatment than during IR CD-LD treatment.

When predose mean MDS-UPDRS Parts I-IV scores were compared by treatment on Day 15, subjects had significantly lower scores for Parts III, II and III, and IV as well as the MDS-UPDRS total score during IPX203 treatment, indicating less PD impairment. Pre-dose on Day 15, when subjects had not had a study treatment for at least 5 hours, the mean MDS-UPDRS Part III score was significantly lower during IPX203 treatment (33.5 vs. 41.6), suggesting that the clinical effects of IPX203 may carry over to the next morning. Analysis of Part IV individual items demonstrated benefits of IPX203 versus IR CD-LD on time spent in 'OFF state' and on functional impact of fluctuations.

On Day 1, subjects receiving IPX203 were 73.3% less likely to receive rescue medication (defined as the 2nd study drug dose of the day) than those receiving IR CD-LD. Similarly, on Day 15, subjects receiving IPX203 were 72.1% less likely to receive a predose than those receiving IR CD-LD.

With regards to PD, the investigator's assessment of the subject's motor state on Day 1 demonstrated significantly less \"OFF\" time and significantly more \"Good ON\" time with IPX203 compared with IR CDLD (2.57 hours difference for each). On Day 15, significant treatment differences were again seen in \"OFF\" time and \"Good ON\" time, although the magnitude of the differences was smaller. During the 10-hour post-dose observation period, 63% of subjects experienced less than 2 hours of 'OFF' time compared to 19% of subjects during the IPX203 and IR CD-LD treatment periods, respectively. Average times to first \"ON\" and first 'Good ON' states after the first dose were not significantly different between treatments on Days 1 or 15.

MDS-UPDRS Part III mean scores on Day 1 were lower during IPX203 treatment than during IR CD-LD treatment from 3 to 8 hours post-dose; across the 8 hours post-dose, the mean scores were 23.6 during IPX203 treatment and 33.0 during IR CD-LD treatment (p&lt;0.0001). Subjects had longer total durations of pharmacodynamic effect during IPX203 treatment than during IR CD-LD treatment, based on minimal improvement thresholds of at least 4, 7, and 13 points on the MDS-UPDRS Part III scale. From 3 to 7 hours post-dose, greater proportions of subjects taking IPX203 than taking IR CD-LD met each of 3 minimal improvement thresholds. On Day 15, across the 10 hours post-dose, the mean MDSUPDRS Part III scores were 18.2 for IPX203 and 22.0 for IR CD-LD (p=0.0226).

The sum of scores from bradykinesia questions from Part III (sum of Questions 4-8, and 14) showed more reduction with IPX203 than IR CD-LD on Day 1 (overall and at Hours 3 through 7) but not on Day 15 (except at Hours 3 and 4).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Deviations from study plan

In total, 28.6% of patients experienced major protocol's deviations during study IPX203-B16-01: 14.3% (4 subjects) had incorrect dosing regimen used on Day 15 visit, 1 subject was given wrong drug at EOS, 1 subject missed IR dose before Day 1 visit, 1 subject used more IPX203 270-mg capsules than expected. Importantly, these protocol's deviations were reviewed and adjudicated prior to database lock to ensure appropriate handling and to confirm that they did not compromise the validity of efficacy or PK/pharmacodynamic analyses.

## 5.4.2. Main studies

## 5.4.2.1. IPX203-B16-02

## Study objective

Study IPX203-B16-02 was a Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-group, prospective, multicentre study that evaluated the safety and efficacy of IPX203 in comparison to IR LD-CD in the treatment of LD-CD subjects with PD who had motor fluctuations, despite being treated with stable regimens of IR LD-CD.

Figure 15: Study IPX203-B16-02 scheme

<!-- image -->

Abbreviations: ET = early termination; IR CD-LD = immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa; PD = Parkinson's disease

## Treatment

The study consisted of an up to 4-week screening period, a 3-week open-label IR CD-LD dose adjustment period, a 4-week open-label period for conversion to IPX203, and a 13-week double-blind, double-dummy treatment period. Subjects were randomised in a 1:1 ratio and stratified by centre to receive either IPX203 (with matching IR CD-LD placebo) or IR CD-LD (with matching IPX203 placebo).

Subjects continued to take permitted non-CD-LD-based PD medications throughout the study if documented in their pre-study regimen and if dosing regimens had been stable for at least 4 weeks prior to Visit 1. A 'stable dosing regimen' meant no change in dose or in dosing frequency.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- o Within 4 weeks following the screening visit, eligible subjects completed their PD diaries on each of the 3 consecutive days immediately prior to Visit 1 (study entry visit).
- o Following Visit 1, qualified subjects entered a 3-week, open-label IR CD-LD treatment period allowing for dose adjustment. The dosing regimen of IR CD-LD could be adjusted during the dose adjustment period to achieve optimal balance of efficacy and tolerability (minimize Off' time without causing troublesome dyskinesia or other dopaminergic side effects). The doses and regimens of the subject's other non-CD-LD PD medications (dopamine agonists, monoamine oxidase [MAO]-B inhibitors, amantadine, anticholinergics) had to remain stable throughout this study. Any adjustments to the IR CD-LD dosing regimen were to be done in consultation with the investigator or sub-investigator and were recorded. Regular phone calls (approximately every 1 to 3 days) to the subjects were made by the Investigator or sub-investigator while the IR CD-LD dose was being adjusted. The IR CD-LD dosing regimen had to be stable for at least 5 days prior to returning for Visit 2. Rescue with additional or modified doses of concomitant PD medications or with use of CD-LD products other than the dispensed study medications was not permitted and triggered discontinuation from the study. Subjects had to complete their 3-day PD Diaries on each of the 3 consecutive days immediately prior to Visit 2.
- o Following completion of the IR CD-LD dose adjustment period, subjects began a 4-week openlabel dose conversion period for conversion from IR CD-LD to IPX203. The initial dosing regimen of IPX203 was based on the most frequent dose of the subject's stable dosing regimen of IR CDLD at the end of the dose adjustment period (Visit 2). A 25-100 mg dose of IR CD-LD was converted to a 70-280 mg CD-LD dose of IPX203 (2 capsules of 35-140 mg CD-LD IPX203), and a 12.5-50 mg (half-tablet) dose of IR CD-LD was converted to a 35-140 mg CD-LD dose of IPX203, but with a longer duration of effect. It was recommended that IPX203 be dosed approximately every 8 hours with the exception that subjects who were currently receiving a TDD of less than 125-500 mg from IR CD-LD at the end of the dose adjustment period had to be initially administered IPX203 every 12 hours. The dosing interval could be reduced to approximately every 8 hours if the subject did not achieve an acceptable duration of effect. The dosing regimen of IPX203 could be adjusted during the dose conversion period to achieve the optimal balance of efficacy and tolerability (minimize 'Off' time without causing troublesome dyskinesia or other dopaminergic side effects). The dosing interval could vary but was not to be more frequent than every 6 hours. The doses and regimens of the subject's other non-CD-LD PD medications (dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, amantadine, anticholinergics) had to remain stable throughout this study. The subject had to be on a stable dosing regimen of IPX203 (no change in dose or in dosing frequency) for at least 5 days prior to returning for Visit 4 (randomization visit). Any adjustments to the IPX203 dosing regimen were to be done in consultation with the investigator or sub-investigator and were recorded. During the dose adjustment period, subjects were to be called by the investigator or sub-investigator to adjust the IPX203 dose further, as needed, and subjects returned to the clinic every 2 weeks for Visit 3 and Visit 4. Subjects were instructed to complete their 3-day PD diaries on each of the 3 consecutive days immediately prior to Visit 4 (randomization visit).
- o At Visit 4, subjects who successfully completed the IPX203 dose conversion period were randomised in a 1:1 ratio, stratified by centre, to one of two parallel treatment arms of IPX203 (with matching IR CD-LD placebo) or IR CD-LD (with matching IPX203 placebo). Subjects underwent 13 weeks of double-blind, double-dummy maintenance therapy with the stable dosing regimen established at the end of Week 3 (Visit 2) for IR CD-LD and at the end of Week 7 (Visit 4) for IPX203. No new dose adjustments could be made in the double-blind maintenance period. Rescue with additional or modified doses of concomitant PD medications or with use of CD-LD products other than the dispensed study medications was not permitted and triggered

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

discontinuation from the study. During the 13-week maintenance therapy period, subjects returned to the clinic for visit 5 (3 weeks after Visit 4), visit 6 (5 weeks after visit 5), and visit 7 (end of study [EOS] visit, 5 weeks after Visit 6). Subjects completed their 3-day PD Diaries on each of the 3 consecutive days immediately prior to each of these visits.

Rescue with additional or modified doses of concomitant PD medications or with use of CD-LD products other than the dispensed study medications was not permitted and triggered discontinuation from the study.

## Randomisation and blinding

On Week 7 at visit 4, subjects were randomised, stratified by centre, in a 1:1 ratio into one of two double blind parallel treatment arms of IPX203 (and matching IR CD-LD placebo) or IR CD-LD (and matching IPX203 placebo).

## Patient population

Patients were enrolled from US, Italy, Spain, France, UK, Czech Republic, Poland and Germany.

Male or female subjects diagnosed at age ≥40 years with PD, consistent with the United Kingdom Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Diagnostic Criteria and who were being treated with stable regimens of LD-CD but experienced motor fluctuations, were enrolled.

## Objectives and estimands

## Primary objectives

1. To evaluate the efficacy of IPX203 in comparison to IR CD-LD in the treatment of CD-LD experienced subjects PD who have motor fluctuations with respect to the change from baseline in 'Good ON' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days, at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination).
2. To evaluate the safety of IPX203 in comparison to IR CD-LD in the treatment of CD-LD experienced subjects with Parkinson's disease (PD) who have motor fluctuations.

## Planned analyses

The primary endpoint and 4 key secondary endpoints were tested in a sequential hierarchical order as follows:

1. The primary endpoint, the mean change from baseline in 'Good ON' time (hours per day), to be tested first at a 0.05 level of significance.
2. If statistical significance is demonstrated, then the first key secondary endpoint, the mean change from baseline in 'OFF' time (hours per day), to be tested next at a 0.05 level of significance.
3. If statistical significance is demonstrated, then the second key secondary endpoint, the proportion of subjects with either 'much improved' or 'very much improved' on the PGI-C, to be tested next at a 0.05 level of significance.
4. If statistical significance is demonstrated, then the third key secondary endpoint, the mean change from baseline in the MDS-UPDRS Part III, to be tested at a 0.05 level of significance.
5. If statistical significance is demonstrated, then the fourth key secondary endpoint, the mean change from baseline in the sum of the MDS-UPDRS Parts II and III combined to be tested next at a 0.05 level of significance.

For the other efficacy endpoints, no adjustment to be made.

## Statistical methods for estimation and sensitivity analysis on primary estimand

## Primary Efficacy Endpoint

The primary efficacy endpoint is the mean change from baseline in 'Good ON' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days, at the end of the double-blind therapy (Visit 7 or early termination). 'Good ON' time is derived from the 3-day PD Diaries. For each day, 'Good on' time is calculated by adding the number of half-hour intervals in which either an 'ON without dyskinesia' or 'ON with nontroublesome dyskinesia' is checked.

The primary efficacy endpoint was analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM). The model included baseline (Visit 4) 'Good ON' time as a covariate, treatment, visit, and pooled centre as fixed effects, and a treatment-by-visit interaction. The model employed an unstructured within subject covariance  matrix  and  a  restricted  maximum  likelihood  (ReML)  estimation  method.  The  degree-offreedom of the denominator was estimated using the Kenward-Roger method (30TKenward and Roger 199730T). The primary analysis population will be the modified intent-to-treat.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Secondary Objectives

To evaluate the efficacy of IPX203 in comparison to IR CD-LD in the treatment of CD-LD experienced subjects with PD who have motor fluctuations with respect to the following key secondary endpoints:

- o Change from baseline in 'OFF' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination)
- o Proportion  of  subjects  with  either  'much  improved'  or  'very  much  improved'  in  Patient  Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) scores at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination)
- o Change from baseline in the MDS-UPDRS Part III at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination)
- o Change from baseline in the sum of MDS-UPDRS Parts II and III at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination).

## Exploratory Objectives

To evaluate the efficacy of IPX203 in comparison to IR CD-LD in the treatment of CD-LD experienced subjects with Parkinson's disease (PD) who have motor fluctuations with respect to the following exploratory endpoints:

- o Percent 'OFF' time during waking hours derived from the 3-day PD Diaries
- o Average duration of each continuous 'Good on' and each continuous 'ON'
- o Hours of (1) 'OFF' time (from Visit 1), (2) 'Good ON' time (from Visit 1), (3) 'ON' time with dyskinesia, (4) 'ON' time with troublesome dyskinesia, and (5) 'ON' time with non-troublesome dyskinesia, and (6) asleep time derived from the 3-day PD Diaries
- o Proportion of subjects with an improvement in 'Good ON' time of at least 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 hours
- o Proportion of subjects with a reduction in 'OFF' time of at least 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 hours
- o Proportions of subjects who are 'ON' upon awakening and 'Good on' upon awakening
- o Average time to 'ON' upon awakening
- o Change from baseline in the average number of motor fluctuations per day averaged over the PD Diary days. A motor fluctuation is defined as a change from 'Off' to 'On' state or from 'ON' to 'OFF' state.
- o MDS-UPDRS total score (sum of Parts I, II, III, and IV) and Parts I, II, and IV separately
- o MDS-UPDRS Part III and Parts II + III combined (from Visit 1)
- o MDS-UPDRS Part II Question 2.9
- o PDQ-39 total score and individual domain scores
- o NMSS total score and individual domains
- o PDSS-2 total score and individual domains
- o PDSS-2 items 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 combined
- o PAS total score and individual domains

## Statistical methods for estimation and sensitivity analysis on the secondary estimands

The first key secondary endpoint was the mean change from baseline in 'OFF' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days, at the end of the double-blind therapy (Visit 7 or early termination). 'OFF' time was derived from the 3-day PD Diaries. For each day, 'OFF' time was calculated by adding the number of half-hour intervals in which an 'OFF' is checked. This endpoint was analysed using a MMRM model with baseline (Visit 4) 'OFF' time as a covariate, treatment, visit, and pooled centre as fixed effects, and a treatment-by-visit interaction. The model employed an unstructured within subject covariance matrix and a restricted maximum likelihood (ReML) estimation method. The degree-offreedom of the denominator was estimated using the Kenward-Roger method (30TKenward and Roger 199730T).

The proportion of subjects with either 'much improved' or 'very much improved' in PGI-C scores at the end of the double-blind therapy (Visit 7 or early termination), the second key secondary endpoint, was analysed using a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test to compare the two treatment groups with pooled centre as a stratification factor.

Key secondary endpoints:

- Change from baseline in 'OFF' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days at the end of doubleblind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination) - Proportion of subjects with either 'much improved' or 'very much improved' in Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) scores at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination).
- Change from baseline in the MDS-UPDRS Part III at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination).
- Change from baseline in the sum of MDS-UPDRS Parts II and III at the end of double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination).

## Tertiary objectives

The following endpoints were evaluated (at the post-randomization visits) as change from baseline (Visit 4) as well as change from the study entry (Visit 1), when applicable, by visits:

- Percent 'OFF' time during waking hours derived from the 3-day PD Diaries
- Average duration of each continuous 'Good ON' and each continuous 'ON'.

## Results

## Participant flow and numbers analysed

A total of 770 subjects were screened; 140 were screen failures and 630 were enrolled in the study. All 630 enrolled subjects entered the IR LD-CD dose adjustment period and there were 41 (6.5%) subject's discontinuations. A total of 589 (93.5%) subjects entered the IPX203 conversion period and there were 83 (13.2%) discontinuations (discussed thereafter in this section). At the end of IPX203

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

dose conversion period, 506 subjects were randomly assigned; 256 subjects to IPX203 and 250 subjects to IR LD-CD. Of these, 449 (88.7%) subjects completed the study; 222 (86.7%) subjects in the IPX203 group and 227 (90.8%) subjects in the IR LD-CD group.

Figure 16: Participant flow

<!-- image -->

## Deviations from study plan

As per study IPX206-B16-02 protocol, rescue(s) with additional or modified doses of concomitant nonLD-CD PD medications were not permitted and constituted a protocol deviation that could trigger discontinuation. While the clinical database did not include a data point specifically labelled as 'discontinued due to rescue treatment' the applicant reviewed all documented reasons for discontinuation to identify subjects whose narratives indicated rescue with additional or modified doses of concomitant non-LD-CD PD medications. Based on this review, 6 subjects discontinued for reasons consistent with the administration of rescue treatment or prohibited medication use, including:

- Requests for ability to change dose (1 subject),
- Inadvertent regimen changes (1 subject),
- Use of PD medication not allowed by protocol (1 subject),
- Modification of study medication dose during maintenance phase (2 subjects),
- Combining study drug with former levodopa medication (1 subject).

These cases were categorised under protocol deviations or dosing non-compliance in the clinical study report. No additional subjects were identified as discontinued for rescue treatment beyond these cases.

## Withdrawals

Out of the 660 subjects enrolled, 589 (93.5%) entered the IPX203 conversion period and 83 (13.2%) discontinued the study.

At the end of the IPX203 dose conversion period, 506 subjects were randomly assigned to IPX203 or IR LD-CD and 57 (11.3%) subjects discontinued early from the double-blind (DB) maintenance period . Out of these 57 subjects who discontinued early from the DB maintenance period 34 (13.3%) were from the IPX203 group and 23 (9.2%) from the IR LD-CD group.

The primary reasons of discontinuation (≥5% of subjects who discontinued) in the IPX203 group were AEs ( 14 [ 41.2 %] subjects), withdrawal by subject ( 10 [29.4%]), lack of efficacy ( 5 [14.7%]), and protocol deviations ( 3 [8.8%]). The primary reasons of discontinuations (≥5% of subjects who discontinued) in the IR LD-CD group were withdrawal by subject ( 11 [47.8%]), lack of efficacy ( 8 [34.8%]), and AEs ( 3 [ 13.0% ]). The difference in the incidence of discontinuations in the DB maintenance period due to AEs was of concern ( 14 AEs [ 41.2 %] in the in the IPX203 group versus 3 AEs [ 13 %] in the IR LD-CD).

The applicant provided information on the reason(s) for subjects' stepping out of the study, especially during the forced conversion period. It is understood that the design put particular stress on this period, and 32 out of the 83 subjects who discontinued while in the IPX203 conversion period had their reason described. The majority reported that the treatment had failed to meet their expectations in terms of efficacy or symptom control. In approximately 15 cases, participants described persistent or worsening symptoms, dissatisfaction with the study drug, or a preference to return to their previous medication (most often Sinemet). These individuals often reported issues such as troublesome dyskinesias, significant \"OFF\" periods, or unpredictable ON/OFF times, all of which contributed to their decision to discontinue.

Adverse events or side effects were also reported, with 6 subjects citing problems such as elevated blood pressure, nausea, anxiety, or other reactions that made continuation undesirable. For some, the challenge was not just the side effects themselves, but the inability to find a satisfactory or effective dose. In 4 cases, difficulty with dose optimisation was explicitly mentioned, sometimes in combination with unpredictable symptom control. Personal and logistical reasons were reported as well, accounting for at least 5 withdrawals. These included family or social stressors, a general unwillingness to continue, or personal circumstances unrelated to the drug's efficacy or safety.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Overall, the impact of the 83 subjects who discontinued during the dose-conversion period of study IPX203-B16-02 on the overall efficacy and safety should be interpreted in the context that IPX203 is a new MR formulation designed to replace IR LD-CD in patients with PD with motor fluctuations. Conversion to IPX203 involved dose titration, including transient lack of efficacy or dopaminergic AEs, which could lead to discontinuation. The initial suggested IPX203 doses in the protocol were based on average bioavailability relative to IR LD-CD. However, most subjects required individualised uptitration or down-titration to achieve an optimal balance of efficacy and tolerability. During the 4-week IPX203 dose-conversion period, these 83 subjects (14.1%) discontinued primarily due to AEs and lack of efficacy. These discontinuations largely reflected the process of establishing a clinically effective and tolerable IPX203 regimen rather than inherent lack of efficacy of IPX203.

These results are in line with Numient/Rytary IPX066-B09-02 study of Robert et al (2013), evaluating safety and efficacy of IPX066 in advanced PD patients, where the largest proportion of dropouts occurred during the 6-week IPX066 dose-conversion period. Specifically, 57 subjects (12.7% of the 450 who entered the period) discontinued early and the remaining 393 were randomised into the maintenance period. AEs were the most common reason for discontinuation during dose conversion (23 subjects). Lack of efficacy was the second most common reason for discontinuation during dose conversion (13 subjects, 2.9%), and a total of 12 subjects (2.7%) withdrew consent during dose conversion.

In study IPX203-B16-02, during the IPX203 conversion period, 229 (38.9%) subjects experienced at least one TEAE. The most frequently reported TEAEs (≥2%) in subjects who received IPX203 were dyskinesia (40 [6.8%] subjects), nausea (29 [4.9%] subjects), dry mouth (25 [4.2%] subjects), dizziness (17 [2.9%] subjects), constipation (12 [2.0%] subjects), and vomiting, fall and insomnia (each 13 [2.2%] subjects). These patterns are consistent with the pharmacologic transition from IR LD-CD to an MR LD-CD formulation.

The impact of these pre-randomisation discontinuations on the overall efficacy and safety conclusions is considered limited because both primary and key secondary efficacy analyses were conducted based on the intention-to-treat principle, i.e., on the randomised population (modified ITT set, N=495), which excluded subjects who discontinued before randomisation.

In summary, the observed discontinuations during the IPX203 conversion period reflected the inherent complexity of transitioning PD patients from a well-established IR regimen to a novel MR formulation under blinded conditions. These discontinuations did not undermine robustness of efficacy and safety conclusions drawn from the randomised DB phase, which demonstrated benefit of IPX203 over IR LDCD.

## Outcomes and estimation

Initially all patients were optimised in their IR LD-CD treatment regimen (Sinemet), followed by the conversion of all patients to IPX203, which led to an increase in 'ON' time compared to the end of IR optimisation (+1.46 h in mean 'Good ON' time after conversion to IPX203) and reduction in 'OFF' time (-1.46 h in mean 'Off' time after conversion to IPX203). Subsequently patients were randomised 1:1 to either continue IPX203 or to be treated with the optimised IR dose. The primary efficacy endpoint of the study was the mean change from baseline (randomisation visit) in 'Good ON' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD Diary days, at the end of the double-blind treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination [ET]). 'Good ON' time was derived from the 3-day PD diaries and was defined as the sum of 'ON time without dyskinesia' and 'ON time with non-troublesome dyskinesia'. Compared to patients treated with IR LD-CD, patients in the IPX203 arm showed maintenance of the previously achieved increase in 'On' time (11.73 h/V4 to +11.35 h/V7), whereas patients randomised to IR LD-CD declined towards their IR optimised 'Good On' time (11.73 h/v4 to 10.77 h/V7).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In the mITT analysis set , subjects receiving IPX203 experienced a lesser decrease in the mean 'Good ON' time from baseline to the end of double-blind therapy (Visit 7/ET) (LS mean: -0.50 hours) compared with those receiving IR LD-CD (LS mean: -1.03 hours). A statistically significant result in 'Good ON' time was noted with IPX203 treatment compared with IR LD-CD treatment ( p=0.0194 ), as outlined e.g., in the table below. A similar trend in 'Good ON' time results was observed in the PP Analysis Set . However, it failed to reach statistical significance ( p=0.1718 ), most likely due to the small size of this analysis set (n=155 for IPX203 group and n=158 for IR LD-CD group).
