Statistically significant results were also noted for the key secondary endpoint of change from baseline in 'OFF' time ( p=0.0252 ). In the mITT analysis set, subjects receiving IPX203 experienced almost maintenance of their previously achieved decrease in mean 'OFF' time from baseline to Visit 7/ET (LS mean: 0.38) compared with the subjects receiving IR LD-CD, who experienced a meaningful increase in 'Off' time (LS mean: 0.86). A similar trend in 'OFF' time results was observed in the PP Analysis Set; however, it failed to reach statistical significance ( p=0.0670 ).

With regard to the key secondary endpoint of Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) scores in the ITT Analysis Set, 56.9% of subjects in the IPX203 group reported improvement in PGI-C scores (defined as 'minimally improved', 'much improved', or 'very much improved') compared with 46.3% of subjects in the IR LD-CD group, at Visit 7/ET. A statistically significant proportion of subjects ( p=0.0015 ) reported 'much improved' or 'very much improved' response with IPX203 treatment (29.7%) compared with IR LD-CD treatment (18.8%). Similar statistically significant results were observed in the PP Analysis Set ( p=0.0161 ).

In terms of the key secondary endpoint of MDS-UPDRS-based endpoints in the ITT Analysis Set, subject scores in both groups increased to a similar degree from baseline to Visit 7/ET (LS mean 0.8 increase in Part III score in both groups; LS mean 1.7 and 1.8 increase, in sum of Parts II and III

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

score, in the IPX203 and IR LD-CD groups, respectively) with no statistically significant difference ( p = 0.9587 for Part III score and p=0.9668 for sum of Parts II and III score). A similar trend was observed in the PP Analysis Set with no statistically significant difference between the IPX203 and IR LD-CD groups in the MDS-UPDRS Part III results ( p=0.7265 ) and sum of MDS-UPDRS Part II and III results (p=0.6785).

The primary endpoint and five key/important secondary endpoints were tested in a sequential hierarchical order (the 'ON' upon awakening endpoint was considered an important secondary endpoint and was included in the sequential hierarchical testing of endpoints). As detailed above, since the endpoint of change from baseline to Visit 7/ET in the MDS-UPDRS Part III score failed to show statistical significance, no claims of superiority can be made on any endpoint further in the hierarchical testing list.

A statistically significant difference was noted in the percentage of subjects who were in the 'ON' state upon awakening for at least 1 of the 3 recorded PD Diary days; IPX203 (53.1%) versus IR LD-CD treatment (44.5%) at Visit 7/ET ( p=0.0046 ). Similar results were noted in the proportion of subjects who were in 'Good ON' state upon awakening at Visit 7/ET (0 days, p=0.0060 ).

With regard to additional endpoints in the mITT Analysis Set, subjects on IPX203 showed greater improvement (lesser decrease) in average duration of continuous 'Good ON' interval from Visit 4/baseline to Visit 7/ EOS when compared with those on IR LD-CD (mean change from Visit 4/baseline to Visit 7/EOS for continuous 'Good ON' interval [hours] for IPX203: -0.07 and IR LDCD: -0.98, p=0.0002 ).

Subjects on IPX203 showed a greater improvement (lesser increase) in the average number of motor fluctuations per day from baseline to Visit 7/EOS when compared with those on IR LD-CD (mean change from Visit 4/baseline to Visit 7/EOS; IPX203: 0.17 and IR LD-CD: 1.47). This difference was statistically significant favouring IPX203 (p&lt;0.0001, difference in LS means: -1.35). Mean number of motor fluctuations per day was 3.75 for IPX203 and 5.14 for IR LD-CD at EOS.

This was a randomised withdrawal study, to assess whether the maintenance of IPX203 was better than the IR LD in keeping the previously optimised oral treatment. In fact, both arms worsened at the double-blind phase (DB). This is the expected placebo effect loss when both the patient and the investigator do not know which treatment the patient is having.

There was some attrition during the DB phase of the study, and several patients were lost for some visits including the EOS visit (up to 27 of 249 in IPX203 and 19 of 246 in IR LD).  In the course of the procedure, as requested, the applicant reviewed the cases where patients missed any visit or the primary endpoint assessment. Overall, missed assessments were infrequent, evenly distributed across treatment arms, and primarily attributable to external circumstances rather than treatment-related factors. No missed assessments occurred at Visit 1 (Week 0) or Visit 4 (Week 7), which represented critical time points for study entry and randomisation during the DB, respectively. The missed assessments were observed mainly at Visit 6 (Week 15) which did not represent a primary timepoint for the analysis. At Week 15, 27 patients (10.8%) in the IPX203 group and 19 patients (7.7%) in the IR-LD-CD group missed the primary endpoint assessment. At Week 20, 14 patients (5.6%) in the IPX203 group and 5 patients (2%) in the IR-LD-CD group missed the assessment. Earlier visits (Weeks 3 and 10) had very few missed assessments (≤1% at Week 3 and approximately 4.5% at Week 10), and these were balanced between treatment arms, as noted in the Table below.

A review of the patient-level information available for a portion of the missed assessments indicated that the majority of missed assessments were due to logistical and external factors, most notably restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Several visits were conducted remotely during periods of site limitations, which prevented collection of PD diaries required for the primary endpoint. Other reasons included early termination due to lack of efficacy or AEs, patient non-compliance or refusal, and isolated cases such as diaries lost in transit or incomplete due to acute medical events. These reasons were unrelated to the treatment assignment and occurred sporadically across both arms.

Given the low frequency of missed assessments, their occurrence at non-critical time points, and the balanced distribution across treatment groups, in the applicant's view, these missing data had no meaningful impact on the study conclusions. Furthermore, the primary endpoint analysis employed a modified intent-to-treat (ITT) approach with appropriate statistical handling of missing data, ensuring robustness and validity of the results.

Th CHMP, having considered the above, noted that there were no missed assessments neither at visit 1 or 4, and most of those which occurred later were at the non-critical visits 5 and 6. It was nonetheless evident that from visit 5 onwards, there was more missingness in the IPX203 arm than in the IR LD arm. The applicant did not discuss such difference. However, since the end of study (EOS) visit 7 had much less missing data and the difference was only of nine patients, corresponding to 5.6% in IPX203 and 2% in IR LD, respectively, the applicant's response was considered satisfactory.

## Ancillary analyses

## Post hoc analyses

Patients entering Phase 3 had in average 2.34 hours of 'ON' time with dyskinesia of which 1.82 hours were categorised as non-troublesome and 0.51 hours were categorized as troublesome dyskinesia. To better understand the effect of IPX203 on patients with clinically meaningful duration of dyskinesia compared to advanced patients with non-relevant durations of dyskinesia the following post hoc analysis was performed.

Patients at study entry were stratified of having more or less than 1 h dyskinesia. In addition, a sensitivity analysis was performed, stratifying patients with more or less of 0.5 h of dyskinesia and patients with having at least 3.5 h 'OFF' time combined with more than 1 h of dyskinesia. At baseline 237 patients had at least 1 h of dyskinesia (in average 4.4 h of dyskinesia, of which 1 h was with troublesome dyskinesia). A total of 267 patients had less than 1 h of dyskinesia (in average 0.5 h of dyskinesia, of which only 0.09 h was with troublesome dyskinesia. Subgroups discriminated well patients having motor fluctuations with or without dyskinesia.

## Analysis of 'ON' time with dyskinesia

During IR LD-CD optimisation phase, time with dyskinesia increased from 4.4 to 4.9 h per day. After conversion to IPX203, mean time with dyskinesia was reduced to 4.6 h per day. During the doubleblind maintenance phase, the change of 'ON' time with dyskinesia was 0.03 h in the IPX203 arm, whereas change in the IR arm was 0.24 h per day (slight increase). Figures for troublesome dyskinesia were similar, increasing from 1 h at baseline, to 1.06 h after optimisation of IR LD-CD. At the end of the conversion to IPX203 (V4), troublesome dyskinesia time was reduced to 0.87 h.

In the double-blind phase, patients in the IPX203 arm showed a further slight decrease of time with troublesome dyskinesia by 0.017 h, whereas patients randomised to IR showed an increase of 0.237 h.

## Analysis of 'Good ON' time

Results for the main efficacy endpoints showed that patients with or without &gt;1 h dyskinesia per day had comparable 'Good ON' time at Visit 1 (9.7 h or 9.5 h, respectively). After optimisations of IR LDCD (Visit 2), 'Good ON' time increased in both groups reaching 10.3 h per day. At the end of the double-blind treatment period (Visit 7), patients on IPX203 retained 1.0 additional hour 'Good ON' time compared to Visit 2, whereas patients randomised to IR LD-CD retained 0.4 hours 'Good ON' time. Overall results were nearly identical for patients with and without dyskinesia.

Major differences were observed in 'Good ON' time with dyskinesia. At Visit 1, patients with dyskinesia had 4.43 h of 'Good ON' time per day, whereas patients without dyskinesia had less 0.49 h per day. 'Good ON' time in patients with dyskinesia increased by approximately half an hour (reaching 4.94 h) by Visit 2 (IR LD-CD optimisation) and subsequently decreased to 4.61 hours by Visit 4 (conversion to IPX203).

'Good ON' time without dyskinesia was virtually unchanged during IR LD-CD optimisation (6.24 hours at Visit 1 and 6.40 hours at Visit 2) but improved by 1.5 hours after conversion to IPX203 (7.92 hours at Visit 4). Thus, in patients with dyskinesia, conversion to from IR LD-CD to IPX203 resulted in an increase in 'Good ON' time without dyskinesia but not in 'Good ON' time with dyskinesia.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In patients having dyskinesia at Visit 2, more than 1 hour of 'Good ON' time, time without dyskinesia was retained after the double-blind period in the IPX203 group, whereas patients re-exposed to IR LDCD retained about 45 minutes (1.09 and 0.77 h, respectively).

## Analysis of 'OFF' time

During IR LD-CD optimisation period, 'OFF' time was reduced by approximately 0.7 hours, reaching 4.74 h for patients with dyskinesia and 6.06 hours for patients without dyskinesia. At Visit 4, 'OFF' time was further reduced to 3.65 h (1.1 h reduction) for patients with dyskinesia and 4.26 h (1.8 h reduction) for patients without dyskinesia. At the end of the double-blind period (Visit 7), patients with &gt;1 h dyskinesia at Visit 2 retained 0.68 and 0.67 h time reduction of 'OFF' time on IPX203 and IR LDCD group, respectively. Patients without dyskinesia or ≤1 hours dyskinesia at Visit 2 showed a n increase of 0.91 h in 'OFF' time versus Visit 4 when re-exposed to IR LD-CD and an increase of 0.28 h when receiving IPX203.

In summary, IPX203 had equally comparable benefits in patients with motor fluctuations with more than 1 hour and with no or less than 1 hour of dyskinesia. Importantly, the gain in 'Good ON' time in patients with more than 1 hour dyskinesia under IPX203 treatment was not associated with an increase in overall time with dyskinesia or time with troublesome dyskinesia. The conversion from IR LD-CD to IPX203 led also to a minor reduction in time with dyskinesia and troublesome dyskinesia.

Treatment effects where overall comparable in patients with more than 1 hour and with no or less than 1 hour of dyskinesia and always favoured IPX203 over IR LD-CD. The only exception was the amount of 'OFF' time in patients with more than 1 hour dyskinesia, which was comparable for both treatments after the end of the double-blind randomisation phase. It is noteworthy that patients on IR LD-CD had a slight increase of dyskinesia and troublesome dyskinesia time compared to IPX203, indicating that the reduction in 'OFF' time was resulting in more dyskinesia in the IR LD-CD group.

Results of the sensitivity analysis in patients with at least 0.5 hours of dyskinesia per day and patients with more than 3.5 hours 'OFF' time and more than 1 hour dyskinesia per day supported the robustness of the findings.

The applicant discussed several post-hoc analyses to support robustness and relevance of the primary endpoint but did not discuss the variation regarding overall time with dyskinesia and variation in time with troublesome dyskinesias as a group. Furthermore, since IPX203may prevent or delay the use of advanced medical therapies for PD, such as duodopa or foslevodopa, to increase robustness of the study data, the applicant was invited to compare study IPX203-B16-02 results with those for these advanced medical therapies for PD.

In the response, the applicant pointed out that, unlike the pivotal studies for LD-CD intestinal gel (LCIG, Duodopa) and foslevodopa/foscarbidopa, IPX203-B16-02 (RISE-PD) employed a withdrawal design, where randomisation took place only after the whole patient population was converted to IPX203. Therefore, a direct comparison of results was not straightforward. To make it meaningful, the applicant focused on the improvements observed during the IPX203 dose conversion period, which most closely corresponds to the double-blind treatment phase of the LCIG and

foslevodopa/foscarbidopa Phase 3 trials. This allowed to compare the incremental benefit of the therapy on top of the optimised IR LD-CD. This approach was justified because the study populations

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

were advanced and comparable across all studies, and IPX203 efficacy was maintained during the DB phase following conversion. It was also important to note that the DB phase for device-aided therapies (DATs) may not have been fully blinded, as dose optimisation and adjustments occurred after blinding. These post-blinding modifications could have revealed to both patients and investigators whether the treatment was active drug or placebo.

During the IPX203 conversion period, patients already optimised on IR LD-CD experienced an improvement in 'Good ON time' of 1.45 h and in 'OFF time' of 1.46 h. In comparison, the foslevodopa/foscarbidopa pivotal trial of Soileau et al , (2022) reported an improvement in 'Good ON' time of 1.75 h and a reduction in 'OFF time' of 1.79 h vs IR LD-CD, while the LCIG pivotal trial of Olanow et al , (2014) demonstrated an increase in 'Good ON' time of 1.86 h and a reduction in 'OFF time' of 1.91 h vs IR LD-CD.

In this context it would also be flagged that, regarding safety, IPX203 demonstrated a TEAE rate of 42.2%, serious TEAE rate of 3.1%, and a total discontinuation rate of 27.4% (14.1% during dose conversion and 13.3% during the DB period). Foslevodopa/foscarbidopa reported a TEAE rate of 85%, serious TEAE rate of 8%, and discontinuation rate of 35.1%, while LCIG reported a TEAE rate of 95%, serious TEAE rate of 14%, and discontinuation rate of 8.8%.

In summary, the applicant's analysis compared accordingly the gains in 'ON time' and reduction in 'OFF time' at the end of the period of forced conversion to IPX203 in the randomised withdrawal study of IPX203, to the results obtained with duodopa or foslevodopa, all versus optimised IR LD-CD. However, since duodopa and foslevodopa studies were conducted longitudinally on a classical prospective parallel study, the shorter forced IPX203 period suffered less placebo effect waning. Furthermore, and in spite of the longer duration of the comparative studies as compared to the forced adjustment to IPX203, the assessors noted that the numerical improvement was higher with the nonoral alternatives than with IPX203. Nevertheless, it could be admitted that the improvement observed was within the same magnitude of effect, although probably less efficacious.

## Concomitant use of dopamine agonists (DA)

In study IPX203-B16-02 concomitant use of dopamine agonists (DA) was allowed. Therefore, available data supporting the use of Hopledo with DA came primarily from the inclusion of DA-treated patients in this trial population.

Clinical and demographic differences between DA-treated and non-DA treated populations are detailed in the Tables below.

DA-treated patients tended to have an earlier age of diagnosis (mean 56.22 vs . 59.99 years), a longer duration of PD (mean 8.84 vs . 7.69 years), and were more frequently from Europe, while non-DA patients were mostly from North America. When comparing the overall IPX203-B16-02 population to the DA-treated subgroup, the treatment effect of IPX203 on 'Good On' time was noted as consistent.

In the overall population who entered the conversion period (N=589), an improvement in 'Good On' time of 1.44 h (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.68; p &lt; 0.0001), compared to Visit 2, was observed. Among patients receiving concomitant DA (N=296), the improvement was 1.30 h (95% CI: 0.94 to 1.65; p &lt; 0.0001), comparable to the overall population. In the double-blind period (modified ITT), the change in 'Good On' Time were -0.50 h (95% CI: -0.86 to -0.14) and -1.03 h (95% CI: -1.39 to -0.67) for IPX203 and IR LD-CD, respectively, with a least squares mean difference of 0.53 h (95% CI: 0.09 to 0.97; p = 0.0194), favouring IPX203. Similarly, among patients using DA, the difference was 0.56 h (95% CI: -0.06 to 1.17; p = 0.0766 ). Although the p-value in the DA subgroup did not reach conventional statistical significance, the magnitude of benefit was comparable to the overall population, and the two CIs overlap.

These findings indicated that concomitant use of DA does not attenuate the efficacy of IPX203. On the contrary, data suggested that patients receiving DA therapy experienced similar improvements in 'Good ON' time compared to those not on DA therapy. In the course of the procedure the applicant provided further reassurance, comparing baseline characteristics of concomitantly treated LD+DA agonists vs . LD alone. Both populations were similar, although DA treated population came mostly from EU and were younger than those on LD alone, which were mostly based in the US and 3 years older. The use of Hopledo yielded similar results. The applicant did not provide the comparison of LD alone vs . LD+DA, but the comparison between the overall population (LD alone + LD and DA agonists). Notwithstanding, the results of the DA treated population had similar difference between use of IPX203 and IRLD: -0.56h in the DA+LD treated vs . -0.50h in those LD alone.

## Gender differences on 'Good ON time'

A statistically significant treatment difference in change from baseline in 'Good ON' time was demonstrated in males in favour of IPX203 vs IR LD - CD (p=0.0208, difference in LS means: 0.67 h [95% CI: 0.10, 1.24]), whereas in females the numerical difference favoured IPX203 but did not reach statistical significance (p=0.3934; difference in LS means: 0.33 h [95% CI: -0.43, 1.08]).

These observed difference between males and females in study IPX203-B16-02 should be perceived as resulting from the exploratory nature of subgroup analyses, differences in LD exposure, and underlying sex - related heterogeneity in Parkinson's disease biology and clinical management. There was a difference in average daily LD dose between males and females throughout the study: females received a lower mean daily dose of LD compared to males in both treatment arms during the DB period.

Literature data indicated several factors that may be responsible for sex differences in PD.  Cattaneo, C., Pagonabarraga, J. (2025) stated that sex differences in PD are multifactorial, involving neurobiological, hormonal, PK and clinical factors. Women tend to have lower body weight, higher LD bioavailability, and a higher risk of LD - induced motor complications and non - motor fluctuations, leading clinicians to preferentially use lower LD equivalent doses to mitigate dyskinesia risk. Oestrogen and other sex hormones exert neuroprotective and dopaminergic modulatory effects, and women often display a different motor and non - motor phenotype, including later onset of motor symptoms and higher prevalence of treatment - related complications compared with men.

Overall, the applicant considered that the sex - subgroup findings in Study IPX203 - B16 - 02 were best explained by the exploratory and underpowered nature of the subgroup analyses, lower LD doses in female participants across study phases, and known biological and clinical sex differences in PD that influence dosing decisions and variability of response. The directionally consistent, albeit non - significant, treatment difference in females, coupled with significant benefit in males and in the overall population, supported a treatment effect of IPX203 in both sexes. Therefore, the lack of statistical significance in women should not be interpreted as lack of efficacy, but as a reflection of multifactorial influences on observed effect size within this subgroup.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

These factors provided biological plausibility for sex - related differences in optimal dosing and clinical response patterns without implying a fundamentally different efficacy of IPX203 per se. In summary, no dose optimalisation in females was considered justified.

## Race - Caucasian vs . Non-Caucasian

The primary study endpoint was met in Caucasians but not in non-Caucasians.

In study IPX203-B16-02 the LS mean difference among non-Caucasian participants was -0.09 h (5.4 minutes), numerically favouring IR LD-CD with no statistical significance (p=0.9473). The nonCaucasian subgroup was notably small (n=19), and the 95% CIs of the LS means were wide and totally overlapping, limiting the interpretability and reliability of this comparison.

Despite the lack of statistical significance and the direction of the primary endpoint in this subgroup, several other efficacy parameters, including 'OFF' time, PGI-C, and motor function assessments, showed numerical trends favouring IPX203 in non-Caucasian subjects. The consistency of these findings across multiple endpoints suggested a potential clinical benefit that may not have been detectable due to the limited sample size and variability within the subgroup.

Importantly, subgroup analyses were exploratory and not powered for formal statistical comparisons. Therefore, the absence of statistical significance should be interpreted cautiously and cannot be taken as evidence of absence of treatment effect. The observed difference in 'Good ON' time among nonCaucasian participants should be viewed in the context of these limitations. The small sample size and large CIs constrain the ability to draw conclusions regarding treatment effect in this subgroup.

## Region / Geography - American vs . European

The North American and European cohorts were balanced in terms of age (mean 58.8 and 57.4 years, respectively), 'Good ON' and 'OFF' time at study entry ('Good ON': 9.44 and 9.63 h/day; OFF: 6.04 and 6.17 h/day), and racial composition (94.0% and 98.4% White/Caucasian, respectively). There were some differences in sex distribution (30.1% female in North America, 38.2% in Europe), duration of PD (7.72 years in North America, 8.84 years in Europe), and Hoehn &amp; Yahr stage (14.9% and 29.3% in HY stage 3-4).

With regard to the primary endpoint of study IPX203-B16-02, measured in hours per day, in the cohort of North American subjects (N=249), IPX203 demonstrated a statistically significant benefit over IR LD-CD, with LS mean difference of +0.79 h (95% CI: 0.19, 1.38; p=0.0096). In the cohort of European subjects (N=246), the difference was +0.28 h (95% CI: -0.39, 0.94; p=0.4135), which, while numerically favouring IPX203, did not reach statistical significance. To be noted that, when focusing on patients with 'OFF time' ≥ 6 h at study entry, the treatment effect of IPX203 was confirmed in North America but it was more pronounced also in Europe: the LS mean difference in 'Good ON' time was +0.67 h (95% CI: -0.18, 1.52; p=0.1213), reinforcing that IPX203 provided benefit even in European patients.

When analysing 'Good ON' time normalised per LD dose at the end of the treatment period (as outlined in the Table below) the treatment effect of IPX203 vs IR LD-CD was consistent and statistically significant in both EU and North American subjects. IPX203 treatment significantly increased 'Good ON' time per dose compared with IR LD-CD treatment (LS means difference 1.38 h [95% CI: 1.11, 1.65] in Europe, 1.73 h [95% CI: 1.49, 1.96] in North America; p &lt; 0.0001 in both regions).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

No statistically significant difference was noted between the two treatments in MDS-UPDRS Part III and sum of MDS-UPDRS Part II and III scores, both in North America and Europe.

A similar pattern like in 'Good ON' time was observed for PGI-C. In North America, 37.7% of IPX203treated subjects were rated as 'much improved' or 'very much improved,' compared to 21.6% for IR LD-CD (p=0.0023). In Europe, the rates were 22.4% for IPX203 and 15.5% for IR LD-CD (p=0.1786).

In summary, while the magnitude of the treatment effect for IPX203 was numerically smaller in Europe, the direction of benefit was consistent with North America and the overall study population. The lack of statistical significance in the European subgroup can be explained by demographic and disease-related factors, rather than any difference in drug response. Considering the safety profiles reported in North America and Europe, the benefit-risk profile for IPX203 was noted as favourable and consistent across regions.

The percentage of females was higher in the EU group compared to North America. All the differences outlined above between the two groups may have contributed to the lower 'Good ON' time observed in the European population.

## Other subgroup analysis

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Based on the results of the performed analyses of the primary endpoint per subgroups, the applicant was requested to justify the efficacy and safety (discussed in section 5.4.12 of this AR) of IPX203 in subjects (with):

- ≥ 65 years
- body weight of &lt;75 kg
- PD duration of ≥ 8 years
- PD onset at ≥ 65 years
- 'Off' time of &lt;6 hours

In the applicant's view, IPX203 overall efficacy (and safety) was preserved across these patient's populations, and no consistent signal of reduced benefit (or excess risk) was identified that would warrant excluding these patients from treatment.

As detailed above, in the overall modified ITT population, IPX203 showed superiority over IR LD - CD in change from baseline to Visit 7/ET in 'Good ON time' (least squares [LS] mean difference 0.53 h, p=0.0194), 'OFF time' (LS mean difference - 0.48 h, p=0.0252), and in the proportion of subjects reporting 'much improved' or 'very much improved' PGI - C (29.7% vs 18.8%, p=0.0015). These effects were accompanied by improvements in several diary-based additional endpoints (e.g., percent 'OFF time', duration of continuous 'Good ON') without worsening of MDS - UPDRS motor scores (or emergence of new safety concerns).

For the primary endpoint, subjects &lt;65 years showed a statistically significant IPX203 benefit in \"Good ON Time' (LS mean - 0.40 h vs - 1.75 h, p=0.0004), whereas in subjects ≥65 years 'Good ON time' had a LS mean of -0.61 h vs -0.57 h, p=0.8852). For the secondary endpoint 'OFF time', in subjects ≥65 years the LS mean was 0.44 h vs 0.57 h with IR CD - LD, (p=0.6423). In this older group, neither the primary endpoint nor the \"OFF\" time and PGI-C secondary endpoints reached statistical significance. These results have been reflected accordingly in the PI, where it is outlined that, particularly in patients aged 75 years and older, the available clinical data do not allow a definitive assessment of potential differences in the clinical response of Hopledo compared with IR levodopa/carbidopa. In this age group, a higher rate of dopaminergic adverse events was observed. Those adverse events were generally mild to moderate in severity and transient. For these reasons, cautious dose conversion with close clinical monitoring is recommended .

In the primary analysis by weight (&lt;75 vs ≥75 kg), 'Good ON' time was significantly improved with IPX203 only in subjects with weight ≥75 kg; in subjects &lt;75 kg, the LS mean changes in 'Good ON' time were similar between treatments with no statistically significant difference (IPX203 - 0.55 h vs IR CD - LD - 0.82 h; p=0.4523). Importantly, primary and secondary endpoints were numerically in favour of IPX203 in the &lt;75 kg subgroup, and there was no evidence of reduced tolerability or excess AEs in lower - weight subjects that would contraindicate IPX203. Given that the trial was not powered for weight - based subgroup hypotheses, the absence of a statistically significant difference in the &lt;75 kg subgroup should be interpreted as a limitation of the sample size and multiplicity rather than a clinically meaningful lack of efficacy.

IPX203 showed an advantage in 'Good ON' time in subjects with PD duration &lt;8 years (LS mean - 0.41 h vs - 1.18 h; difference 0.77 h; p=0.0207), whereas in subjects with PD duration ≥8 years 'Good ON' time changes were similar between treatments ( - 0.55 h vs - 0.88 h; p=0.2996). However, when examining 'OFF time' in the PD duration ≥8 years subgroup, this result is non-significant and near zero (0.58 h versus 0.59 h, respectively; p=0.9595).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In this longer - duration subgroup, a higher proportion of subjects on IPX203 were 'much' or 'very much' improved on PGI - C compared with IR CD - LD (p=0.0489), with no deterioration in MDS - UPDRS motor scores.

It is important to also flag in this context a safety aspect: it is well-known that LD PK may be altered by gastrointestinal dysfunctions such as dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, constipation, bacterial infection, gut dysbiosis, diet, comorbidities and concomitant medication intake (Leta et al , 2023). These factors may contribute to non-optimal LD response, symptoms fluctuations and unpredictable dyskinesia, and are more common in older patients and those with a PD onset in advanced age. Due to these 'confounding' factors, the results of these post-hoc analyses should be interpreted cautiously.

Subgroup analyses by age at PD onset showed that, in subjects with onset &lt;65 years, 'Good ON' time decreased less with IPX203 (LS mean -0.45 h) than with IR LD-CD (LS mean -1.29 h), with a statistically significant treatment difference of 0.84 h (95% CI: 0.33, 1.34; p=0.0013). In subjects with PD onset ≥65 years , the LS mean change in 'Good ON' time was -0.74 h with IPX203 vs -0.27 h with IR LD-CD (treatment difference -0.47 h [95% CI: -1.43, 0.49]; p=0.3351); non-significant patterns were also seen for 'OFF time' (treatment difference 0.13 h [95% CI: -0.72, 0.98]; p=0.7646), PGI-C (% much/very much improved: 19.4% vs 25.8%; difference -6.4% [95% CI: -20.8, 8.0]; p=0.8984), and MDS-UPDRS Part III/Part II+III scores. These results should be interpreted cautiously given the exploratory nature of the subgroup analyses, smaller sample size, and wide CIs indicating no clear signals. Of note that, as discussed in section 5.4.6 of this AR, safety profiles were comparable across subgroups. Hence, in the applicant's view, no evidence-based reason could be identified to exclude subjects with PD onset ≥65 years from IPX203 treatment.

In subjects with baseline 'OFF time' ≥6 hours , IPX203 increased 'Good ON' time (LS mean -0.64 h vs -1.66 h; difference 1.02 h; p=0.0010) and attenuated 'OFF time' increase versus IR LD-CD (LS mean 0.15 h vs 0.98 h; difference -0.83 h; p=0.0202), with a higher proportion of subjects reporting \"much\" or \"very much\" improved PGI-C. In the complementary subgroup with baseline 'OFF time' &lt;6 h, treatment differences were smaller and non-significant for 'Good ON' time (LS mean -0.30 h vs - 0.41 h; difference 0.10 h; p=0.7539) and 'OFF time' (LS mean 0.27 h vs 0.31 h; difference -0.04 h; p=0.9015). Importantly, there was no indication of deterioration with IPX203; 'Good ON', 'OFF time', and PGI-C remained comparable between treatments.

In addition to the exploratory nature of the subgroup analyses, one further known limitation, especially relevant for this subgroup of patients, was that the study did not allow IPX203 administration more frequently than every 6 hours. Some participants might have experienced a greater increase in 'Good ON' time and reduction in 'OFF time' with more frequent dose than every 6 h or if dosing frequency could have been titrated to clinical response. When analysing 'Good ON' time per LD dose at the end of the treatment period (as outlined in the Table below), IPX203 consistently showed a statistically significant benefit over IR LD-CD in both groups: those with less than 6 h and those with 6 h or more of 'OFF time'. Specifically, IPX203 led to significantly more 'Good ON' time per dose compared to IR LD-CD treatment (p&lt;0.0001, LS mean difference: 1.65 h [95% CI: 1.38, 1.92] for 'OFF time' &lt;6 h; and 1.48 h [95% CI: 1.25, 1.71] for 'OFF time' ≥ 6 h).

In conclusion, while subgroup analyses suggest attenuation of the primary 'Good ON' effect in certain highly overlapping subgroups (older age, lower weight, longer disease duration, later onset, lower baseline OFF), these analyses were exploratory, underpowered, and affected by strong correlations between covariates. Within these subgroups, IPX203 generally maintained favourable effects on 'Good ON time', 'OFF time', and PGI - C (and did not exhibit new safety concerns - as discussed in the dedicated safety section of this AR), even when formal statistical superiority versus IR CD - LD was not demonstrated.

## 5.4.2.2. Study IPX203-B16-03

## Study objective

IPX203-B16-03 was a Phase 3, 9-month, multicenter, open-label safety extension study to evaluate the long-term safety and clinical utility of IPX203 in the treatment of subjects with advanced PD who had motor fluctuations.

. Subjects who had successfully completed the randomised controlled trial IPX203-B16-02 had the opportunity to enrol in this open-label study.

The study consisted of a baseline visit (no 1) followed by 3 visits (no 2 to 4) spaced at approximately 3-month intervals. For subjects who had successfully completed Study IPX203-B16-02, the baseline visit (of this study coincided with the EOS Visit 7 of the preceding study (with an allowed window of + 7 days). Subjects were initially started on the final IPX203 dosing regimen determined during the IPX203 dose conversion period of study IPX203-B16-02. Investigators were permitted to adjust the dosing regimen of IPX203 during this study to achieve the optimal balance of efficacy and safety and any changes were recorded. Subjects continued to take their non-LD containing PD concomitant medications (including dopamine agonists, amantadine, selective monoamine oxidase [MAO]-B inhibitors [safinamide, rasagiline, and selegiline]) during study IPX203-B16-03. Changes in doses or in dosing regimens of all non-CD-LD PD medications and/or the addition of new non-CD-LD PD medications were also captured. Supplemental CD and benserazide, apomorphine, and the addition of COMT inhibitors (e.g., entacapone, opicapone, and tolcapone) could likewise be initiated during this study.

Adverse events, supine and standing orthostatic vital signs, and concomitant medications were evaluated throughout the course of the study. Electrocardiograms (ECGs), clinical laboratory tests, physical examinations, the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) and Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index (GCSI), were also considered.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The following clinical utility measures were assessed: Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Parts I to IV, Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S), Clinician Global Impression of Severity (CGI-S), the 39-item Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ39), Parkinson Anxiety Scale (PAS), Non-Motor Symptom assessment scale (NMSS) for Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale 2 (PDSS-2), Treatment Satisfaction Assessment (TSA), 12Item Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI-12), and Early Morning Symptoms Questionnaire (EMSQ). Visit 4 was the EOS visit.

## Diagnosis and Main Criteria for Inclusion

## Inclusion Criteria:

1. Successfully completed Study IPX203-B16-02;
2. Able to provide written informed consent prior to the conduct of any study-specific procedures;
3. Female subjects of childbearing potential were to have a negative urine pregnancy test at the Baseline visit (Visit 1);
4. Agreed to use a medically acceptable method of contraception throughout the study and for 6 weeks after completing the study.

## Exclusion Criteria:

1. Intended to use any doses of Rytary® or Duopa™ during this study;
2. Planned to use an investigational treatment other than IPX203 during the course of this study;
3. Neurosurgical  ablation  treatment  for  PD  planned  or  anticipated  during  the  study  period. Implantation of a deep brain stimulator (DBS) for the treatment of PD was permitted during this study;
5. Subjects who, in the opinion of the clinical investigator, were not to participate in the study.

## Clinical Utility Measures:

MDS-UPDRS Part I to IV, PGI-S, CGI-S, PDQ-39, PAS, NMSS, PDSS-2, TSA, ZBI-12, and EMSQ were assessed at every visit.

## Statistics

Subjects were assigned to treatment group defined by the treatment received in the DB phase of the previous IPX203-B16-02 study (IPX203 or IR CD-LD). Data were summarised using descriptive statistics for continuous variables. Unless otherwise specified, statistics included number of subjects, mean, standard deviation (SD), minimum, median, and maximum. Tables of categorical variables, counts and percentages were displayed accordingly by the applicant. Baseline was defined as the last assessment obtained prior to the first dose of the open-label drug in this IPX203-B16-03 study.

The study electronic case report form (eCRF) did not explicitly capture when the subject took the first open-label study drug dose. Therefore, it was assumed that this dose had been taken on the day of Visit 1, after all study assessments.

The analysis' populations used in this study were:

- Safety Analysis Set (SAS): it included all subjects treated with the open-label study drug in the study.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The study eCRF did not explicitly capture if a subject took the open-label study drug. Thus, it was assumed that a subject took the open-label study drug if (and only if) the study drug was dispensed to the subject at one of the study visits.

- Intent-to-Treat (ITT) Analysis Set: it included all subjects treated with the open-label study drug in the study and had at least one post-baseline clinical utility assessment.

## Clinical Utility Analysis

Analysis of the clinical utility endpoints was performed on the ITT population.

The Total MDS-UPDRS and each of its components (Parts I through IV), and Parts II and III combined, PGI-S, CGI-S, PDQ-39, PAS, NMSS, PDSS-2, TSA, ZBI-12, and EMSQ scores, as well as the changes from baseline in these scores, were summarised by visit and treatment group, as well as for both treatment groups combined. A summary of the study entry baseline of Study IPX203-B16-02 was also included.

A total of 419 subjects were enrolled: 206 from the previous IPX203 randomised group and 213 from the previous IR LD-CD randomised group (in the double-blind period of Study IPX203-B16-02). A total of 352 (84%) subjects completed the study: 179 (86.9%) from the previous IPX203 group and 173 (81.2%) from the previous IR LD-CD group, respectively. Overall, 67 (16.0%) subjects discontinued the study: 27 (13.1%) from the previous IPX203 group and 40 (18.8%) from the previous IR LD-CD group, respectively . The primary reasons of study discontinuations (≥20% of total subjects who discontinued) were subject withdrawal (22 [32.8%] subjects), AEs (20 [29.9%] subjects), and lack of efficacy (14 [20.9%] subjects).

The demographic and baseline characteristics were comparable among the subjects from the previous IPX203 IR CD-LD groups. Overall, the mean (SD) age of subjects was 66.9 (8.86) years, majority were male (279 [66.6%]) and white (406 [96.9%]) The mean (SD) BMI of the subjects was 27.472

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

(5.0074) kg/m 2 . The mean (SD) age of onset of PD was 58.0 (9.32) years, and the mean (SD) duration of PD was 8.8 (4.84) years.

All clinical utility measures were stable, and efficacy was maintained for the full duration of the study, (throughout the 9 months). Overall, there were minor changes in mean (SD) TDD of LD or in dosing frequency over the 9 months of treatment. After 3 months, most subjects had found a stable dosing regimen and maintained that regimen for the remainder of the study. This was an indication that the efficacy/safety profile of IPX203 was acceptable and could be maintained over a long period of time. No notable difference was observed in any of the clinical utility measures scores from baseline to EOS (Visit 4/Month 9). The scores were also comparable over the 9-month treatment period between the subjects previously randomised to IPX203 compared to those previously randomised to IR LD-CD (in the DB period of Study IPX203-B16-02) as detailed below.

At baseline, the two groups were well balanced in demographic and clinical characteristics and demonstrated comparable efficacy profiles throughout the extension.

Age distribution was similar across groups. The mean age was 66.7 years in the prior IPX203 group and 67.1 years in the prior IR LD-CD group, while the median age was identical, at 68 years in both cohorts. Gender distribution was also aligned: the IPX203 group included 131 males (63.6%) and 75 females (36.4%), whereas the IR LD-CD group comprised 148 males (69.5%) and 65 females (30.5%). Most participants were white (97.1% in the IPX203 group and 96.7% in the IR LD-CD group). Anthropometric measures were closely matched, with mean BMI of 27.6 kg/m² for IPX203 and 27.4 kg/m² for IR LD-CD, respectively.

Disease history was comparable between groups. The mean time since diagnosis was 8.9 years for IPX203 and 8.8 years for IR LD-CD, and the mean age at PD onset was 57.7 years for IPX203 and 58.3 years for IR LD-CD respectively.

Baseline disease severity was also similar across multiple measures: the mean MDS-UPDRS total score was 57.3 for IPX203 and 56.7 for IR LD-CD. Sub-scores were nearly identical, with Part I averaging 10.0 in both groups; Part II at 13.1 for IPX203 and 12.6 for IR LD-CD; Part III at 27.8 and 27.3; and Part IV at 6.5 and 6.8, respectively. Hoehn and Yahr stage averaged 2.2 in both groups, and most subjects were classified as stage 2 (69.4% for IPX203 and 73.9% for IR LD-CD).

Subjects initiated IPX203 at the regimen determined at the end of the double-blind phase, and the dosing remained stable throughout the 9-month extension. The mean TDD at baseline was 1477.1 mg for prior IPX203 subjects and 1483.5 mg for prior IR LD-CD subjects, with minimal increases by month 9 (+100.8 mg and +64.3 mg, respectively). Dose adjustments occurred but returned to baseline levels in 10.2% and 8.2% of subjects, respectively.

Study completion rates were slightly higher in the prior IPX203 group (86.9%) compared to the prior IR LD-CD group (81.2%). Discontinuations were more frequent among prior IR LD-CD subjects (18.8% versus 13.1%), primarily due to AEs (14 subjects, 35.0% vs 6 subjects, 22.2%). Conversely, discontinuations due to lack of efficacy were more common in the prior IPX203 group (9 subjects, 33.3% vs 5 subjects, 12.5%). Subjects' withdrawals accounted for approximately one-third of discontinuations in both groups.

Efficacy was assessed primarily through changes in MDS-UPDRS scores and other patient-reported outcomes. MDS-UPDRS total scores increased slightly from baseline to Month 9 (+2.5 points for prior IPX203; +2.0 points for prior IR LD-CD). Scores remained comparable throughout the study: Month 3 (57.0 vs 55.9), Month 6 (56.5 vs 55.6), and Month 9 (58.9 vs 58.6). Part I and II scores were stable, with no clinically meaningful changes. For Part I, baseline scores were 9.9 vs 9.8, rising to 11.1 vs

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

10.9 at Month 9 (mean change: +1.4 vs +1.0; overall +1.2). Part II started at 13.0 vs 12.6 and ended at 13.6 vs 13.5 (mean change: +0.8 vs +0.7; overall +0.8). Part III remained unchanged, moving from 27.8 vs 27.1 at baseline to 28.1 vs 27.8 at Month 9 (mean change: +0.4 both). Motor complications (Part IV) decreased slightly, from 6.4 vs 6.8 at baseline to 6.2 vs 6.4 at Month 9 (mean change: -0.1 vs -0.2).

Non-motor symptoms and quality-of-life measures were similarly stable:

- Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S) remained at around 3.7 in both groups by Month 9 (mean change: 0 vs -0.1).
- Clinical Global Impression of Severity (CGI-S) decreased marginally (baseline 3.8 vs 3.9; Month 9: 3.8 vs 3.7; overall -0.1).
- 39-item Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39) total score increased by 4.1 points overall (IPX203 +5.3; IR LD-CD +2.9).
- Parkinson Anxiety Scale (PAS) total rose by 0.8 (IPX203 +0.7; IR LD-CD +0.8).
- Non-Motor Symptom Assessment Scale (NMSS) increased by 3.9 points (IPX203 +4.0; IR LD-CD +3.8).
- Sleep quality, assessed by PD Sleep Scale-2 (PDSS2), showed negligible change (-0.1 overall, IPX203 0; IR LDCD -0.2). Domain changes: Disturbed Sleep +0.3 both; Motor Symptoms at Night -0.2 total (-0.1 IPX203; -0.4 IR LD - CD); PD Symptoms at Night -0.2 both.

Overall, the open-label extension of study IPX203-B16-02 did not show any critical issues in efficacy, as it would be expected after a randomised withdrawal study to similar active components and return to the expected best treatment. Notwithstanding, it would have been expected that the subgroup of patients who had previously been in IR-LD would improve slightly under IPX203 again.

The pivotal IPX203-B16-02 (RISE-PD) study employed the Hauser diary to capture daily fluctuations in motor state, specifically 'Good On time' and 'OFF time', highly sensitive indicators of treatment benefit in PD. In contrast, the OLE (IPX203-B16-03) did not include Hauser diary assessments, relying instead on clinic-based scales such as the MDS-UPDRS. This approach was not optimal.

At the end of RISE-PD, the difference between groups in 'Good On time' and 'OFF time' was only approximately 30 minutes, as the IR LD-CD group unexpectedly did not return to its pre-conversion level, suggesting a carryover effect. All patients entering the OLE had been previously optimised on both IR LD-CD and IPX203 during the parent study, which further minimised baseline differences. Given this minimal difference at OLE entry, any incremental improvement in the prior IR LD-CD group after switching to IPX203 was expected to be small and clinically subtle and unlikely to be detected by clinic-based instruments such as the MDS-UPDRS.

These scales, while appropriate for global severity assessment, are less sensitive to short-term changes in motor fluctuations compared to the Hauser diary. Therefore, the absence of measurable differences between subgroups in the OLE reflects both the small difference in disease control at baseline and the limited responsiveness of the scales used. Importantly, the OLE was not designed to compare efficacy between prior IR LD-CD and IPX203 groups, so differences were not expected. Rather its purpose was to evaluate long-term safety, tolerability, and stability of IPX203.

The results confirmed that IPX203 maintained stable efficacy and tolerability over 9 months, regardless of prior treatment assignment. Switching between formulations did not harm patients, supporting treatment flexibility in clinical practice.

## 5.4.10. Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical efficacy

## 5.4.10.1. Discussion

Key information on IPX203 efficacy is outlined below. This should be read in conjunction with section 5.2.6.

The applicant conducted two Phase 2 (Studies IPX203-B14-02 and IPX203-B16-01 ) and two Phase 3 (Studies IPX203-B16-02 and IPX203-B16-03 ) studies to support this initial MAA. The primary objective of the Phase 2 study IPX203-B16-01 was to compare the PK of single and multiple doses of IPX203 with immediate-release (IR) CD-LD in subjects with advanced PD. Levodopa and CD were administered at a fixed ratio of 4:1.

Idiopathic PD patients, aged ≥40 years, chronically treated with stable regimens of LD -CD but experiencing motor complications, were randomised to one of two dosing sequences: IPX203 followed by IR CD-LD or vice versa. Each treatment period lasted 15 days, separated by a 1-week washout when subjects received their usual stable pre-study PD medications. The study consisted of four visits

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

after screening: at Day 1 (visits 1 and 3) and 15 (visits 2 and 4) of each treatment period.

Twenty-eight subjects were randomised; 27 (96.4%) completed the study. One withdrew because of an AE while on IPX203, and did not receive IR CD-LD. The subjects mean (SD) age was 66.4 (10.1) years. Males slightly outnumbered females (16 versus 12). The majority (92.9%) of subjects were white.

Initial IPX203 doses were chosen based on previous PK data with IPX203 and IR CD-LD in advanced PD patients: a LD dose of approximately 270 to 360 mg from IPX203 was expected to provide peak LD concentrations comparable to those of 100 mg LD from IR CD-LD. This approach was considered acceptable.

During IPX203 treatment, on average, IPX203 treatment was associated with approximately 2.3 hours less \"OFF time' than IR CD-LD. Most of this improvement (1.9 hours) was on \"Good ON\" time. Durations of \"Good ON\" episodes or any \"ON\" episodes were longer with IPX203 (LS means differences: 2.89 h and 3.79 h, respectively). IPX203 treatment was also associated with fewer motor fluctuations per day. A higher proportion of subjects experienced a reduction in \"OFF' time of at least 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 hours during IPX203 than during IR CD-LD treatment.

When predose mean MDS-UPDRS Parts I-IV scores were compared by treatment on Day 15, subjects had lower scores for Parts III, II and III, and IV as well as the MDS-UPDRS total score with IPX203, indicating less PD impairment.

At predose on Day 15, when subjects had not had a study treatment for at least 5 hours, the mean MDS-UPDRS Part III score was lower during IPX203 than IR CD-LD treatment (33.5 versus. 41.6), suggesting that IPX203 clinical effects may carry over to the next morning.

Analysis of Part IV individual items also demonstrated benefits of IPX203 versus IR CD-LD, both in terms of time spent in 'OFF' state and functional impact of fluctuations.

On Day 1, subjects receiving IPX203 were 73.3% less likely to receive rescue medication; on Day 15, these subjects were 72.1% less likely to receive a predose than those receiving IR CD-LD.

The investigator's assessment of the subject's motor state on Day 1 demonstrated less \"OFF' time and significantly more \"Good ON\" time with IPX203 compared with IR CD-LD (2.57 h difference for each). On Day 15, treatment differences were again seen in \"OFF' time and \"Good ON\" time, although the magnitude of these differences was smaller.

During the 10-hour postdose observation period, 63% of subjects on IPX203 treatment period experienced less than 2 hours of 'OFF' time compared to 19% during IR CD-LD treatment period. Average times to first \"ON\" and first 'Good ON' states after the first dose were not significantly different between treatments on Days 1 or 15.

MDS-UPDRS Part III mean scores on Day 1 were lower during IPX203 treatment than during IR CD-LD treatment from 3 to 8 hours postdose; across the 8 hours post-dose, the mean scores were 23.6 during IPX203 and 33.0 during IR CD-LD treatment (p&lt;0.0001). Subjects had longer total durations of PD effect during IPX203 than during IR CD-LD treatment, based on minimal improvement thresholds of at least 4, 7, and 13 points on the MDS-UPDRS Part III scale. From 3 to 7 hours postdose, greater proportions of subjects taking IPX203 than taking IR CD-LD met each of 3 minimal improvement thresholds. On Day 15, across the 10 hours postdose, the mean MDS-UPDRS Part III scores were 18.2 for IPX203 and 22.0 for IR CD-LD (p=0.0226), respectively.

The sum of scores from bradykinesia questions from Part III (sum of Questions 4-8, and 14) showed more reduction with IPX203 than IR CD-LD on Day 1 (overall and at hours 3 through 7) but not on Day 15 (except at hours 3 and 4).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The pivotal Phase 3 study IPX203-B16-02 evaluated safety and efficacy of IPX203 (in comparison to IR LD-CD) in the treatment of LD-CD-experienced subjects with PD, with motor fluctuations aged ≥ 40 years.

The study population accurately reflected IPX203 the proposed target population and indication for use (revised in the course of the procedure, as detailed in section 8.1.1.). This trial consisted of an up to 4-week screening period, a 3-week open-label (OL) IR CD-LD dose adjustment period, followed by a 4-week OL period for conversion to IPX203, and a 13-week double-blind (DB), double-dummy treatment period. Subjects were randomised in a 1:1 ratio, stratified by center, to receive either IPX203 (with matching IR CD-LD placebo) or IR CD-LD (with matching IPX203 placebo).

The study primary endpoint (PEP) was a mean change from baseline in 'Good ON' time in hours per day, averaged over the PD diary days, at the end of the DB treatment period (Visit 7 or early termination). 'Good ON' time was derived from the 3-day PD diaries and defined as the sum of 'ON time without dyskinesia' and 'ON time with non-troublesome dyskinesia'.  No medication adjustments were allowed after randomisation and during the study DB phase. This approach was considered acceptable.

The study design, the choice of endpoints and hierarchy were also considered adequate.

Usually, improving 'ON time' is frequently done at the cost of increased sleep time or increased dyskinesias. The effect on sleep and the harmonised 'ON time' deals with the first aspect. However, the details regarding frequency and severity were not provided. No dedicated tool to measure dyskinesias were used.

Six-hundred and thirty subjects were enrolled and entered the IR CD-LD dose adjustment period.

Forty-one (6.5%) dropped out. Thereafter, of the 589 who entered the IPX203 conversion period, 83 (13.2%) withdrew from the study. The primary reasons for discontinuation were AEs ( 35 [ 42.2% ] subjects), withdrawal by subject ( 32 [ 38.6% ]), and lack of efficacy ( 10 [ 12.0% ]). The applicant clarified the reasons behind 'withdrawals by subject': most were due to the stabilisation falling behind the patients' expectations. This may be related to the rigid drug scheme required.

Further, 506 subjects were randomised to IPX203 (256) and IR CD-LD (250); 449 completed the study: 222 (86.7%) in IPX203 group and 227 (90.8%) in IR CD-LD group.

Fifty-seven (11.3%) subjects discontinued early from the DB maintenance period: 34 (13.3%) from IPX203 and 23 (9.2%) from IR CD-LD group, respectively. The primary reasons for discontinuations in IPX203 group were AEs (14 [41.2%] subjects), withdrawal by subject (10 [29.4%]), lack of efficacy (5 [14.7%]) and protocol deviations (3 [8.8%]). The primary reasons for discontinuations in IR CD-LD group were withdrawal by subject (11 [47.8%]), lack of efficacy (8 [34.8%]), and AEs (3 [13.0%]). The number of subjects, who discontinued IPX203 in study IPX203-B16-02, considered very high, raised concerns (especially, the 83 during dose conversion period, of whom 10 due to lack efficacy, also looking at the overall higher number of subjects who discontinued from the DB maintenance period). Particularly, the difference in an incidence of discontinuations due to AEs (41.2% vs 13%) was flagged to the applicant for further analysis.

It was agreed that the impact on the overall efficacy and safety of the 83 subjects who discontinued during the dose-conversion period of study IPX203-B16-02 should be interpreted in the context of IPX203 as new MR formulation designed to replace IR LD-CD in patients with PD with motor fluctuations. Conversion to IPX203 involved dose titration, including transient lack of efficacy or dopaminergic AEs, which could lead to discontinuation. The initial suggested IPX203 doses in the protocol were based on average bioavailability relative to IR LD-CD. However, most subjects required individualised up-titration or down-titration to achieve an optimal balance of efficacy and tolerability.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

During the 4-week IPX203 dose-conversion period, 83 subjects (14.1%) discontinued primarily due to AEs and lack of efficacy. These discontinuations largely reflected the process of establishing a clinically effective and tolerable IPX203 regimen rather than inherent lack of efficacy of IPX203.

In addition, the applicant provided information on AEs during IPX203 conversion period: 229 (38.9%) subjects experienced at least one TEAE. The most frequently reported TEAEs (≥2%) in subjects who received IPX203 were dyskinesia (40 [6.8%]), nausea (29 [4.9%]), dry mouth (25 [4.2%]), dizziness (17 [2.9%]), constipation (12 [2.0%]), vomiting, fall and insomnia (each 13 [2.2%]). Overall, the above is consistent with what expected upon transitioning from IR to MR LD.

Subjects receiving IPX203 showed a greater improvement in the mean 'Good ON' time from baseline to the end of DB therapy (Visit 7/ET) when compared with those receiving IR CD-LD (mean change from baseline to Visit 7/ET; IPX203: -0.39 h and IR CD-LD: -0.97 h). 'Good ON' time decreased less in the IPX203 group (LS mean: -0.50 h) when compared with IR CD-LD group (LS mean: -1.03 h). IPX203 treatment resulted in significantly more hours of 'Good ON' time compared with IR CD-LD treatment (p=0.0194, difference in LS means: 0.53 h [95% CI: 0.09, 0.97]). However, in the perprotocol (PP) analysis set, no statistical significance was observed in 'Good ON' results.

Subjects receiving IPX203 showed a greater improvement in the mean 'OFF' time from baseline to Visit 7/ET when compared with those receiving IR CD-LD (IPX203: 0.29 h and IR CD-LD: 0.76 h). 'OFF' time increased less in the IPX203 group (LS mean: 0.38 h) when compared with IR CD-LD group (LS mean: 0.86 h). IPX203 treatment resulted in significantly less 'OFF' time compared with IR CD-LD treatment (p=0.0252, difference in LS means: -0.48 h [95% CI: -0.90, -0.06]). However, in the PP analysis set statistical significance was not reached.

At Visit 7/ET, higher number of subjects in IPX203 group reported improvement in PGI-C scores (56.9%) compared with IR CD-LD group (46.3%). Moreover, a statistically significant proportion of subjects (p=0.0015) reported 'much improved' or 'very much improved' response with IPX203 treatment (29.7%) compared to IR CD-LD treatment (18.8%). Similar statistically significant results were observed in the PP analysis set (p=0.0161): 32.9% of subjects reported 'much improved' or 'very much improved' response with IPX203 treatment compared to 22.2% of those with IR CD-LD treatment. However, no statistically significant difference in MDS-UPDRS Part III scores from baseline to Visit 7/ET was reached with IPX203 versus IR CD-LD (p=0.9587). Also, no statistically significant difference in sum of MDS-UPDRS Part II and III scores was reported with IPX203 versus IR CD-LD (p=0.9668).

A lesser increase in the mean percent 'OFF time' during waking hours from baseline to Visit 7/ET was observed in subjects receiving IPX203 versus those receiving IR CD-LD (mean change from baseline to Visit 7/ET; IPX203: 1.75 and IR CD-LD: 4.55).

Likewise, a lesser decrease from double-blind baseline to Visit 7/ET was reported in the mean 'ON time' without dyskinesia in subjects on IPX203 compared with those on IR CD-LD (mean change from double-blind baseline to Visit 7/ET; IPX203: -0.43 h and IR CD-LD: -0.97 h).

There were no significant differences between IPX203 and IR CD-LD groups from the DB baseline to Visit 7/ET in the mean 'ON time' with troublesome dyskinesia, in the mean 'asleep' time and in proportion of subjects with an improvement in 'Good On' time as per PD Diary.

A 36.2% of subjects in the IPX203 group had a reduction of at least 0.5 hours in 'OFF time' at Visit 7/ET compared with 33.6% in the IR CD-LD group. Significantly fewer subjects in IPX203 group (11.9%) compared to IR CD-LD group (18.7%) had a reduction of ≥ 2 hours (p=0.0309) at Visit 7/ET.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The percentage of subjects in the 'ON' state upon awakening for at least 1 of the 3 recorded PD diary days at Visit 7/ET was statistically significantly higher in IPX203 group (53.1%) compared to IR CDLD group (44.5%) (p=0.0046). Moreover, the proportion of those in 'Good ON' state upon awakening at Visit 7/ET was also higher in IPX203 group compared to IR CD-LD group (p=0.0060).

Subjects receiving IPX203 showed a lesser increase in the average number of motor fluctuations per day from baseline to Visit 7/ET when compared with those receiving IR CD-LD (p&lt;0.0001, difference in LS means: -1.35 [95% CI: -1.72, -0.97]).

No statistically significant difference was noted with IPX203 versus IR CD-LD treatment in MDSUPDRS total score (p=0.9639), Part I (p=0.5549), Part II (p=0.9186), or Part IV scores (p=0.8735): subjects in both groups had a similar degree of change.

No differences were noted with IPX203 compared to IR CD-LD in the PDQ-39 total score. However, a statistically significant difference was reported in favour of IPX203 for the emotional well-being score.

There were no differences in IPX203 versus IR CD-LD treatment in the NMSS total score, except for a statistically significant difference in perceptual problems/hallucinations score (p=0.0094, difference in LS means: 0.6 [95% CI: 0.1, 1.0]).

To increase robustness of data, the applicant compared study IPX203-B16-02 results with those of advanced medical therapies for PD, namely Duodopa and Foslevodopa. Since a direct comparison was not possible due to different study design (IPX203-B16-02 was a randomised withdrawal while the others were prospective), the applicant focused on the improvements observed during IPX203 dose conversion period, which most closely corresponds to the DB treatment phase of the LCIG and Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Phase 3 trials. This allowed to compare the incremental benefit of the therapy on top of the optimised IR LD-CD.

There are several strategies to improve motor control. Of these, the use of dopamine agonists (DA) is very common in patients with motor fluctuations / dyskinesias, concomitantly being treated with LD. Available data supporting the concomitant use of IPX203 with DA, and whether the use of oral or transdermic formulations showed a different response pattern, was also sufficiently presented.

During IPX203 conversion period, patients already optimised on IR LD-CD experienced an improvement in 'Good ON time' of 1.45 h and in OFF time of 1.46 h. In comparison, the Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa pivotal trial of Soileau et al (2022) reported an improvement in 'Good ON time' of 1.75 h and a reduction in 'OFF time' of 1.79 h vs IR LD-CD, while the LCIG pivotal trial of Olanow n . (2014) demonstrated an increase in 'Good On time' of 1.86 h and a reduction in 'OFF time' of 1.91 h vs IR LD-CD. The IPX203 forced conversion period, however, was much shorter than the FU provided in Duodopa and Foslevodopa studies, making them probably more effective. Therefore, it can only be admitted that the observed improvement is in the same magnitude of effect as the non-oral alternatives.

A statistically significant result in ' Good ON ' time was achieved in IPX203 group compared with IR CD-LD group only in subjects &lt;65 years (p=0.0004, difference in LS means: 1.35 h [95% CI: 0.62, 2.08]). In subjects ≥ 65 years no statistically significant difference was noted between groups. The CHMP could agree that, although in subjects ≥65 years 'Good ON time' was comparable between treatments and statistical significance was not reached, benefits of treatment in this population can be expected based on results of other endpoints (e.g., 'OFF time' and PGI - C).

Statistically significant result in 'Good ON' time was achieved in males treated with IPX203 compared with those treated with IR CD-LD but not in females. However, these differences should be perceived as resulting from the exploratory nature of the subgroup analyses, differences in LD exposure, and underlying sex - related heterogeneity in PD biology and clinical management. There was a difference in average daily levodopa dose between males and females throughout study IPX203-B16-02: females received a lower mean daily dose of LD compared to males in both treatment arms during the DB Based on these aspects, no dose optimalisation in females was considered justified.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Similarly, a statistically significant difference was shown in subjects with a PD onset at &lt;65 years. In subjects with PD onset ≥65 years , the LS mean change in 'Good ON' time was -0.74 h with IPX203 vs -0.27 h with IR LD-CD (treatment difference -0.47 h [95% CI: -1.43, 0.49]; p=0.3351). Non-significant patterns were also seen for 'OFF time' (treatment difference 0.13 h [95% CI: -0.72, 0.98]; p=0.7646), PGI-C (% much/very much improved: 19.4% vs 25.8%; difference -6.4% [95% CI: -20.8, 8.0]; p=0.8984), and MDS-UPDRS Part III/Part II+III scores. However, the results should and wide CIs indicating no clear signals. Of note, as discussed in section 5.4.6 of this AR, safety could be identified to exclude subjects with PD onset ≥65 years from IPX203 treat significant difference in ' Good ON ' time was shown in IPX203 subjects with a ' OFF ' time of ≥ 6 hours versus IR CD-LD subjects) and no statistically significant difference was reported in subjects with a ' OFF time' of ≥ 6 hours at study entry.

period. Literature data also indicated several factors that may be responsible for sex differences in PD. Similarly, the primary endpoint was met in Caucasians but not in non-Caucasians. However, the nonCaucasian subgroup was very small (n=19), which largely limits interpretability of the comparison to Caucasians. Nevertheless, several efficacy parameters ('OFF time', PGI-C and motor function assessments), showed numerical trends favouring IPX203 in non-Caucasians. The primary endpoint was not met in EU subjects. In North American subjects, 'Good ON' time decreased less in IPX203 (LS mean: -0.39 h) when compared with IR CD-LD group (LS mean: -1.18 h). A statistically significant result in 'Good ON' time was achieved in IPX203 group when compared with IR CD-LD group (p=0.0096). Looking at the identified differences between North American and EU subjects, the more pronounced benefit in US patients seemed related to the more widespread use of concomitant medications such as dopamine agonists (DAs) and monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), and to the fact that in the EU population, although with the disease for longer time and with higher H&amp;Y score than those in US, but the duration of 'OFF time', was lower. When comparing those with more severity, there was a similar magnitude of improvement, even favouring EU patients. Body weight was also shown to affect the study results. A statistically significant result in ' Good ON ' time was achieved only in subjects with a body weight of ≥ 75 kg treated with IPX203 versus those treated with IR CD-LD. The applicant justified that most intrinsic patient's factors (identified as being possible discriminators between treatment responses) have been thoroughly discussed in the literature (gender, BMI, disease severity and age), and none justifies a reappreciation of the B/R or a recommendation for different posology. The CHMP could agree that, although in subjects &lt;75 kg no statistically significant difference was shown in the LS mean changes in 'Good ON time', numerical difference was observed. Moreover, no signs of worse tolerability or higher incidence of AEs in this group of patients was observed. In subjects with a PD duration of &lt;8 years , a statistically significant difference in 'Good ON' time was achieved with IPX203 rather than IR CD-LD treatment (p=0.0207, difference in LS means: 0.77 h [95% CI: 0.12, 1.42]). Importantly, there was no indication of deterioration with IPX203; 'Good ON time,' 'OFF time', and PGI-C remained comparable between treatments. In addition to the exploratory nature of the subgroup analyses, one further known limitation, especially relevant for this subgroup of patients, was that the study did not allow IPX203 administration more frequently than every 6 hours. Some participants might have experienced a greater increase in 'Good ON' time and reduction in 'OFF time' with more frequent dose than every 6 hours or if dosing frequency could have been titrated to clinical response. When analysing 'Good ON' time per LD dose at the end of the treatment period, IPX203 consistently showed a statistically significant benefit over IR LD-CD in both groups: those with less than 6 h and those with 6 h or more of 'OFF time'.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In conclusion, while these subgroup analyses suggest attenuation of the primary 'Good ON' effect in certain highly overlapping subgroups (older age, lower weight, longer disease duration, later onset, lower baseline 'OFF'), these analyses were exploratory, underpowered, and affected by strong correlations between covariates. Within these subgroups, IPX203 generally maintained favourable effects on 'Good ON time', 'OFF time', and PGI - C and did not exhibit new safety concerns, even when formal statistical superiority versus IR CD - LD was not demonstrated.

Overall, the observed magnitude of effect of IPX203 was small (0.53 hour) as compared to IR-LD, but IPX203 was administered three times a day while IR-LD was to be taken five times a day. The fact that the 3 oral formulations of IPX203 performed better than the 5 of IR-LD suggested that the time of intake is less critical for IPX203 than with IR-LD, representing an inherent advantage in the target patient's population.

IPX203-B16-03 was a Phase 3, 9-month, OLE study evaluating long-term safety and clinical utility of IPX203 in patients who had successfully completed the pivotal study IPX203-B16-02. It consisted of a baseline visit (no 1) followed by 3 others (no 2 to 4) approximately every 3-months.

A total of 419 subjects (of which 71.7% had a baseline Hoehn and Yahr Stage 2) were enrolled: 206 from previous IPX203 and 213 from previous IR CD-LD group. Of those enrolled, 352 (84%) completed the study: 179 (86.9%) from previous IPX203 and 173 (81.2%) from previous IR CD-LD group.

Sixty-seven (16.0%) subjects withdrew: 27 (13.1%) from previous IPX203 and 40 (18.8%) from previous IR CD-LD group.

Overall, the mean MDS-UPDRS total scores were stable throughout the treatment period. No notable difference was observed in the mean MDS-UPDRS total score from baseline to EOS (Visit 4/Month 9) (mean change from baseline to Visit 4; total: 2.3, previous IPX203 group: 2.5, and previous IR CD-LD: 2.0). The total scores were also comparable between previous IPX203 and IR CDLD subjects over the treatment period.

The mean MDS-UPDRS Part I, Part II, Part III and Part IV scores were also stable and comparable between groups. Moreover, no differences in PGI-S, CGI-S, PD Questionnaire-39, Parkinson Anxiety Scale, PD Sleep Scale-2 and Early Morning Symptoms Questionnaire scores were observed from baseline to EOS (Visit 4/ET), and between previous IPX203 and IR CD-LD subjects over the treatment period.

The indication was revised accordingly.

## 5.4.10.2. Conclusions on the clinical efficacy

Overall, the clinical development programme is considered acceptable.

It can be agreed that efficacy of IPX203 has been demonstrated, in terms of a benefit over IR LD-CD, expressed on longer duration of 'Good ON time', without significant worsening of sleep time or time with troublesome dyskinesias. The smaller number of intakes per day may also be an inherent advantage in the target patient's population.

## 5.5. Clinical safety

Please refer to the Table(s) of studies in section 5.1.2 of this AR.

For the purpose of this document, the following definitions apply:

- 'Adverse event - AE' means any untoward medical occurrence in a subject to whom a medicinal product is administered, and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with this treatment.
- 'Serious adverse event - SAE' means any untoward medical occurrence that at any dose requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation, results in persistent or significant disability or incapacity, results in a congenital anomaly or birth defect, is lifethreatening, or results in death. The definition (in line with ICH E2A) includes important medical events that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalisation but may jeopardise the patient or may require intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed in the definition above.
- 'Adverse drug reaction - ADR' means any untoward and unintended response to a medicinal product related to any dose administered, for which, after a thorough assessment, a causal relationship between the medicinal product and the adverse event is at least a reasonable possibility, based for example, on their comparative incidence in clinical trials, or findings from epidemiological studies and/or on an evaluation of causality from individual case reports.

## 5.5.1. Safety data collection

The safety of IPX203 has been evaluated in  the clinical development program comprising seven studies: three Phase 1 pharmacokinetics (PK) studies in healthy volunteers (Studies IPX203-B16-04 , IPX203-B16-05 and IPX203-B16-06 ), a Phase 2 single-dose PK, pharmacodynamics/efficacy and safety study in advanced PD patients (Study IPX203-B14-02 ), a Phase 2 study to evaluate the PK, PD, efficacy, and safety of single and multiple doses of IPX203 in advanced PD patients (Study IPX203-B16-01 ), a Phase 3, randomised, controlled trial to evaluate safety and efficacy in PD patients who have motor fluctuations (Study IPX203-B16-02 ) and its open-label, 9-month extension (Study IPX203-B16-03 ).

Additionally, two Phase 1 studies have been conducted to assess the safety and tolerability of carbidopa, with focus on safety of its high doses. However, as only CD was used, these were not added to the pooled safety analyses.

Furthermore, in the course of this initial MAA procedure, the applicant supplied new interim data from a Phase 4 RWE study conducted in the US (ELEVATE -PD study interim analysis with 111 patients), evaluating the performance of the IR-to-IPX203 conversion algorithm in routine clinical practice.

The seven clinical studies were pooled into the following analyses pools. The grouping of studies was based on the subject population characteristics and study duration:

- P1HLT : Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers, 1 day dosing (Study IPX203-B16-04, Study IPX203-B16-05, Study IPX203-B16-06)
- P2APD : Phase 2 studies in advanced PD Patients, 1 to 14 days of dosing
- P3PDMF : Phase 3 studies in PD patients with motor fluctuations, long-term dosing (Study IPX203-B16-02, Study IPX203-B16-03)
- P123ALL : All the studies in the pools defined above

Overall, the demographic and baseline characteristics were comparable among IPX203 and IR CD-LD groups. For the IPX203 group, the mean (SD) age of subjects was 66.3 (8.90) years, and majority were males (372 [63.2%] subjects). Their mean (SD) BMI was 27.31 (4.948) kg/m2. The majority of subjects (69.4%) had Hoehn and Yahr Stage 2, and a mean (SD) screening Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) score of 27.2 (1.80). The mean (SD) age of onset of PD was 58.0 (9.29) years, and the mean (SD) duration of PD was 8.4 (4.82) years.

Table 44: Overall summary of adverse events across the IPX203 studies (Safety Population)

<!-- image -->

In the Phase 1 studies pool in healthy volunteers, three (3.2%) IPX203 subjects experienced three treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) that were mild and treatment-related. One (1.1%) IPX203 subject experienced TEAE that led to discontinuation of the study drug. No serious TEAEs or deaths were reported.

In the Phase 2 studies pool in advanced PD patients, 14 (29.2%) IPX203 subjects experienced 32 TEAEs (15 mild, 17 moderate). Of these, 10 (20.8%) IPX203 subjects experienced 25 TEAEs that were treatment related. One (2.1%) IPX203 subject each experienced a serious TEAE and a TEAE that led to discontinuation of the study drug. No deaths were reported.

In the Phase 3 studies pool in PD patients with motor fluctuations, 397 (67.4%) of All-IPX203 subjects experienced 1355 TEAEs (837 mild, 419 moderate, 99 severe). Of these, 205 (34.8%) All-IPX203 subjects experienced 471 TEAEs that were treatment-related. Sixty (10.2%) All-IPX203 subjects experienced 102 serious TEAEs, of which 11 treatment-related. Eighty (13.6%) All-IPX203 subjects experienced 139 TEAEs that led to discontinuation of the study drug. Six (1.0%) subjects died during Phase 3 studies.

The TEAEs reported by System Organ Class (SOC) and Preferred Term (PT) for at least 2% of subjects in any treatment group are presented in the following Tables, for the pooled IPX203 studies and the open-label and double-blind periods in Phase 3 studies, respectively.

In the Phase 1 studies pool, 3 (3.2%) IPX203 subjects experienced three TEAEs, mild and treatment related. These TEAEs included vomiting, blood cholesterol increased (, and dizziness (1 [1.1%] subject each).

In the Phase 2 studies pool, 14 (29.2%) IPX203 subjects experienced 32 TEAEs. The most commonly reported TEAEs (≥5% subjects) in these subjects were dyskinesia (6 [12.5%]), dizziness and hypertension (3 [6.3%] subjects each).

In the Phase 3 studies pool, 397 (67.4%) of All-IPX203 subjects experienced 1355 TEAEs. The most commonly reported TEAEs (≥5% subjects) in these subjects were dyskinesia (63 [10.7%] subjects), nausea (44 [7.5%]), fall (35 [5.9%]), and urinary tract infection (31 [5.3%]).
